items.title: Pogačar’s Viral Booty Band Warm-Up Routine Might Just Be a Placebo
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Should cyclists warm up with mini bands? Why the placebo effect might outweigh any true muscle 'activation,' and how riders can make better use of glute bands.
items.lbText:
Tadej Pogačar made “booty bands” everybody’s favorite warm-up ritual when he was filmed twerking and squatting his way through a pre-race routine, bands around his knees.

But it turns out that these wildly popular pre-ride workouts might largely be a placebo .

Waddling, lunging, and squatting through a mini-band session before a ride doesn’t “activate your glutes” or prime you to push max power.

According to WorldTour experts, the power of glute bands might largely be in the mind.

“These mini band moves are beneficial, but it’s more from a pseudo-science perspective. Someone riders might feel like, ‘Oh, I’m doing something , I’m preparing myself to ride’ by doing them,” Jayco-AlUla physiotherapist Dan Guillemette told Velo .

“But in terms of actual performance, it’s really unlikely there’s any actual benefit.”

So how have mini-bands become one of sport’s most popular primers?

They’ve become no-brainers for WorldTour and triathlon pros, TikTok influencers, 4w/kg Velo writers [ ahem ], and everyone in between.

Here’s why mini band warm-ups might not be worth your time – unless you’re already doing them – and how to make better use of these wildly popular home workout tools.

Pogačar’s pre-race warm-up video was one of the viral cycling clips of 2025. The meme pages loved it.

The Instagram reel shows Pogačar and his teammate Juan Molano working through a series of mini band exercises ahead of a stage at the UAE Tour. Pogi’s now-famous “bum to the sky” hip opener was a particular highlight.

It was a rare behind-the-scenes glimpse at how pros prepare to push wild watts for hours on end.

Since then, clips of Matteo Jorgenson , Jonas Abrahamsen , and Remco Evenepoel doing similar routines have reinforced the thinking that a few minutes inside a mini band will push you to new performance peaks.

And unlike a set of Pogačar-approved 165mm cranks or an indoor trainer “heat suit,” there’s no expensive equipment, excess sweat, or annoying apps involved.

All you need is a $10 band from Walmart and one of the routines being pumped into your cycling social feed.

The big selling point of booty band routines for cyclists and endurance athletes?

That they waken your glutes from their slumber after too long being sat on. A few minutes pushing at a mini band will buzz your butt into “workout mode.”

Strength expert Chris Peden burst that bubble when he spoke to Velo .

Peden, the head of S&C at Decathlon CMA-CGM, said pros and amateurs alike have been fooled by a misapplication of the term “sleepy glutes.”

“These routines are always advertised as ‘you’ve got weak glutes, your glutes don’t work, or are ‘asleep.’ That’s the result of medical terms transferring to the performance world that don’t really apply,” Peden told Velo . “It’s a medical term from those who are extremely inactive, not somebody who does even a low level of training.

“And anyway, muscles don’t ‘switch on’ or ‘switch off,’” Peden continued. “Your neuromuscular system is always working. Your brain knows exactly what to recruit at any one time,” Peden said.

“A band workout does not make that signal ‘better’ or ‘cleaner,’ as some suggest. It’s unlikely to have any benefit at all.”

If you’re reading this post, you’re likely interested in bikes and maybe ride one every so often.

A second misconception? That squeezing some torque out of your glutes with an oversized elastic band will ready you for your 400-watt interval workout.

That’s founded in another misapplication, this time of the term “PAP.”

PAP, or Post Activation Potentiation, refers to the acute boost in muscular performance following a previous activity. A set of heavy back squats before attempting a maximum vertical jump is a common real-world application of PAP.

But sadly, a set of waddling “monster walks” won’t come close to delivering the muscular force or speed required for any meaningful PAP.

In the world’s biggest bike races, turbo trainers – not mini bands – are used to provide an effective potentiation.

These torture devices are wheeled out of team trucks ahead of time trials, hard uphill starts, or for those wanting to make the day’s early break. Riders work through a progressive build before a series of short submaximal efforts that fully stimulate the muscles for a fast racing start.

So, wait one sec. If the popular theories behind booty bands are a load of BS, why are they still so popular in the dialed-down, scientifically-backed WorldTour?

Even Peden admitted his own athletes on Decathlon CMA-CGM do them, even though he dismisses their direct impact on performance. Both he and Guillemette at Jayco-AlUla think that for many riders, the gains are all in the mind.

For many, workout bands became part of their pre-ride routine as juniors, either as a misguided warm-up tool or as a minimal dose of strength work.

“Psychologically, the placebo effect is massive,” Peden said. “Our riders still do them regardless of what we might say. They’ve been told to do it since they were 15 years old, and that it’s beneficial to them. So I can’t turn around to tell them to suddenly stop.

“They’re not doing any harm, but they’re not achieving anything meaningful as a supposed ‘activation,’” he continued. “If they’re proving some psychological benefit and riders believe they help, I’m not going to hold them back. However, I might try to suggest they include some more useful practices, instead – say, around mobility.”

Guillemette, who worked at Team Sky before he joined Jayco-AlUla, added that a band routine can also help riders transition out of inactivity.

They prime the mind and loosen the body.

“It’s really unlikely that there’s any benefit to using bands in terms of race performance,” Guillemette said.…

items.title: Yankees news: Boone considering changes to the lineup
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
NY Daily News | James O’Connell: The Yankees ran out the same exact lineup in Games 1 and 2 of their ALDS matchup against the Rays, but aside from Ben Rice and his pair of home runs no one else is really contributing. As the series shifts over to New York for Game 3 tonight, manager Aaron Boone was amenable to some lineup tinkering though he wouldn’t get into specifics of who could find their way in and who would get sent to the bench. Some of the more likely candidates to sit include those who both haven’t found their way into a hit yet and also fumbled the ball around in their atrocious Game 2 showing, such as Ryan McMahon and Jazz Chisholm Jr.

NY Post | Mark W. Sanchez: Max Fried is lined up to start tonight on the mound in Game 3, but there was the potential for that to not be the case. Fried’s partner is due to give birth in the coming days and there was the possibility that Fried would have to miss this start, but the lefty confirmed that he will be there for the team adding that he’s “got a really supportive family that understands that this is my job.” Fried’s focus is leaving it all on the line for his team as the Yankees face elimination, and hopefully that dedication pays off for him.

MLB.com | Matthew Leach: So the Yankees are down in an 0-2 hole, but is there any hope of a comeback? There’s a few reasons to believe in a turnaround, namely that they largely beat themselves in Game 2 and have an elite pitching staff that could lock down opposing bats so long as the defense stops putzing the ball around. Getting out of Tropicana Field is also a big plus, and even though a potential Game 5 would see them return to that house of horrors, they’ve got to win the first two before worrying about that.

MLB.com | Mike Lupica: The Yankees are certainly not strangers to reverse sweeping in an ALDS, as Lupica takes us through the history of the team’s ability to flip the script. Unfortunately, that history all lies in the recent past as Aaron Boone’s squads have largely been unable to answer back after getting punched in the face in a series — let’s see if they can change that narrative this time around.

The Big Lead | J.P. Hoornstra: Sadly, we end our notes with the passing of ‘Sudden’ Sam McDowell, who died on Monday. McDowell was a six-time All-Star throughout his 15-year MLB career, and he played for the Yankees at the tail end of his career for the 1973-74 seasons. From all of us here at Pinstripe Alley, we send our condolences to Sam’s family and friends.

items.title: Mercedes to run old + new car spec in Singapore amid upgrade doubts
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Mercedes is to run a back-to-back comparison between its new and old Formula 1 aero packages in Singapore to better understand whether or not its latest upgrade has worked.

The manufacturer had arrived at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia hopeful that a new development step for its W17 would lift it clear at the front of F1.

However, the expected 0.3-second improvement did not materialise, and team principal Toto Wolff reckoned it had instead dropped its performance by up to half a second.

That left the door open for Red Bull's Max Verstappen to take his first pole position and victory of the season for Red Bull.

The surprise lack of pace from Mercedes prompted some deep post-race analysis to understand what went wrong, and whether what played out was entirely down to the aero package or was linked to the rough track surface.

That work has exposed that there are areas of its car that Mercedes needs to better understand, which is why it will bring back some older specification parts in Singapore this weekend for testing.

The team will run comparison tests between the new and old parts to help build a better understanding of what has happened.

Wolff said: "We have identified several areas we need to investigate further, but F1 doesn't offer simple answers and we need more evidence before drawing firm conclusions.

"Singapore gives us an immediate opportunity to continue that work. The characteristics of the circuit are very different and that will help us build a clearer picture of where we are.

"That is why we will evaluate both the latest update package and our previous specification across the weekend to ensure we fully understand the direction we need to take."

Mercedes is due to split its old and new packages across its two cars for the entire weekend.

As the Singapore GP is a sprint weekend, there is only a single practice session before sprint qualifying on Friday evening.

The plan to do some back-to-back testing of its aero packages comes amid confirmation that George Russell will take an engine grid penalty as well, following the failure he suffered in Malaysia.

That change of components will put him at the back of the grid at a venue that is notoriously difficult to overtake on.

Wolff added: "That is particularly frustrating given the way he drove last weekend and the result he deserved to be fighting for.

"Unfortunately, these things are part of the sport and our focus now is on giving him the best possible car and opportunities to fight back through the field."

items.title: Save $127 on the Wahoo Kickr V6 – our top choice for a smart trainer is at its lowest price of the year in the Amazon Prime Big Deal Days sale
items.author: paul.brett@futurenet.com (Paul Brett)
items.content:
The Wahoo Kickr V6 remains a standout leader among the best smart trainers and is our premium recommendation for Zwift racing. While it missed the overall top spot to its more budget-friendly stablemate, the Kickr Core 2, this flagship model delivers top-tier performance for serious indoor riding.

This is the lowest price the Kickr V6 has been all year, and if you're looking to invest or upgrade, we think it warrants serious consideration at this price.

TheWahoo Kickr V6 has hit the lowest price we've seen this year. If you're in the market for one of the best smart trainers, then this is an excellent purchase. It delivers incredibly accurate power readings (+/- 1%), an excellent ride feel, and lightning-fast connectivity, making it a superb way to enjoy indoor training.

The Kickr V6 still earned a perfect 5-out-of-5-star review from associate editor Josh Croxton. At the time of testing, Josh was torn between the Elite Justo 2 and the Kickr V6 as his top choice, and both are excellent top-of-the-line smart trainers.

The Elite Justo has a slightly better max power (2,300 watts vs 2,200 watts) and higher max simulated grade (24% vs 20%). I'd still opt for the Wahoo, as I love Wahoo products, and especially at this discounted price.

The Wahoo Kickr V6 deal applies to US shoppers only, and there are currently no reductions on Amazon UK. The Wahoo Kickr Core 2 is down to £449.49, from £549.99, which matches the best price from earlier in the year.

Below are the best Wahoo deals, from other retailers, relevant to your location and currency.

items.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
items.content:
As I did yesterday I'll spend my day furiously hunting for things that fit the brief of a) actually good products that are b) decently discounted, as well as being c) available in an acceptable range of sizes to save the click-through disappointment.

I'll focus on Amazon, but also sprinkle in options from elsewhere as many places have concurrent sales to try and take some of Jeff's thunder. Naturally for the Prime Day deals you'll need to sign up for an Amazon Prime membership, but you can quickly cancel it after we won't snitch.

The Prime Day sale runs until the end of today (midnight), so there's plenty more time to take advantage of some sweet discounts.

USA: Prime Day bike deals

The current price for the Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is an all-time low. A perfect chance to get your indoor setup for winter sorted. This is a fantastic indoor trainer.View Deal

This is the cheapest Wahoo's smallest computer has been all year, so it's a great time to nab one if you need an upgrade. It doesn't have the touchscreen of the Roam below, but it's lighter and basically has all the same features. last year at full price, so it's even more of a good buy now. The easy navigation and classically friction-free user interface of Wahoo tech were standout features, plus all the usual training aids you'd expect from a device used in the WorldTour. View Deal

Not as big a discount in percentage terms as the Bolt, but the Roam, but in cash terms they're both about the same. Unless you want the weight savings, and as long as you can afford it, then I'd get the Roam; it's what I use as my own bike computer, and I also gave it 4.5 stars in my review.

What sets it apart for me, along with all the things that make the Bolt great, is the brilliant mapping. It's so clear, and the integration of things like Strava Live Segments is excellent for those who like to have a hit out on random lanes at any given moment.

View Deal

Think is a brilliant light for the money, despite not being the most up-to-date model.

It has a huge 200-hour runtime and a smart motion sensor. Plus it's very bright, you won't be dissapointed on this light.

View Deal

This is as cheap as Apple's top tier in-ear headphones have been this year so it's a perfect time to buy them if you want to beat the inevitable Black Friday rush. Packed with features, including an in-built heart rate monitor that our testing shows to match the accuracy of a watch, plus the brilliant sound quality and noise cancellation you've come to expect. View Deal

It's OK; I won't tell anyone if you do a bit of running on the side. I do, on occasion, and a running watch helps a lot to pace yourself as much as anything. The Forerunner 165 is about all you need for regular jogging, and eschews all of the Garmin bells and whistles in terms of internal multisport features to keep the cost down.View Deal

The Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is also discounted by around £100. It's a good-quality trainer that comes with handy dropout adaptors, and the Cog and Click system means you can run it with nearly any bike you want to. View Deal

Here's the UK version for the SEEMEE 300 deal. For £35.52, this is a really excellent little light that does everything well; it's one of our favourite cycling products of the last few years.View Deal

As someone who uses Qobuz rather than Spotify so I can listen to my music in HD, they've been a revelation, and the battery life and comfort aren't half bad, too. I can't go back to other headphones now, which is a bit annoying. View Deal

OK it's not Amazon, but this deal is too big to not include. I described the Gabba R as 'close to faultless for its intended use' when I reviewed it back in 2024, and if you want to ride hard in the rain, it's really hard to beat, especially with such a massive discount.

The aesthetics won't be for everyone, but when it's raining, it looks less shiny than it does in the catalogue.

View Deal

Throw in a few spare batteries so you don't have to stop filming to recharge, and a selfie stick, and you're well on your way to making some sweet, sweet content.

items.title: 'You can't simply borrow road metrics' - Colnago launches new G5-X gravel bike
items.author: Emily Tillett
items.content:
Colnago has released a brand new G5-X gravel bike today, which builds on its existing G4-X gravel platform, which launched back in 2024.

Colnago says, “You can't simply borrow road metrics - weight, stiffness, aerodynamics - and apply them just as easily to a gravel bike.”

The Italian brand has focused on creating a bike that can excel across a broad range of gravel racing. It highlights events including the Traka 200, Unbound 200, Badlands and GranGuanche Audax as examples of the different types of racing the G5-X is designed to handle.

The G5-X embraces the trend towards wider tyres, offering clearance for 53mm tyres, not class-leading, but an improvement of 8mm over the outgoing G4-X. Colnago ships all models with 50mm tyres fitted, making use of the frame's increased tyre clearance, which is something I like to see.

The frame is still relatively traditional-looking, though, which may please Colnago purists. The brand has decided on a round 27.2mm seatpost to boost comfort and open up dropper post options.

Another new feature is integrated frame storage within the downtube, which is said to fit a tube, CO₂ canister, tools and a plug kit.

The G5-X also gets mounting points on the top tube, downtube and fork - six in total, including two additional fork mounts designed with ultra-distance and bikepacking races in mind.

Colnago has carried over its integrated CC.01 Wide cockpit, which has more flare than the standard CC.01, at 3cm rather than 1cm per side. Like the standard CC.01, it's a carbon monocoque design intended to keep weight down while maintaining stiffness.

The new bike also comes with the option of Fidlock Twist Lock technology, allowing you to use either conventional bottles or Fidlock-compatible accessories. The mechanical attachment is designed to keep bottles securely in place over rough terrain, reducing the risk of losing a bottle, while the side-loading system can be useful on smaller frames or when the bike is loaded up and space is limited.

Colnago hasn't pushed the boundaries in any one particular area with the G5-X. Instead, you're getting a gravel race bike that should do everything you need it to do, and nothing you don't - a "fast yet capable bike" as Colnago puts it.

Geometry, specs, and pricing

The G5-X will be available in five sizes, from 45cm to 57cm, three bike builds and two colour options.

Compared with the G4-X, the G5-X has longer chainstays and a longer wheelbase. The head tube angle is also slightly slacker, while the reach is marginally longer, changes that Colnago says offer “more stability even in a compact position”.

The bottom bracket is also lower on the G5-X to help improve stability at speed, with the BB drop increasing from 70mm to 77.5mm on a 54cm frame.

As for pricing, the entry-level model (if such a thing can ever be said of a Colnago) is built with SRAM Rival XPLR and Vision TC45 Carbon wheels, costing $5,500 / €4,900 / £5,299.99.

A more expensive SRAM Force XPLR build, also with Vision TC45 Carbon wheels, is available for $7,500 / €5,750 / £6,299.99.

The range topper is a SRAM Red XPLR AXS build with Zipp 303 XPLR SW wheels for $10,500 / €9,200 / £9,999.99.

Interestingly, this is less than the flagship Specialized S-Works Crux in a SRAM Red build, which costs $13,999.99 / £11,999.

items.title: F1's cost cap fix: What's actually proposed, and for when
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Formula 1 teams are set to discuss a potential overhaul of financial regulations for 2027 aimed at ending what has been labelled a “cost cap trap” for smaller squads.

The Race has learned that the idea of a catch-up mechanism being added to the cost cap is set to be raised at the next meeting of the F1 Commission, which takes place in November.

The plan is being pushed for by Williams boss James Vowles, who wants revised cost cap rules in place for the start of next season to avoid what he thinks has become a “two-tiered” F1, where the big four teams have pulled away from the chasing pack.

Vowles sees this situation as a consequence of legacy advantages having been locked in.

Vowles fears that the more this becomes bedded in, then the bigger the risk that the divide becomes permanent.

Should teams not have the chance to mix it with those at the front, they will become less attractive for sponsors and there will be less incentive to invest. That will stop progress, lead to even worse results and see team valuations go down.

Williams is not calling for an end to the cost cap, which it thinks has been hugely positive in bringing financial stability to F1 and adding value to all the current teams because there is no longer an arms race of spending.

Instead, Vowles’ idea is to have a sliding scale catch-up system within the cost cap that allows the teams outside of the top four to spend more.

He wants it in place for 2027 because, with its impact probably going to take three years to come through the system, it needs to be there for the next rules cycle that begins in either 2030 or 2031.

The specifics of what sliding scale may be adopted depend on how talks develop within the F1 Commission or F1’s Financial Advisory Committee (FAC), but there are a few ways of doing it.

It could be implemented in a similar way to F1’s Aerodynamic Testing Restrictions, so that the team that is bottom of the standings gets the most extra allowance, with the spending freedom behind steadily reduced up until the fifth team.

Or it could be done with a tier system like happens with F1’s Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) engine catch-up mechanism. So, teams within a certain percentage range of points of the big squads are grouped together to get extra spending allowances.

Another way of doing it could be to base it on a scale that is directly related to points gaps - with it perhaps only being triggered for teams that are 100 points off the top four.

This would ensure that the system would not benefit a team that finished a close fifth and would only come into force if there was a genuine step between the 'big four' and the rest.

Is there support for his plan?

For Vowles’ plan to go through, it will need to secure support from teams in the F1 Commission.

Under F1’s current governance structure, for changes to take place at this stage for 2027, it is understood they would need support from the FIA, FOM plus six of the current 11 teams - so Williams and five others. This will secure what is known as a super majority.

However, changes to the rules for 2028 could be pushed through if there is support from the FIA, FOM plus four teams in total - so Williams and three others. This is known as a simple majority.

It is obvious that Vowles’ plan will not have universal backing – especially from the big four teams, who are unlikely to be supportive of moves that could potentially allow others to catch up.

The bigger teams are up for changes to cost cap rules, but this is more focused on pushing for areas that are currently inside the cap being moved outside.

Most recently, for example, there have been discussions about moving cybersecurity spending outside the cap.

Other squads, like Alpine, have pushed back against this and suggested that the situation should be the opposite – and all team spending should be inside the cost cap.

Mercedes thinks more thought needs to be put into how the cost cap is squeezing staff wages, as teams are limited in attracting the best staff because they cannot afford them or they are losing them to other industries.

Deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: “Every team is having to trade investing in its people against investing in its car. And that's the most difficult and uncomfortable of the trade-offs that the cost cap imposes.”

The Race understands that as part of the discussions Vowles has had about his idea, four squads have indicated broad support. These teams are Audi, Aston Martin, Alpine and Cadillac.

Sources suggest Haas is against the move as the Banbury-based team is already running a tight ship and is not at the cost cap limit. Therefore, supporting any extra freedoms for spending will simply be a green light to help the opposition.

Right now, that leaves Vowles one vote short of the super majority needed to get changes in place for 2027.

Key then will be what Racing Bulls does. Getting it on board could rest on convincing Red Bull chiefs that it may be in their interest to help their second team.

Even if Racing Bulls cannot be won over, getting majority support for 2028 - so those four votes - is possible. But Vowles wants this in place for next year, so he needs to win more support.

The matter seems finely poised right now, which is why the intensity of conversations in the paddock is set to ramp up from Singapore this weekend ahead of that crunch F1 Commission gathering next month.

What is causing the 'trap'

Vowles says his experience of working at both Williams and previously Mercedes is illustrative of how smaller squads suffer disadvantages under F1’s cost cap.

That is because there is a combination of factors in play that mean smaller teams have less headroom for spending on development each year compared to the big teams – plus it costs them more to produce the same things.

As Vowles said: “One car is about 30% more expensive compared to what I remember from a previous team.”

There are many ways that this expenditure offset happens.

One example is processes and manufacturing. Big teams have been able to improve efficiency through big finance departments to make sure that there is no wastage in the system.

Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen said earlier this year that key to his squad moving forward was exploiting the cost cap more as it was coming off a period of under-investment under previous owners.

He told The Race that its finance department was “under-resourced” and that “there are all sorts of areas of the budget cap which we haven't really explored properly”. “We're doing that now,” he insisted.

Nielsen said that when money was being wasted through inefficiencies in one area, that then directly limited the amount of money that could be spent on upgrades.

“If you leave stuff on the table in the budget cap, that's basically stuff that could have paid for a new front wing or a new floor or a new rear wing,” he said.

Expanding a team tomorrow to create a more efficient system for the long term is expensive. Invest a lot of money doing it, and that money has to come out of current car build and development - so results in the present dip.

Another way the bigger teams save money is by manufacturing more parts in-house. Smaller teams that do not have that luxury have to use external suppliers, which can be much more expensive.

But it is not just in cost cap spending compared to the big teams where the smaller outfits feel they are being held back.

One bone of contention has been allowances for capital expenditure, which permit teams to build the infrastructure where they can make improvements.

From F1’s cost cap coming into force in March 2020 until the end of 2025, CapEx was limited - with a broad $36 million limit from 2022-2025, although some extra concessions were given to help smaller teams in late 2023.

The system has changed since the start of 2026, but it’s still not straightforward.

CapEx limits were removed completely from the start of this year and all spending on this front was placed inside the wider $215 million overall cap.

However, any expenditure on this front has to be allocated in the cost cap through depreciation on a standardised straight-line method.

This means, for example, that if a team spends $25 million on a new windtunnel, then that money is written off over a set period. If a 10-year timescale is chosen, it would mean that $2.5 million would have to be taken into account each year.

So, if a team has made $100 million of investment on CapEx projects to improve machinery and systems, then that means $10 million more coming out of its development budget each year - compared to a bigger team that already has that infrastructure in place.

At least part of why Williams hasn’t been able to replicate McLaren’s revival is that its own infrastructures and systems had slipped badly behind the times over the last 20 years.

Whereas McLaren’s still remained very good - it was just not making the most of them.

This was proven when McLaren’s technical restructuring was initiated in 2023 under Andrea Stella’s leadership and its development work suddenly became massively more impressive even before it switched to a new windtunnel and simulator McLaren had been developing since 2019.

Williams fell much further behind the curve, which in turn held back its processes - and it was also not staffed to the same quantity or quality as McLaren either.

Even with the money from owner Dorilton, it would take time to build the team back up - and the CapEx limits were an obvious additional hurdle here, as Williams could not pump money into its factory even if it wanted to.

items.title: Gravel grid anomalies, national teams in name only and self funding – Explaining the workings of a UCI Gravel World Championships
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
The UCI Road World Championships have nearly a century of history and in mountain bike there have been decades to carve out the lay of the land. However, the global cycling body has only introduced a gravel battle for the rainbow jersey in recent years, making the discipline of uneven surfaces also one where the ins and outs of the competition for the title also aren't as smoothly paved into the collective memory of the cycling world.

The handlebars may be curled and road racers may have dominated the top steps, but there are some vast differences between the race for a road rainbow jersey and a gravel one, not least of all the role of national teams. Nor does it replicate the set-up of mountain bike title races, where riders from other disciplines are often completely on the back foot because of the grid position which leaves them well back on the start grid.

Gravel has carved out a path all of its own. It is one that has kept evolving since the first edition in 2022 as the process of identifying pitfalls and problems continues.

The changes also aren't likely to be at an end, as the relatively new introduction has delivered a scale of popularity and attention on the UCI Gravel World Championships that means it's not going anywhere soon, but it also exists in an environment that is far from settled. There is a tug of war between the sanctioned and unsanctioned system, an evolution of the professionalism plus an inconsistent and complex environment when it comes to teamwork, or the lack of it.

There are many complications, nuances and barriers but somehow what has evolved as riders, teams, federations and the UCI work through them all has captured the imagination. Read on to find out a little more on the environment, rules, racing dynamics and history of gravel racing.

First, before we get into the ins and outs of the race for a gravel rainbow jersey a little context may be required for those who have been introduced to the discipline through the UCI races. It's not like gravel didn't exist before the cycling body attached its name to the sport in 2022, creating a global series stringing together a series of events through the year that ultimately culminated in the UCI Gravel World Championships.

In fact, it was already huge at that point, it's just that it wasn't operating under one unified banner. In fact the lack of oversight was often a matter of pride, and for some a part of the appeal, with the sense of community and much vaunted "spirit of gravel" a key attraction.

Gravel races, big and small, had been playing out for decades across the globe but nowhere was it more established than in the United States, which is the home of the crown jewel of gravel, Unbound Gravel, and also Gravel Worlds, a popular Nebraska event that had trademarked the name before the UCI event came on the scene. Lauf Gravel Worlds plays heavily into its pirate-status event, with a sword trophy and tongue in cheek attitude.

In gravel federations have 10 elite slots allocated across the men's and women's events, with no rankings requirement, and the host nation has 20 places. Gravel national and continental champions also gain an automatic place, along with the defending world champions.

But that is far from where it ends, as a rider can also qualiy via the UCI Gravel World Series, with a swathe of rounds across the year and world to choose from and plenty of opportunities to snare a spot by qualifying in the top 25%.

This combination of qualifying options, with the wild card scenario often opening the door to big name riders from other disciplines, means you can end up with a scenario like last year where the field is heavy on riders from specific nations.

For example the women's field last year was just about a quarter Dutch while also overwhelming dominated by a handful of nations, In the men's field among the 279 riders there were 45 riders from Belgium, 36 from the Netherlands and 32 from Germany, with the three nations accounting for not that much under half the field.

There is money on the table in gravel racing, with races like Unbound Gravel delivering $10,000 for the elite winners and the US-based Lauf Gravel Worlds delivering a substantial pay packet of $25,000 to the elite winners while the Life Time Grand Prix series gets $50,000.

There is also money in UCI-sanctioned World Championships, although not a great deal, with the elite men's and women's road race winners, for example, getting €8,000 each. Go looking for the prize money at the Gravel World Championships in the technical guide and it is an entry you won't find. There is a reason for that; there isn't any.

What's more at the road event, riders are also far more likely to be supported by their national federations to race, with everything from travel expenses, uniforms and support staff covered. In gravel, however, with just some exceptions, the costs are largely borne by either individual privateer athletes or, in the case of the fortunate ones, their trade teams - even though they are racing in national colours.

When riders head to the UCI Road World Championships, it's with the clear expectation that they are racing for their nations, and if that means completely sacrificing themselves to work for a greater goal then it is exactly what they will do. In fact, for most the chance to go for glory themselves will never have even been a consideration, with the squad selected to support a leader. That all makes sense, and is the norm, in road racing but that's not the case in gravel.

For a start, the gravel discipline as a whole has come from a far less-organised and team oriented place. While teamwork is starting to become a greater element, it's not that widespread, being more the exception than the rule. Also, in what - depending on the course - is often not a bunched up race but an attritional affair, it perhaps doesn't play out in quite the same way.

Then there is also the issue of how riders end up at the UCI Gravel World Championships. In other disciplines nations have strict quotas, based on rankings, which deliver a limited number of riders with national federations selecting, and often funding, the spots.

As mentioned above, there is an alternate path in gravel with riders able to earn their own spot in the UCI Gravel World Series, so if they don't need to be selected by their national federation and that diminishes their ability to call the shots. So does the fact that riders are often likely to be paying their own way as privateers or perhaps they may be fortunate enough to have either a gravel team – like Specialized Off-road or Factor – or a squad from another discipline supporting them. It's a scenario that raises the question of why should they race for a national teammate's glory when the whole reason they have funding to be there is either for their own sponsors or trade team?

That also raises another issue. While riders may be racing in their nation's jersey could they instead work on trade team orders? For example Specialized Off-road has three key favourites in the men's elite race and are in Australia to support them – with Keegan Swenson (United States), Mads Würtz Schmidt (Denmark) and Matt Beers (South Africa) – but they are all from different nations. Are they really going to race against each other given the circumstances surrounding their participation in the event? We shall soon see.

There has been a considerable contrast in what's on offer at Unbound 200, the most revered of gravel races, and the courses that have been delivered for the UCI Gravel World Championships so far. For a start Unbound Gravel is long, really long, with the 200 miles converting to 322 km while in contrast the UCI Gravel World Championships so far have been in the range of 141km for the elite ment to 194km and between 123km to 149km for the elite women.

That aligns far more closely with the distances that road riders are typically riding, which is advantage one to the road contingent at the rainbow jersey race, and a disadvantage for them at Unbound. Another big one is the terrain.

Thus far the Gravel World Championships have had a fair chunk of either road and other non-gravel surfaces as part of the course, like cobblestones and singletrack, where as the long stretches of gravel roads at Unbound throw up an entirely different challenge. The mud can be brutal if there is rain on the run in, the sharp flint vicious on tyres and the long stretches between feed zones a race killer, particularly for a rider who is used to a support car behind and hasn't long practiced all the tricks of the trade to nurse or redeem the situation when things go wrong.

Certainly there still isn't the same support as road riders are used to, but with the shorter distances, tech zones and perhaps slightly less brutal conditions at what we've seen from the Gravel World Championships so far it isn't as big an issue.

Then there are the points. Unbound Gravel might be one of the biggest things in gravel but it and races like it count for nought in terms of UCI points. That means if riders are focussed on the non-sanctioned gravel world they are likely to be on the back foot from the very start as they will be back on the grid at the UCI Gravel World Championships.

Then you add in the dynamic of courses in recent years, which have delivered some not inconsiderable similarities to a road Classic and its terrain where road riders may feel more at home in then their gravel brethren. That, however, may change this year as there will be more gravel, more climbing and plenty of chances to pass and help work back from an inconvenient grid position. Plus there will be smaller fields to work through given the long trip. There is a chance this could be the year the road domination changes.

The start grid is decide by who has the most points, with gravel riders getting 100 percent of their UCI points and riders from other disciplines having it pared back to 50 percent. This can matter because gravel racing doesn't work the same way as the road with big groups so often working together for the largest portion of the race. The unpredictability of the discipline can mean the field gets split up and reduced far earlier and also if there are thin sections a bottleneck can quickly ruin the chances of the riders behind.

To be fair, the Nannup course's generous width and the smaller fields, given the effort it takes to get out to Australia, will probably make start position a little less crucial this time.

There aren't follow cars in gravel like on the road but that doesn't mean the rider is completely without any form of help or support. For a start there are feed zones out on the Nannup course, where riders can get food and mechanical assistance – though no bike changes are allowed – however that is not the limit of where it can occur.

The UCI outlines in its regulation on gravel racing that: "Mechanical assistance can be provided everywhere throughout the course. Any person providing assistance shall be stationary on the side of the road of vehicle circulation."

Still, the feed zones are the "strongly encouraged" option and there are also some exclusions on the feeding outside these zones, such as not feeding on the downhill or in the last 10km.

There is a chequered history to the broadcast of the UCI Gravel World Championships, with uproar in 2023 when, after a late change of organiser, only part of the men's elite race was broadcast live and the women's was not at all. After that it was written in as a condition for organisers in the bid document that there must be broadcasts for both.

Nannup, of course had already been long awarded the championships by that point, but they will without question be delivering anyway. Despite the enormous technical difficulties of providing the coverage in a remote location, the organisers have been diligent in working through the bugs over the years in the lead in. That means both the elite women and elite men are set to get a live broadcast, running from 13:00 to 18:00 AEDT on SBS on Demand and outside Australia on the UCI YouTube channel.

items.title: 'It's more a personal battle' - Sofia Gomez Villafañe locked in all year for significant climbing and 'wide open gravel' at UCI Gravel World Championships
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Sofia Gomez Villafañe's proverbial ladder of success has led to more than 20 major off-road victories on three continents so far, over the past five-and-a-half seasons. This year she put a bullseye on Nannup for the UCI Gravel World Championships.

She has won multiple national titles for the two countries she represents with dual citizenship - as a collegiate racer in mountain bike and cyclo-cross for the US and MTB cross-country for Argentina. In 2021, she made history for Argentina as the first female to compete in XCO mountain bike at the Olympic Games since 2004, finishing top 25. With bigger stakes this season, she trained and raced for the ultimate rainbow reward.

"We've actually had it targeted as an event for almost a year. It's not a last-minute decision. It's not something that we sprinkled in," Villafañe told

Since moving from the one-hour power outputs of the World Cup MTB scene to long-distance off-road challenges in 2021, the 32-year-old has signature victories at Unbound Gravel 200, The Traka 200 and Cape Epic - winning each event twice. In North America, she has a crowded trophy case with seven Belgian Waffle Ride wins, a sweep of all three editions of Valley of Tears, a win at Leadville Trail 100 and many others.

The most significant mark of being 'the best' is to be a world champion, and a rainbow jersey remains elusive, in any discipline, for one of the world's most dominant off-road cyclists.

Twice before, Villafañe has competed at the UCI Gravel World Championships for Argentina, her best finish 12th on Italian races that did not compare to the high-elevation, long-distance courses to which she was accustomed in North America. So when the UCI Gravel Worlds announced the courses a year ago for Western Australia, Villafañe locked in.

"So the decision to target this year's World Championship actually got solidified in October, November of last year with my coach. We have been really needing to set some big goals behind the season," Villafañe told before she left the US for Australia.

"I've been really committed to the Life Time Grand Prix. Knowing the past two years the [Worlds] courses really didn't suit me, we thought the courses in Australia might."

It's hard to realise that her first outing in an off-road endurance race was Crusher in the Tushar in Utah, where she didn't even have a gravel bike. With some tyre adjustments and a larger chainring, she won solo in the 69-mile event with more than 10,000 feet of climbing. A month later, she won solo again, this time at the mixed-surface Belgian Waffle Ride North Carolina using a Specialized Diverge borrowed from Katerina Nash.

Once she had all equipment set with Specialized Off-road and made the cut as part of the inaugural, invitation-only Life Time Grand Prix series for 2022, the upward trajectory began. She's won the Grand Prix three times and sits at the top of the leaderboard for 2026.

The trip to Australia means that Villafañe will have to miss Little Sugar MTB in Arkansas, as that round of the Life Time Grand Prix takes place on the same weekend as Worlds. It will be the one 'drop race' of the series for the three-time winner, leaving the 100-mile Big Sugar Classic on October 17 to determine final standings.

"We're getting to Australia early, so we're flying the 29th, getting there October 1st. So really giving the body time to adjust," she told about travelling with her husband Keegan Swenson, also part of the Grand Prix and will represent Team USA at Worlds.

"And then the plan is to fly out Sunday evening because all the flights from Australia are at like 11 p.m. at night. Basically everything's packed as Keegan [Swenson] finishes, and we go straight to the airport, so we could arrive Monday late afternoon in Bentonville and have a few days to get the body recovered ahead of Big Sugar."

Elite women will again have a dedicated start on October 10 with 78 miles (125.6km). The race is the shortest distance for the women's race in the five-year history of UCI Gravel Worlds, the longest in 2023 at 141km in Veneto, but it has heavy climbing, 3,179 metres (10,429 feet) worth, and 84% on wide, dirt roads.

"It's being dubbed as the first real gravel World Championships in terms of a course. I think it's exciting for it to be somewhere new. The fact that it's outside of Europe adds a new element.

"I think you are gonna have hills and wide-open gravel, which is a little bit more like the American gravel that I'm used to. Yeah, I think it's gonna be a really good course."

Even an Unbound winner has to qualify for Worlds

The squeeze play for a week of October races, separated by 10,743 miles (17,289 kilometers), was set in motion in February in Spain, where Villafañe stayed to race a UCI Gravel World Series qualifier.

"When I went to Spain in February to race Santa Val, we added a UCI gravel race so I can make sure I could qualify and not have to go through the federation and all those things. It's definitely been a targeted race," she explained.

She swept both stages and the overall at Santa Vall. Then she took off after the first 16km of the 97km Castellón Gravel Race and won solo, giving her automatic qualification to Worlds.

"I'm pretty sure Argentina would have given me a spot, like they always have for whatever world championships I've had to do. But it was nice to earn it, have my ticket, and have some UCI points," she said, though she'll have work to do from the start grid.

"I mean, I think I'll be pretty far back because I've only done one [UCI gravel world series event]. We have riders that race almost the entire calendar, so it's better than zero, so I'll take it."

A second trip to Santa Vall this year was the barometre for her off-season training. She said workouts don't always "translate to good races".

"I mean opening up the season in Santa Val like I did, I knew we had, with my coach, done a lot of hard work in the base season. So to really be able to climb and attack the way that I did at Santa Val was very rewarding. I mean, Spain just treats me really well."

It may be easier to list what she didn't win rather than what she conquered, but we'll start with the Life Time Grand Prix. She won Sea Otter Classic Gravel and a second Unbound 200, then after seventh place at Leadville 100, she won Chequamegon MTB. Her spring in the US included wins at The Mid South and Valley of Tears and plus a second SBT GRVL in between summer Grand Prix races.

"I had a phenomenal start to the first half of the year, and then in the summer we kind of had to take a little bit slower. Then in the past like two weeks, I've been firing again. So I'm really hopeful that I'm showing up really well prepared," she said.

"For me, it's more a personal battle [at Worlds]. I just have never been able to put it together at a world championship level race."

It will be her first trip to Australia, and she said the biggest appeal was the hilly course. The competition includes Life Time Grand Prix rival Karolina Migoń (Poland), who is fourth in the overall standings. Rosa Klöser (Germany) has withdrawn from the Grand Prix but will be in Nannup as a formidable opponent, finishing second to Villafañe at Santa Vall but then better at Lauf Gravel Worlds with second, two spots better than Villafañe. And then there's a stacked Dutch team with her Specialized Off-road teammate Geerike Schreurs and former gravel World Champion and last year's silver medallist Marianne Vos confirmed to start.

That firing on all engines was evident yet again at the fourth round of the Life Time Grand Prix in Wisconsin on September 19, where Villafañe overcame a crash in the mud and fought back to win the elite women's race at Chequamegon MTB. This was her third win in four series starts to give her a firm 18-point lead in the Grand Prix overall standings, now just Big Sugar remaining on her calendar.

"Now I just need to stay healthy and hopefully have smooth travel down there, smooth adaptation. And really just have a stress-free environment come pre-race day because that's really what affects me the most. If there's stress around me, then I get stressed. But if it's chilled, then I'm chilled."

It's only been five years since she started racing gravel and didn't even have a gravel bike. She's proven with consistent performances, versatility across disciplines and competitive drive to be the leading off-road rider for these Worlds.

So far across her dominant season, Villafañe said wins at The Traka and Unbound Gravel 200 have been her highlights of the year, and "each race had its little moment to celebrate". When asked if there was a third so far, she just left that open, hoping to complete the answer to that question later with a rainbow jersey.

items.title: Thoughts on the maddening first two Yankees-Rays ALDS games
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The Yankees have found themselves in an all-too-familiar situation once again and will fight for survival as they return to the Bronx to face the Rays in an elimination game.

Who’s to blame? Well, let’s look at the facts. The Yankees’ pitching rotation isn’t first on the list, with both Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler allowing two or fewer earned runs, but the offense appears to be on life support. Ben Rice is one of the few saving graces for this team, but the infield’s inability to execute has put the whole squad in a distressing situation.

Starting Ryan McMahon at third backfired for the Yankees almost immediately in the first inning, when the third baseman fumbled a routine ground ball that allowed Yandy Díaz to reach safely instead of throwing him out at first. It would be astounding to see him start again on Wednesday night over José Caballero or Anthony Volpe.

Jazz Chisholm Jr. also made an egregious error worth noting in Game 2, completely misfiring his throw to Luis García Jr., which gave Tampa Bay their first run of the evening. His response to the error was even more shocking following the game, when the second baseman admitted that he’d still make the throw despite having his back turned to properly execute it. Chisholm Jr. remains hitless in this series and has yet to make an impact on either side of the ball.

Gerrit Cole battled through a solid five innings in the first game of the series, striking out five batters and giving up only one run. Jonathan Aranda’s long ball was the only scoring on either side, and I’d say that the Yankees’ offense was far more at fault for the 1-0 loss in Game 1.

Cam Schlittler got through 4.1 innings, striking out two and allowing two earned runs in 76 pitches during Game 2, and held back the Rays’ offense long enough for the Yankees’ infield to throw away any hopes of evening the series for their return to the Bronx.

The offense is lifeless in the ALDS

Despite coming off two electric wins scoring a combined 18 runs in the Wild Card Series, the Yankees’ offense was no match for Rays’ ace Drew Rasmussen, who completely dominated the Yankees with 10 strikeouts and a no-hitter through 7.2 innings in Game 1.

Spencer Jones, Trent Grisham, and Cody Bellinger all struck out twice in the first meeting of the ALDS, and the Yankees’ only hit of the night came from Austin Wells with a double in the eighth inning. He unfortunately made the poor decision to ignore coach Luis Rojas’ stop sign and go for the triple, and was tagged out at third by Rays’ third baseman Junior Caminero following an elite play from shortstop Taylor Walls.

Taking a deeper dive into the Pinstripes’ offense, Ben Rice has been one of the only players in the lineup who’s shown up in this series, with a game-tying home run in the fourth of Game 2 and another late home run that cut the deficit. Bellinger was one of two other Yankees who got a hit on Monday night with a single following Rice’s first homer, and gave fans a sliver of hope that this offense might come alive. He also crushed one deep into center, which would’ve been a grand slam in 12 of the 30 ballparks, but it flew into the glove of Jonny DeLuca to send the game into the bottom of the fifth.

Wells got the only other hit of the night, redemption from his erroneous decision-making that was one of the reasons preventing the Yankees from making any headway in Game 1.

It’s clear that the depleted Yankees’ offense and egregious errors cost them their shot at evening the series. This is not an unfamiliar situation, as they’ve started several series on the road down 2-0 in the last five years. The last team in franchise history to erase the 2-0 deficit in a Division Series was the 2017 Yankees, who defeated the Guardians in five and later fell short in the ALCS to the Astros in seven.

Aaron Boone, after sending out an unchanged lineup for most of the postseason so far, must take the heat for failing to lead this team down a different path this time. They’ve been down this grueling road before, but there is little change from each postseason run that ends in the same demoralizing fate year after year. The Yankees ended the 2025 season, notably including a healthy Aaron Judge on the roster, with a four-game ALDS loss and were outscored by the Blue Jays in a combined total of 37-16.

Right now, it’s obvious that this team is completely depleted of offensive momentum, and it’s about time to shuffle the order as the Yankees go into survival mode.

Down 2-0 in the series with a looming return to the Bronx, the Yankees have their work cut out for them to continue this postseason run.

items.title: 11 Prime Day Cycling Deals Actually Worth Buying in 2026
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Navigating Amazon's cynical retail holiday is an exhausting chore. Here are 11 genuine 2026 discounts on cycling tech, smart trainers, and nutrition from Wahoo, Garmin, and GoPro that I recommend at full price.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Welcome to Velo Deals. We sift through the retail landscape to bring you deals worth paying attention to. It might be a discount or it might just be a product so good you should grab it. Either way, if it’s worth your time, you’ll see it here. If you’d like to see the rest of the category, check all our Velo Deals coverage.

Amazon Prime Day is perhaps the most cynical holiday of all time. Despite that, if you were going to buy something anyway, you might as well save money. I went looking for products I know and love that are also on sale. I managed to find 11 cycling Prime Day deals on gear I’d tell you to buy any day of the year, now offered for less. There’s a bit of a tech lean to Prime Day, so you will see that represented here, but I’ve got some cycling nutrition in the mix as well.

Wahoo bike computers are all about simplicity. They are simple to use but don’t skimp on what you need. The last piece of the puzzle Wahoo has lacked was self-training off the bike computer, and now there’s access to Wahoo and Coros training dashboards. The ELEMNT Bolt 3 is likely going to be my best budget bike computer in future best bike computer buying guides , and at 36% off, nothing else competes.

If you like to listen to music while you ride, the absolute best way to do it is with bone conduction headphones, and SHOKZ is the market leader. You can still hear what is happening around you, and on top of that, they can’t fall off, they’ve got tons of battery life, and if you want to stop your music, a single button press lets them disappear without having to stash them in a pocket.

The one challenge with bone conduction headphones is that they aren’t the best choice off the bike, and the mic performance is universally bad. If you are looking for something that will stay secure on the bike (use just a single earbud) and works well in regular life, then Apple users want the AirPods Pro 3. I’ve also tested these on a trainer with a fan at my face, and for the Apple ecosystem, this is what you want.

Winter is coming and that means Zwift for a lot of people. Wahoo is far and away the market leader when it comes to indoor trainers but the brand has a bit of a challenge on it’s hands. The offerings have gotten so good over the years that it’s hard to recommend the more expensive options. Adding the Cog and Click makes it even easier to add your outdoor bike. I have this as the best smart trainer for Zwift in my best smart trainers buyers guide and that means the best overall in my mind. Grab a great deal now before winter really hits.

One of the keys to eating enough on long rides is mixing textures and flavors. I generally drink my calories when riding, but I always carry chews so I can stop briefly and chew something.

Like I said, I tend to prefer to drink my calories on the bike, and this is my go-to choice. There’s a decent amount of sodium and a sweet, but not sickly, flavor profile. You can also choose an option with caffeine if that is your preference.

There’s science behind the idea that cramps come from a hyper-excited motor neuron repeatedly misfiring and locking the muscle up, rather than just dehydration or an electrolyte imbalance, and that it’s possible to make it stop with a shock to the vagus nerve. That shock comes from sour foods, so I also carry sour Salt Stick Energy Gummies with me. To be clear, Salt Stick doesn’t make this claim, and its gummies might not be sour enough. I don’t worry too much though because they still taste delicious and the cramp relief is just a potential bonus. You also get 130 mg of salt per packet, so that helps with cramps too.

If you aren’t in the Apple ecosystem, then I find the choice for headphones that are perfect for on and off the bike to be a lot more wide open. I’ve gone back and forth with different companies who offer a little more this or that, but in the end, I keep coming back to the Pixel Buds Pro 2 because the mic is really good and there’s such easy access to Gemini. For Android users who want headphones that will work just as well off the bike as on, this is my choice.

If you enjoy the videos that I put out for Velo, this is one of the two cameras that I use. Insta360 has a huge range of fantastic products, but I’ve settled into the GO Ultra as my second camera, which I attach to my jersey for a second point of view. It’s also a fantastic choice for regular life as you can use it as a tiny still/video travel camera when it’s docked. You can read my full Insta360 GO Ultra review for more info.

The other camera I use to make videos is the Mission 1 Pro. As good as Insta360 and DJI are, nothing else currently competes with the quality of the Mission 1 Pro. This is a professional-level tool for anyone serious about the best quality content. You can read more in my full GoPro Mission 1 Pro review .

One of the best things about Garmin is the way that the ecosystem lets you move between devices seamlessly. I don’t have to wear a strap or a watch while I ride because I have a Garmin bike computer (not on sale for Prime Day). When I get off the bike and put on the watch, the data seamlessly switches so that’s all uninterrupted in Garmin Connect. That opens up a small need for something different in my watch, though. I want something that looks good and works as a smartwatch as much as a fitness watch. That’s where the Garmin Venu X1 fits in.…

items.title: Anthony Rizzo shares insight as an analyst during AL Wild Card Series
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The former Yankee joined NBC Sports broadcast team as an “Inside the Pitch” analyst this season and shared his perspective from the booth as the Yankees swept the Red Sox in two games. He’s been back at Yankee Stadium for a few games during the season, but Rizzo explained that returning to the Bronx this time in late September felt a lot different.

“The drive to the stadium for the first game was a different feeling,” Rizzo told Pinstripe Alley. “I was like ‘Oh wow, I’m driving into a playoff game but I’m not playing.‘ I had a little bit of adrenaline going, but had to relax because I’m on the broadcast team now.”

However, after watching Payton Tolle ply his craft and Cam Schlittler throw consistently over 100 mph throughout the battle in Game 1, Rizzo admitted he was ultimately glad he wasn’t facing either. He also shared that the atmosphere in the Bronx during the playoffs is so uniquely intense that it makes a huge impact in every at bat.

“When the momentum is going it’s all sunshine and rainbows,” Rizzo said. “On the other end, when it’s not going well, that Yankee Stadium crowd can suffocate the home team. It’s really important as a player to get the crowd behind you in a good way, because we all know that Yankees fans are very passionate and will let you know how they’re feeling immediately. When the Bronx Zoo is Bronx Zooing, there’s no better place.”

Following the series sweep that sent the Yankees to face the Rays in the ALDS, Rizzo shared his key to get ahead of Tampa Bay as they look to advance to their first ALCS since Rizzo’s own playing days in pinstripes, back in 2024.

“If they can keep the Rays’ big three, Díaz, Aranda, and Caminero Jr. at bay, I think they have a great chance. At the end of the day, it’s all about timely hitting.”

Down 0-2 in the series following the 5-2 loss, the Yankees will look to stay alive as they return to the electric Bronx atmosphere for Game 3 on Wednesday night.
