items.title: Is Nannup delivering the first 'real' UCI Gravel World Championships?
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
It is clear that Nannup in Western Australia is going to be a UCI Gravel World Championships unlike any we have seen before, with it hardly possible to make a bigger detour in location after four European-based editions.

The change, however, runs far deeper than a position on the map, with the race also taking full advantage of its remote location, which offers one crucial natural resource in abundance: endless gravel roads.

It delivers a course that fits a more traditional archetype of what a rainbow-jersey race in the discipline should look like. That has created expectations that, after years of domination by road professionals since it started in 2022, the rainbow jersey could, in fact, end up on the back of a rider who races the discipline as their bread and butter this October.

"It's being dubbed as the first real Gravel World Championships in terms of a course. I think it's exciting for it to be somewhere new," Sofia Gómez Villafañe told with the leading player in the unsanctioned world of gravel who skipped the world title race the last two editions, this time turning it into a key target for the season.

She won't be the only one switching from a calendar largely filled with more traditional gravel events, with Specialized Off-Road teammate Matt Beers returning to the race for the first time since the opening edition, while Keegan Swenson is also back after skipping the 2023 and 2024 editions.

They will also be joined by the in-form men's gravel rider of the season, Mads Würtz Schmidt, who earlier this year said: "I think a World Championships with an Unbound peloton would be pretty special, so I hope the guys will come over and see the opportunity that it is to have a really cool, actual Gravel World Championships."

The flow of riders mentioned as starters does, in fact, include quite a number of Unbound Gravel 200 winners and podium finishers, from this year's victors Würtz Schmidt and Villafañe to previous years' Swenson, Rosa Klöser, and Carolin Schiff.

However, the top gravel riders certainly won't have the field to themselves, as plenty of others from across disciplines also think it's worth the trip. That includes the prolific rainbow title winner Marianne Vos, defending champion and WorldTour rider Florian Vermeersch, and riders who frequently mix road and gravel, like Tiffany Cromwell and Connor Swift.

"Hopefully, with the demands of the course, everybody sees an opportunity that they have not maybe seen in the previous years, with the European type racing, which has, let's say, a more singular dynamic as regards to the person who can win it," the Nannup UCI Gravel World Championships race director Stephen Gallagher told in the weeks before the event.

"This year has a lot more variance around the type of rider who can win."

What's different? Gridding, course and more

When Nannup first applied for the World Championships, the event's popularity and format were unknown, but with a big slab of road riders joining the gravel specialists. Even from the first edition of the UCI-sanctioned Worlds in Italy, it was well attended and fiercely competitive. It was then – and has continued to be – one where the podium is dominated by road professionals.

Initially, there was controversy over the way the start grids worked, with UCI points deciding the positions even though there were no points at that stage on offer for the UCI's own gravel series, and certainly not for the US-based, non-UCI gravel events.

That meant road, mountain bike and cyclo-cross riders hit the front row while the specialists were allocated spots down the back of the grid, although some last-minute lobbying meant some were moved up into the second and third row, but ultimately it was still a system which put gravel riders at a considerable disadvantage.

That situation has since changed, with riders like Nicole Frain, who are sitting right near the top of the UCI Gravel World Series, likely to get a position at the front of the field, as now the series allocates points and riders from other disciplines, where often there are far more race days packed into a season, get half their points taken into consideration. That, of course, still doesn't help riders who race a gravel calendar that largely focuses on the unsanctioned events, like Life Time Grand Prix participants Swenson and Villafañe.

What they do have running to their advantage this year, however, is the shape of the race, both in terms of the course and the participants. For a start, this year the gravel roads are wide, which means far more opportunities to work the way up through the field.

Plus, the field isn't likely to be as large in the first place, with the location outside Europe making it far more of an effort for the road professionals based there to just duck into the discipline for the weekend, or as dominated by teams from one nation.

For example, last year in Limburg, 279 riders started the elite men's race: 45 from Belgium, 36 from the Netherlands, and 32 from Germany; in the women's field of 107, Dutch riders made up nearly a quarter of the starters. Based on the registered riders, it looks like the field will be far more evenly balanced this year.

The next factor is the type of terrain and road surface riders will be facing. Other years have delivered a significant amount of the race off traditional smooth paved roads, but never as much as what will be offered on October 10 and 11. On top of that, this year those surfaces are actually all gravel roads, with previous editions including cobbles and single-track in the unpaved portions as organisers had to make do with what was available in the more heavily populated areas where the events were held.

Around the remote township of Nannup, however, organisers were spoilt for choice as they carved out an elite men's course with the 144km route, 85% gravel and 3,713m of elevation gain and an elite women's race with 84% gravel across the 125.6km and 3,179m of elevation gain.

"It's in a forest. It's endless gravel roads. So it's a cross between what you can find in parts of Europe and what you find in America," said Tiffany Cromwell, who won the SEVEN UCI Gravel World Series race on the course earlier this year.

"It gives more the feeling that it's not about positioning; it's not about short accelerations. The course is relentless, the climbs are steep, it's a lot of climbing – total climbing, but it's not long climbs, they're just steep – and I think that kind of hard draining course makes it more towards what typical gravel races usually are."

Cromwell, who is also a race ambassador, certainly wasn't going to be drawn into the narrative of it being the first 'real' UCI Gravel World Championships as "gravel is always interpretation of what you have in the place that you're in".

But she did make it clear that she believed that there is something on offer in 2026 for her retirement race that, as a rider who has competed in every edition of the UCI Gravel World Championships, she hasn't seen before in the rainbow jersey battle.

"It's the first time we're going to potentially see a gravel rider maybe win," Cromwell told . "It's the one that feels more like a gravel race than a Belgian Classic."

Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. Subscribers get unlimited access to exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

items.title: Yankees At-Bat of the Week: George Lombard Jr. (9/30)
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
Welp, the Yankees forgot to bring their bats to Game 1 against the Rays and now they forgot their gloves in Game 2. Five errors in the first five innings destroyed any advantage they might have gained from Cam Schlittler starting, their self-immolation eerily reminiscent of the fifth inning collapse in Game 5 of the 2024 World Series. In an attempt to cling on to a positive memory of these playoffs, I present our first At-Bat of the Week of the 2026 postseason, this edition featuring George Lombard Jr. in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.

We join Lombard with no outs in the sixth inning last Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. The Yankees blew Boston’s doors off in Game 1, 9-0, on the back of Ben Rice’s historic two home run, six-RBI performance. That game was close until the Yankees blew things open in the eighth, and this game is following a similar pattern with Max Fried and Sonny Gray largely holding both offenses in check.

And just like in Game 1, Chad Tracy came out with a quick hook for his starter, which is how we see Garrett Crochet pitching out of the bullpen to open the sixth. Crochet hadn’t thrown an MLB pitch since April, missing most of the season with a left shoulder injury, but made it back just in time to sneak onto the Wild Card roster. Spencer Jones stands on first after reaching on a leadoff strikeout wild pitch, and as we’ll soon see his hustle down the line will prove to be the turning point in the game.

I can almost guarantee that Lombard and everyone else in the stadium is expecting Crochet’s first MLB pitch in over five months to be his overpowering four-seamer. Perhaps Crochet looks to play off this expectation, because he introduces a wrinkle with a first pitch cutter trying to get a hitter sitting four-seamer to chase below the zone.

The intent is sound but the execution isn’t quite there. This pitch starts as a ball low out of Crochet’s hand and never looks like a strike. Lombard isn’t tempted to chase and spits on this cutter for ball one.

After showing Lombard a fastball that breaks glove-side, there is an opportunity for Crochet to steal a called strike inside. His four-seamer breaks in the opposite direction as the cutter, so a pitch that starts a little in off the plate and tails back to the inside edge should freeze the hitter.

It’s clear Crochet’s command is rusty given he misses his target on the opposite side of the plate. He wants to get this four-seamer in under Lombard’s hands but instead lands it low and away, just out of the zone. It still requires an impressively disciplined take from Lombard given it lands mere inches from the outside edge, made doubly difficult considering it immediately follows a cutter that breaks toward the plate from outside to in.

Lombard has worked the count leverage in his favor, 2-0. You’d expect most pitchers to come into the zone with a heater to avoid falling behind, 3-0, especially a pitcher with as blazing a fastball as Crochet’s.

Lombard completely sells out for the four-seamer and is made to look a little bit foolish on this back foot cutter. Make no mistake, this is a filthy pitch from Crochet. It looks like a strike middle-down out of the hand before the late movement zips it down and in under Lombard’s bat.

So far, the cutter appears to be coming out of Crochet’s hand a lot better than the four-seamer. After getting the chase and whiff on the previous one, he doubles up with another back foot cutter.

Crochet is able to pinpoint the bottom rail of the zone with this cutter for called strike two. Lombard is taking all the way to give Jones the opportunity to steal second . It’s a good thing he didn’t swing, because an errant throw to second from Adley Rutschman allows Jones to take the extra base, putting him 90 feet away from scoring an invaluable insurance run. Even if Jones hadn’t been running on the play, I still like this take from Lombard — this pitch had tailor-made groundball written all over it.

In the span of two pitches, Crochet has swung the count leverage in his favor, from 2-0 to 2-2. Having shown Lombard three cutters out of four pitches and with his first chance for a strikeout, Crochet attempts to gas a four-seamer by the Yankees rookie, the pitch coming in seven mph faster and with eleven inches less drop than the cutter.

What a swing by Lombard! This is a nasty heater from Crochet, 98 mph and just off the corner up and away. The situational hitting by Lombard is mature well beyond his 21 years. Living by the old adage of hitting the ball back the way it came, Lombard stays through this outside heater and shoots it to the opposite field for an RBI single. It’s such a simple approach and swing — short and compact to the pitch making sure to stay behind the baseball — the rookie not trying to do anything more than the pitch will allow him to do, knowing that solid contact the other way is almost certain to get the run in.

Proper credit has to be awarded to Jones as the precursor to this AB. Not giving up on the play when he struck out, the wheels to steal second and then the awareness to see the ball rolling into center and take off for third put Crochet on the ropes, and Lombard’s single opened the floodgates. To get that kind of mature contribution from a pair of your homegrown rookies in the playoffs against your age old rival is such a shot in the arm for the rest of the team. And returning to Lombard, I cannot say enough about how mature his approach was in this AB. It would be easy for any player, especially a 21-year-old rookie in his first postseason, to let the tension and stress creep in after Crochet quickly flipped the count from 2-0 to 2-2. However, he clutched up and came through with one of the finer pieces of situational hitting you are likely to see this postseason, giving his team an indispensable two-run cushion and setting the stage for the fireworks that would follow later in the frame.

items.title: The very second apron that paved the way for their title seeks to destroy the Knicks
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
Sports are cyclical. It’s very rare for a team to stay on top for a prolonged period of time, just the same as it’s rare for a team to stay in the doldrums for a long time. Smart organizations can keep championship windows open, and dumb organizations can keep shooting themselves in the foot, but in every sport, the bill eventually comes due.

The second apron, an invention of the latest CBA, has been the NBA’s attempt to speed up the cycle. They don’t want teams like the Warriors spending five years at the top of the sport with their all-time collection of talent. They want championship windows to be shorter, but also more volatile. It’s like a conveyor belt; they want these teams to all get a taste of glory before going back to the hunt.

As the current NBA champions, the Knicks are the latest team to fight a battle with the second apron. James Dolan says he does not want to exceed it, something that very few teams have done since it was introduced. They find themselves with a core that wants to be compensated as champions, but have a finite amount of money to get there.

It’s easy to curse the second apron for what they’re doing to muddy up the Knicks’ title defense and beyond, but in doing that, we have to remember that the construction and reason behind this team even reaching the mountaintop was the second apron.

The Minnesota Timberwolves were coming off a trip to the Western Conference Finals, but faced a massive crisis entering the 2024-25 season with their financial table. Some players needed extensions, some players had massive raises kicking in, and they were doomed to spend the season above the second apron. You can spend one year there and survive, but doing two or more years there is a death sentence. Hence, they needed to shed long-term salary.

That’s how Karl-Anthony Towns became a Knick.

The Boston Celtics were the type of unstoppable superteam that the league looked to avoid in 2023-24, boasting a starting five full of players who could create their own shot and hold their own defensively, an extremely rare blend. All of that was bolstered by an elite coach who maximized offensive efficiency with the three-pointer.

It was expensive to keep that team together the following season, and they did it in the second apron, but they knew they had to make changes after 2024-25 to avoid dooming themselves long term with a still-young superstar in Jayson Tatum. When the Knicks took out a bruised, battered Celtics team that May, they offloaded Kristaps Porzingis and Jrue Holiday and lost Al Horford and Luke Kornet to free agency, destroying that unstoppable ceiling and paving the way for the Knicks to take their place at the top of the totem pole.

The second apron unraveled the Celtics and Timberwolves, feeding a Knicks team that was excellently built and simply waited until their time to strike. Now, the Robin Hood nature of the second apron has come around to collect from the champs.

Karl-Anthony Towns wants an extension. Deuce McBride wants an extension. Josh Hart (who’s less of a priority due to a team option in 2027-28) wants an extension. Jalen Brunson is due at least $290 million down the road in a future extension (and could be up to $411 million). There’s not enough room under the second apron to keep them all happy.

The second apron already threw a right hook at the Knicks’ underbelly by forcing them to let go of Mitchell Robinson, but now they could come back and take McBride from them next season (or force them to trade him). The desire to keep the band together has caused a lowballing of Towns, something that is openly frustrating him in the media.

And now, we’re getting reports that both he and Hart could be trade chips in February if we can’t get a deal done? What happened to all the good vibes???

No matter how much “power of friendship” you have, money is the universal divider. I’m not calling Towns greedy for wanting to make more than residential losing players, Trae Young and De’Aaron Fox, but I’m also not going to call the Knicks prudish.

The second apron is extremely restrictive and, at most, you can exceed it one time before its vice grips start to sink in. I’m not sure if Dolan knows that fact, but if he does, you have to be very careful with how you use it.

It unfortunately seems like this will be a distraction for the Knicks in their title defense with how rigid the two sides seem to be. As much as it sucks, that’s the second apron.

It steals from the rich and gives to the poor.

items.title: 'I was mad' – Tom Pidcock says two teammates were hit by police motorbike driving against peloton at Tre Valli Varesine
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Tom Pidcock has stated that two of his teammates were struck by a police motorbike driving against the direction of the peloton during the Tre Valli Varesine race on Tuesday.

Pidcock was giving a post-race interview to Eurosport and describing the early phase of the race when he mentioned the incident.

"A police motorbike was going the wrong way down the course and crashed into two of our guys. So from this point... well, first of all I wanted to stop racing myself. I was mad. The guys all riding in front of me, for me, and two of them on the floor."

Pidcock revealed that the two riders in question were Marcel Camprubi and his fellow Briton Thomas Gloag.

"Luckily Marcel was ok, he could continue," Pidcock explained.

"Tom was also ok, in the end, but he stopped the race, and he has some stitches in the knee."

Rider safety has been a major talking point in recent years, and vehicle traffic in races has been high up the safety agenda since the death of Finlay Tarling in August.

"Things like this shouldn’t happen," Pidcock added.

items.title: Ezra Caudell Leaves the Hospital 31 Days After Philadelphia Crash
items.author: ahood
items.content: Modern Adventure rider Ezra Caudell will begin intensive rehabilitation as his recovery from the Philadelphia crash progresses, officials confirmed Tuesday.
items.lbText:
Ezra Caudell, shown here this spring, has left a hospital after a month following his crash. (Photo: Gautier Demouveaux/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Ezra Caudell has left the hospital and is transferring into intensive rehabilitation some 31 days after his traumatic crash at the Philadelphia Cycling Classic .

The Modern Adventure Pro Cycling rider was discharged late last week and will continue his recovery at Magee Rehabilitation Hospital in Philadelphia, officials confirmed.

Caudell, 20, was already walking the hospital halls before his discharge , according to the recovery update shared by his family and team.

“Just as encouraging has been his neurologic recovery. Ezra continues to show significant improvement from the injury to his brain, with progress in his strength, cognition, communication, and independence each day,” an update read.

“His recovery will take time, but his progress over the past month has been remarkable, and to see him now walking, interacting with those around him, and moving on to rehabilitation represents an enormous milestone.”

Caudell crashed on August 30 while racing the Philadelphia Cycling Classic.

The move into rehabilitation marks a major step for Caudell, though the team update on Tuesday emphasized that a long recovery still lies ahead.

The medical team expects his lung contusions and his fractures to continue healing without the need for further intervention, officials said.

His family and Modern Adventure Pro Cycling thanked supporters for their continued support as the popular rider begins the next phase of recovery.

“Ezra’s family and the Modern Adventure Pro Cycling team have every confidence in him and remain deeply grateful for the continued support he has received,” a note read.

items.title: Tre Valli Varesine: Jarno Widar pulls off surprise win in three-up sprint with Tom Pidcock and Matteo Jorgenson
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Jarno Widar (Lotto-Intermarché) pulled off the first victory of his hugely-promising young career on Tuesday, getting the better of Tom Pidcock (Pinarello-Q36.5) and Matteo Jorgenson (Visma-Lease a Bike) to win the Tre Valli Varesine.

The 20-year-old Belgian, who turned professional at the start of the year after a string of big results on the U23 scene, pulled off something of a shock as he sailed clear in a three-man sprint to the line.

Pidcock, who had created the winning move with an attack on the penultimate climb of a punchy circuit-based course, was surely considered the favourite as they prepared to sprint it out, being the fastest proven finisher.

But Widar sprang a surprise, and it paid off. He jumped from the back of the trio with well over 200 metres to go and opened a huge gap. Pidcock jumped into action but the damage was done, and he didn’t seem to have the legs anyway, sitting up as Widar continued to put the power down all the way to the line.

There was even a one-second gap measured between them as Pidcock had to settle for another second place after his runner-up finish at the Giro dell’Emilia, with Jorgenson trailing him across the line for third place.

Only a couple of seconds behind, Quinn Simmons (Lidl-Trek) led home the vastly-reduced peloton of around 20 riders.

The 105th edition of the Tre Valli Varesine, part of a string of late-season Italian one-day races, took place on a 196km route that was made up of six laps of a 15.9km circuit centered on the punchy Montello climb, and then two laps of a 31.4km circuit that also took in another climb after the Montello and before the draggy final haul towards the finish line.

The day’s five-man breakaway was reeled in on the second lap of the longer circuit, with Mikkel Honoré (EF Education-EasyPost) opening up the race from 44km out with an attack that was later joined, on the final Montello ascent, by Simmons and Davide Piganzoli (Visma-Lease a Bike).

But things had been pretty much been stitched back together by the time they hit the irregular penultimate climb to Barasso with 16km to go, which would prove crucial.

The world champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates) launched a big attack after Simmons’ final roll of the dice had been dealt with. When the group came back together, Pidcock took advantage of a lull to hit out with a huge acceleration. Widar and Jorgenson went with him, but there was quickly a gap to the rest.

Pidcock produced a monstrous turn to drive the move forward on the gentler top section of the climb, with Widar coming through but Jorgenson initially refusing to collaborate. When the US rider suddenly attacked instead of pulling, Pidcock did not hide his frustration.

Eventually, with 11km to go as they started to tilt downhill, Jorgenson started working and though McNulty attacked again to drag a 10-man chase clear, the reduced bunch came back together and lacked impetus, allowing the leading trio to start the haul towards the line with 3.4km to go with a lead of some 30 seconds.

The trio kept pushing up the climb until they reached the final kilometre, where thoughts turned to the sprint. Jorgenson was always the underdog, Pidcock was the favourite, but Widar sprang a surprise, and pulled off a stunning first victory of a career that will surely see many more.

items.title: I love the Kärcher OC3 Foldable – it's perfect for bike cleaning, and at a best-ever 32% off in the Amazon Prime Big Deal Days sale
items.author: paul.brett@futurenet.com (Paul Brett)
items.content:
The Kärcher OC3 Foldable really impressed me in testing, and I scored it a 4.5 out of 5-star rating. It only missed out on what would have been a perfect score due to its price.

Right now, in the Amazon Prime Big Deal Days sale, it's discounted by a whopping 32%, down to just £95.11, and a saving of £44.88 on the usual $139.99.

I think the Kärcher OC3 Foldable is a perfect option for washing your bike, especially if you're short on space. The beauty of this is that, folded down, it takes up absolutely zero space, either at home or in your car or van. As it's self-contained with an 8-litre water tank and built-in battery, it comes into its own if you lack an outdoor tap and suitable access to mains power.

As this deal is time-limited, I'd advise snapping one up for yourself while you can. Amazon Prime Big Deal Days run from 6-7 October, so the clock is ticking.

Built around an 8-litre collapsible water tank, this portable, low-pressure washer has been a total game-changer for post-ride cleaning. With a 5-bar (approx. 72.5 PSI) pressure rating, it's powerful enough to safely handle a quick post-ride clean-down, easily removing mud and debris. The battery lasts for around 15 minutes, meaning you can get a good few cleans in before charging.View Deal

The beauty of the OC3 Foldable is that it collapses to almost nothing. At just 108 mm (4.25 in) tall when folded, a 60% reduction in vertical profile. You can easily store it in a small kitchen drawer or keep it in the car. Expanded, it stands at 271 mm (10.7 in), with a static footprint of 305 x 298 mm (12.0 x 11.7 in).

In my Kärcher OC3 Foldable Mobile Cleaner review, some of the other testing highlights included the continuous battery runtime of 15 minutes, it's 8-litre silicone (or thermoplastic elastomer) tank, and the lightweight, even when filled, meaning its a breeze to carry around. It's easy to hold in one hand while in use.

The generous 1.8-metre length adds to the walkability in use, and the pressure gun feels great in the hand, operating with a simple trigger pull.

At this price, I think it's a bargain buy for anyone after a versatile low-pressure washer which handles basic grime effortlessly, and I was hard-pressed to find a single fault in this brilliant piece of kit

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Rubén Sierra
items.author: Jonathan Farrar
items.content:
After bursting onto the scene as a young All-Star in the late 1980s, Rubén Sierra went on to play for nine franchises over the course of his 20-year Major League career. The Yankees got to see two different stints from him over all those years, and had two very different experiences.

Rubén Angel Sierra Garcia October 6, 1965 (Rio Piedras, Puerto Rico): 1995-96, 2003-05

Born in Puerto Rico, Sierra lost his father when he was just four years old. Growing up in the Jardines Selles projects inspired Sierra to do one thing: get him and his family out of there. Excelling as a multisport athlete in high school, Sierra was signed by the Texas Rangers in 1982 and started his professional journey at just 17 years old in 1983.

Sierra, an outfielder who batted from both sides of the plate, quickly climbed through the Rangers system. So quickly that in 1986, the barely-not-a-teenager found himself on the doorstep of the majors in Triple-A. Later that summer, the Rangers called the kid up, and he homered in his second big league at-bat. Sierra went on to play in 113 games, launching 16 homers to go along with 13 doubles and 10 triples, for a baseball triple-double, if you will, good enough for a sixth-place finish in the American League Rookie of the Year voting.

That performance his rookie season was good enough to make him stick with the big league club moving forward. Sierra followed up his rookie campaign by hitting 30 home runs in 1987 and had a decent season again in 1988. The 1989 season would go down as one of Sierra’s best. He batted .306 with 29 big flies and led the major leagues with 14 triples and RBIs with 119. For the first time, he was selected as an All-Star and finished second to Robin Yount in the MVP race. Sierra cried and argued he deserved the MVP in a moment that would have been meme’d and gone viral if it had happened 30 years later.

Following the meltdown, Sierra had a down season. However, the still-young rising star rebounded in 1991. Making his second All-Star team, he hit 25 homers with 116 RBIs while batting .307 on the year. Following the season, Sierra fought with the club over salary and eventually won in arbitration. However, Sierra took the process very personally. An already-rocky relationship with manager Bobby Valentine finally came to a head, and a frustrated Rangers front office fired Valentine. Sierra was then traded, a few weeks after his third All-Star appearance, to the Oakland A’s on August 31st, with Jeff Russell and Bobby Witt for Jose Canseco.

Sierra played in Oakland for the rest of the 1992 season and into the 1995 season. While in Oakland, Sierra clashed with another manager, this time Hall of Famer Tony La Russa. The two openly fought in the sports pages, with Sierra bashing the get-on-base approach La Russa wanted. Despite playing well enough to be an All-Star again in 1994, the club had soured on Sierra to the point where they traded him with Jason Beverlin to the Yankees for another disgruntled player, Danny Tartabull.

The first stint in the Bronx for Sierra started in 1995 and ended almost a year to the date in 1996. The reason for the short stint was manager conflict again. Sierra clashed with Buck Showalter after he started using Sierra in a platoon role with Darryl Strawberry. Sierra had his agent call Showalter to complain, which set off Showalter.

By October, they had at least reached an uneasy truce, and while Sierra was held to a .174 showing in the five-game ALDS loss to Seattle, he did hit a pair of big home runs, the second tag-teaming with captain Don Mattingly to almost literally shake the Bronx in Game 2.

Joe Torre took over the Yankees in 1996, and Sierra again found a way to immediately get off on the wrong foot with the skipper. Torre would later say Sierra was the hardest player he ever had to coach and said he only cared about statistics and did not understand baseball. After one calendar year, the Yankees had enough and traded him with prospect Matt Drews to the Detroit Tigers for slugger Cecil Fielder.

Following his trade to Detroit, Sierra embarked on a four-year stretch playing for five different clubs. His production plummeted during this journeyman phase, eventually forcing him into a brief hiatus from the major leagues to completely retool his swing. Sierra found himself playing in Mexico, and over this stretch, his attitude changed and he started showing maturity, reaching out to mend a lot of broken relationships, including burying the hatchet with Torre.

Sierra got his swing back on track and was given a chance to revive his career back with the Rangers. In his comeback season, he won the 2001 American League Comeback Player of the Year award. Sierra then made a one-year pit stop in Seattle before bouncing back to the Rangers for the 2003 season. In June of 2003, he was dealt by Texas back to New York for Marcus Thames.

The second stint in the Bronx saw a reinvented Sierra. He was selfless and a productive veteran bench piece who became a beloved clubhouse presence for Torre. Sierra delivered a few clutch moments for the Bombers, including a pinch-hit game-tying triple in the ninth inning of 2003 World Series Game 4 against the Marlins’ Ugueth Urbina, and a three-run home run at the Metrodome off Juan Rincón to knot up Game 4 of the 2004 ALDS.

By the time his second stint concluded after the 2005 season, Sierra had rewritten his legacy in New York. Across five seasons in pinstripes, Sierra hit 45 home runs while batting .254 over the span of 383 games.

Over his 20-year career, Sierra got 2,152 hits and had a .268 career batting average. He hit 306 home runs and drove in 1,322 RBIs across 2,186 games. After his playing days, Sierra started focusing on his lifelong love for salsa music. He has released several salsa albums and spent much of his retirement actively touring, performing, and singing at live music venues and events. Sierra was inducted into the Texas Rangers Hall of Fame in 2009.

items.title: Binche-Chimay-Binche: Paul Magnier slams the door on Lotto-Intermarché duo for winning sprint
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) triumphed at Binche-Chimay-Binche, winning the sprint finish to score his 12th victory of the 2026 season.

Lotto-Intermarché set up the lead-out in the final kilometre after the two Belgian teams caught lone late attacker Lewis Askey (NSN) with just over one kilometre to go.

The team couldn't outpace Giro d'Italia points winner Magnier, though, as he came off the wheel of Jenno Berckmoes to blast past to win in the final metres of the hilly 206.8km race. Berckmoes had to settle for second place as his lead-out man Lionel Taiminiaux rounded out the podium in third.

Early on in the day, a seven-man break went clear, with Siebe Deweirdt (Flanders-Baloise), Paul Conor (TotalEnergies), Victor Hannes (Aarco), Rokas Adomaitis (Energus), Harry Lasker (Modern Adventure), Léo Schyns (Color Code-Alu Center), and Kévin Avoine (Van Rysel Roubaix) all making it away.

The breakaway riders never got more than three minutes up the road, however, and Lasker, Schyns, and Avoine dropped away before the race hit the finishing circuit. At 65km to go, Deweirdt, Conor, Hannes, and Adomaitis had 1:20 on the peloton, which was led by Soudal-QuickStep.

That advantage quickly faded as a group including Jasper Stuyven (Soudal-QuickStep) and Per Strand Hagenes (Visma-Lease a Bike) moved across the gap. With 50km to run, the break was caught for good.

A group of seven including Toms Skujinš (Lidl-Trek), Lukáš Kubiš (Unibet Rose Rockets), Gianni Vermeersch (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), and Laurenz Rex (Soudal-QuickStep) went clear at 41km to go as Magnier crashed before rejoining the peloton.

At 32km to go, the move came to an end as the peloton brought it back. More attacks came and went, but nothing stuck as the riders prepared to tackle the final lap of the race. Several riders attacked early on the lap with 12km to go, with Stuyven, Thibaud Gruel (Groupama-FDJ United), Christophe Laporte (Visma-Lease a Bike), and Søren Kragh Andersen (Lidl-Trek) getting away.

Kragh Andersen went solo off the front into the final 10km before Stuyven, Gruel, and Laporte came back along with several others 6km from the line. Jonas Abrahamsen (Uno-X Mobility) and Lewis Askey (NSN) were also up there in a new 10-man leading group.

The group didn't survive out front until the finish, however, with the peloton making the catch at 2km to go as Askey took off alone. He couldn't hold off the might of Soudal-QuickStep and Lotto-Intermarché in the chase, and so the final sprint was set up with Lotto leading the way.

UEC European Championships: France storm to elite mixed relay TTT victory
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Riding the 44km course in 1:00:29, they obliterated the World Champion Italian team, beating them by a whopping 1:12. The battle for third place was much closer, with the Luxembourg team taking the bronze medal, 27 seconds faster than the Polish team in fourth place.

Despite losing one of their number early in the first leg, the French men’s squad of Bruno Amirail, Remi Cavagna and Thibault Guernalec led from start to finish, setting the fastest time at each of the time checks and handing over to the women in a clear first place.

Anchored by Juliette Berthet, Cédrine Kerbaol and Maeva Squiban, the French continued to fly, putting more time into the Italian team and even catching the Polish team, who started four minutes ahead of them.

For their part, the Italian squad of Mattia Cattaneo, Marco Frigo, Matteo Sobrero, Elisa Longo Borghini, Monica Trinca Colonel and Alessia Vigilia held on for the first lap, but when Trinca Colonel was dropped early on lap two, they lost time quickly.

“It’s really cool. I think there is kind of a prophecy,” Cédrine Kerbaol said. “We did three times second in Worlds and now it’s the third time we get the title at Europeans, so we are really happy. For sure, it was not won in advance, the Italians are really, really strong, and the last days have been a bit hard with recovery from the Worlds."

Cavagna offered the slightest insight into the French excellence in the discipline, saying, “We train a lot for this, it’s really important for France because we love this, we always race here for win. We always work together to be strong and to be the strongest, and today we were the strongest.”

Only six nations took to the start on Šenčur for the 44km race, the equal fewest which comprised two laps of the circuit used to close all the road races, which included the climb to Možjanca and its brutal gradients up to 15%. Each nation field a six-rider team, their three men riding the first 22km lap, with the women starting their once the second man completed his race. The team’s time was taken when the second woman crossed the line.

The home Slovenian squad were first off, their three men heading down the ramp at 15:30 local time and setting a time of 30:18 at the changeover. Behind them, though, France were flying, seeing a fastest time of 13:15 at the opening split, 8km into their ride, some 26 seconds quicker than World Champions Italy, the final team to set off.

At the change, the French were by far the fastest team, eclipsing the Slovenians, stopping the clock at 28:03, more than two minutes faster than the Slovenians and some 24 seconds faster than the Italians, who had failed to make up any time from the first time check.

Further down the running order, some of the other teams struggled badly, their stronger riders being forced to slow for their compatriots to ensure two riders were together at the finish.

While the Italian team had two changes from the six riders who won the World Championships in Canada last month - meaning four of them ride in the rainbow stripes and two in the azure of the Italian team - the French had only one substitution, Jordan Labrosse being replaced by Guernalec, allowing them more continuity.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Definitely heartbreaking’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The New York Knicks officially unofficially played basketball yesterday, and I can’t be happier about an opponent’s win.

As Russell said in his Scenes, we’ll give them belt when it counts, but for now, all I needed was some Orange and Blue hoops in my screen.

Here’s the latest from NYK world coming off Monday’s loss. Get well soon, Huk.

On playing everyone available in the preseason opener:

“Everybody’s been busting their behind in camp. Everybody’s good people, and it’s our first game. So I’m gonna play everybody. Twenty guys. Jose’s not playing.”

On the Knicks’ lack of physicality in the preseason loss to Philadelphia:

“Most of it, I was okay with (the performance). I just listed things that I saw that I know we can be better at. What bothers me is our lack of physicality throughout the ballgame, and that’s the whole roster, up and down. We weren’t great on the ball physically, and we weren’t great with our defensive positioning physically.

“That I’m concerned about, and I don’t wanna see it happen (again). The rest of the stuff, it’s coach-talk. It’s real, but it’s coach-talk that we’ll clean up watching film and all that stuff. I can’t help with the physicality. That they got to find it individually, which will then turn into collectively. That’s how you find minutes. That’s how you make the team. That’s how you contribute.”

On evaluating the Knicks’ options at center:

“I think just it’s just kind of gut feel. And then we’ll look at production because they’re gonna probably give us different levels of protection in different areas. Tony is just a really smart guy that has a great feel for the game, and when you watch him play, they’re not necessarily sexy, but he’s extremely efficient, and then there are times when it’s like, ‘Oh, my God, he kicked our ass [in the past].

“When you look at Wiseman, he’s younger, he’s a little more raw, he’s a vertical threat. He’s one of the best runners I’ve been around. You can see and feel his length and his athleticism and his potential.

“Then when you look at Drew, just a toughness about him, and you know what you’re gonna get, not tonight, but every fricking night that you go out there, ’cause he’s got a great feel, a great sense of toughness about him, and again, he’s not afraid to do anything against anybody, and his belief is at a pretty high level.

“So they’ll all initially bring something a little bit different, and we’ll just see, at the end of the day, if any of them, in terms of the center spot, fit well enough to be on our team.”

On Mikal Bridges attacking the rim:

“It’s great. He’s long, athletic and smart. He can finish at the rim. He’s capable of playing off of two feet and making a spray because he has a tremendous feel for the game.”

On creating more offensive opportunities for OG Anunoby:

“We have to try and put him in those positions a bit more, but he also has to have a good feel of what he wants and get to his spots. With him being in the system for a year, he’s got a better feel. … We also have a better feel on how to use him. I don’t call a lot of plays, and now he can find the small areas where he can be aggressive offensively. … His natural ability, especially with how hard he works, is showing.”

On wishing Ariel Hukporti a speedy recovery:

“We hope Ariel — whatever is wrong with him — he has a speedy recovery and he’s back on the floor. You hate to see anybody go down with an injury, but especially somebody who is a caliber person who Ariel is.”

On the 76ers’ roster and their status as an Eastern Conference contender:

“You look at their roster, man, it’s just loaded: multiple-time All-Star, multiple-time All-Star, multiple-time All-Star, MVP candidate, MVP candidate, MVP candidate. I remember back in the day, Pop said — when I was an assistant for him — there is a change from having two All-Stars on your team to having three. He brought it to our attention as a staff. He was like, you made at least three NBA All-Stars, and not just one-offs, but perennial All-Stars to go win a championship.

“And this is when we were going against Kobe [Bryant] and Shaq[uille O’Neal] and their [Lakers] team and all that.

“You look at this [Philly] team here, and they’ve got as many All-Stars or guys of that nature as they had in Miami when LeBron was down there. So they’re definitely a deep team, a talented team. Nick Nurse does a phenomenal job. He’s a championship-level coach, and they’re definitely going to be one of the teams that are contending in the East.

“In my opinion, it just got harder for everybody with the team that they assembled here.”

On LeBron James reaching his 24th NBA season:

“The first thing, I guess like year 24 is insane. It’s unheard of. It’s not human. People talk about Wemby being not human because of what he can do for his size. You got to throw LeBron in that category because of his durability and still doing it at the age that he has at a high level. It’s amazing to watch, but if there’s anybody that’s going to do it, he’s going to do it because even when he was young, he was really diligent about taking care of his body and he was not afraid to ask the vets, like Zydrunas Ilgauskas, who was one of the best in terms of taking care of his body, he was not afraid to ask him what he does daily and then follow his lead. So just an amazing, amazing run for one of the all-time greats.”

On the championship-level upgrade to his travel toiletries kit:

“Something has changed: This is kind of cool. So, our equipment guys are great, Kyle, Steve, Will, shout out to them. One of the best in the league, and they give me a toothbrush and toothpaste, mouthwash, and lotion, and all that. And they put it in my locker area, and they usually just carry it in a paper bag or a plastic bag.

“[Now] they put it in one of those travel things. And they set it really nice on my desk, and I go in there today, and these freaking guys, they made a travel case. Like this is where my lotion is. This is where the Kleenex goes. The two travel Listerines, the deodorant, and Sensodyne toothpaste in the back.

“And, it’s foam. It’s in a case, and not only that, you can’t see it, but right here, it says lotion. Right here, it says deodorant. So this is what championship level coaches get, right? I guarantee Nick [Nurse] has this s–t, too.”

On what he wants from a Knicks contract extension:

“Simply put, I want to do something that can keep the team together and that can work with the Knicks, but also values me. And none of those things have come close to happening.”

On wanting to be paid according to his value after winning a championship and not making concessions:

“No s–t, Sherlock. I just got a championship, you thought it’d be pretty easy… unless you guys think I got anything else to prove?”

On the outlook for reaching an extension before the regular season:

“It don’t look good. I mean in my experience, you just appreciate the moments right now and let it go where it goes.”

On how he is handling the lack of an extension:

On the Knicks’ preseason opener:

“It’s a good first step. Not a great first step, but as long as we’re making strides in the right direction, it’s something to be happy about. Still a lot for us to learn and be better at early”

On Ariel Hukporti’s injury:

“Definitely heartbreaking. When I came back in the locker room, I went to go check on him. Sad to see. Obviously, we’ll pray for him.”

On his first game with the

“It felt good just trying to contribute to the team”

On Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart potentially becoming trade candidates if they remain unsigned:

“Josh Hart has already hinted that, as this gets closer to February, which is around the trade deadline.

“The temperature could rise if Karl-Anthony Towns and Hart himself are not extended. So far, these sides are not close.”

MLB Playoff Roundup: Sean Burke shoves as White Sox go up 2-0
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
It was an American League-only night on Monday, and the Yankees fumbled their way into an 0-2 hole. Four errors gave the Rays far too many opportunities to capitalize, and while Cody Bellinger came a few feet away from a grand slam the only actual results the lineup could produce came on a pair of Ben Rice solo shots. With only one other game going on, let’s take a look at the other side of the AL bracket.

AL Division Series Game 2

Chicago White Sox 4, Cleveland Guardians 3(Chicago leads, 2-0)

The Guardians knew they needed to respond facing the potential of going on the road to Chicago down 0-2, and they jumped ahead in the first inning against Anthony Kay. Steven Kwan led off with a single and José Ramírez worked a walk to put runners on, and after a seven-pitch battle that culminated in a ground out moving the runners up Kay’s day was done. Will Venable went to Sean Newcomb knowing he’d need to get a ton of mileage out of his bullpen but Newcomb did him no favors out the gate, spiking a throw to first that turned a fielder’s choice into a two-run lead for Cleveland.

Trailing for the first time this postseason, the White Sox took a bit to get going against Gavin Williams. Williams struck out 11 batters over the course of five innings, looking especially sharp through the first three, but the cracks started to form in the fourth inning. Kyle Teel led off with a single and Miguel Vargas walked to move him into scoring position for Munetaka Murakami, who turned on a triple-digit heater to smoke an RBI single out to right field.

Williams worked around a leadoff single in the fifth by striking out the side, but after he started the sixth off with another single Steven Vogt had seen enough and went to his bullpen. Erik Sabrowski was the choice, and though he managed to get a grounder out of Murakami he was still in trouble and about to make it worse. Pinch-hitter Randal Grichuk worked a walk and a wild pitch put both runners in scoring position before Tommy Pham flew out shallow enough to not bring home the lead runner. That put the pressure on Braden Montgomery to deliver, and he provided with a two-run double slicing down the right field line. That chased Sabrowski from the game, but Hunter Gaddis couldn’t get out of the inning before Chase Meidroth added on with an RBI single to make it 4-2.

The White Sox had the lead, and they’d held Cleveland from scoring after their initial outburst thanks largely to one man. Newcomb gave Chicago two innings before turning the ball over to Sean Burke, their Game 2 starter against the Astros in the Wild Card Series, and he managed to have a better outing coming out of the ‘pen than he did starting that game. Burke pitched 5.1 innings for the Southsiders, striking out six and retiring 16 of the first 17 batters he faced. Chase DeLautner broke that streak up with a single to left, and Venable decided it was time to get his closer Grant Taylor into the game for a four-out save. Jo Adell greeted him with an RBI triple to cut the deficit in half, but Taylor got Nathaniel Lowe to fly out harmlessly to strand the tying run. Cleveland’s rally wouldn’t continue in the ninth as they went down in order, putting Chicago on the doorstep of an ALCS berth.

items.title: One of the best rear bike lights we've ever used has 41% off, but only for 48 hours in the Amazon Prime Big Deal Days sale
items.author: paul.brett@futurenet.com (Paul Brett)
items.content:
When it comes to the best rear light, the Magicshine SEEMEE 300 has set the standard for many years. It recently lost its crown in bike light buying advice to the newer SEEMEE 400. However, if battery life is your main requirement, then the older 300 actually lasts longer than its far more expensive sibling.

A price gap that is now even wider thanks to the Amazon Prime Big Deal Days sales. It sees the SEEMEE 300 drop to just £35.52, a massive 41% off the list price of £59.99.

Our Senior Tech Writer, Will Jones, scored the SEEMEE 300 with an almost faultless 96% during his testing and was hard-pushed to critique the Magicshine. Will only marked it down for the slightly confusing mode selections and its potentially dazzling brightness (for other riders) on full power, being very minor quibbles.

I love the SEEMEE 300, and have highlighted many Amazon deals for as long as I've been a deals hunter on . For me, maximum brightness on a rear light, as far as my own safety goes, is an actual box-ticking feature (sorry other riders).

As this deal is time-limited, I'd advise snapping one up for yourself while you can.

The UK Amazon Prime Big Deal Days discount drops the SEEMEE 300 to just £35. It comes loaded with features, including two LEDs that combine with a bonus downward-facing LED and project a beam directly onto the ground below you, massively increasing your overall visibility.View Deal

It may have been superseded by its 400 sibling as our best rear bike light, but the older model still has what it takes, especially at this price. With a 200-hour runtime and enhanced safety features, including a smart motion sensor that cleverly adjusts the brightness when you brake, it offers incredible value.View Deal

The SEEMEE 300 has one of the best battery lives of any rear light on the market at a whopping 200 hours. That even beats the latest SEEMEE 400 (107 hours) because of the higher overall power output of the 400, with, of course, 400 lumens.

Smart features include auto-dim, which dims the light to suit the ambient lighting conditions and prolongs the already impressive battery life. Another cool addition is the motion sensor, which acts as a brake light, something that is really useful if you're a regular commuter riding in traffic.

However, the feather in the SEEMEE 300s cap is the unique downward-facing LED light that illuminates a large cone below you, giving 360 degrees of effective visibility.

items.title: 'Real-world control over deep tube shapes' - Look's G85 Cezal gets the RS treatment with high-modulus carbon fibre
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
Look has launched a G85 Cezal RS gravel race bike today, building on the G85 Cezal foundation it built earlier in the year.

It feels like new race-oriented gravel bikes are being released pretty much constantly, and the requirements for a competitive gravel race bike seem to get more specific and purposeful with every passing season.

Look launched its G85 Cezal all-rounder back in April, and we covered that launch with a first-ride impressions piece, after swinging a leg over the new machine in Italy.

Fast forward to now, and Look has given the Cezal a race tune and 'RS' model update with some boosted clearances and High Modulus carbon fibre.

The French brand says that the Cezal RS is 'engineered specifically for riders seeking precision, reactivity and speed across medium and long distances'. Gravel racer Russell Finsterwald has played a hand in the bike's development and rode to a top 20 Traka 360 result on a prototype of the bike earlier in the year.

You will notice the Cezal has non-dropped seatstays for a more traditional look, and Look has given it relatively normal 50mm rear and 57mm front tyre clearances.

On paper, the bike may not look as cutting-edge as some of its competitors, and that mismatched tyre clearance figure may disappoint some, but Look argues it has drawn on real-world riding scenarios to come up with a highly competitive gravel machine that's the right tool for the job.

Look claims the Cezal RS has been built around three core pillars: Versatile performance, responsive handling, and balanced component selection. The brand also said that it will provide a 'competition-ready setup for 99% of race scenarios'.

Those core pillars sound sensible. We attended a pre-launch video call on the new bike, and it sounded as though creating a well-rounded bike informed by real-world race experience, not just one that would light up the comments sections, was a priority.

The RS has the same geometry as the G85 Cezal, and Look says it stuck with the non-dropped seatstays and a round seatpost to improve the bike's handling, citing the need for real-world control over deep tube shapes.

The carbon fibre used in construction has been upgraded, though; the RS has a High Modulus (HM) carbon fibre layup, which saves a healthy 200 grams off the frame weight compared to the standard G85 Cezal.

Claimed weight for the medium frame is 1000 grams for the frame with hardware.

This HM layup provides a very stiff headtube, which Look says is stiffer than its Blade RS3 road bike.

The upgraded layup is said to boost bottom bracket stiffness by 19% and headtube stiffness by 20%.

The brand claims the rear seatstays 'filter 15% of vibrations', but there's no further context on that number.

Tyre clearance is 57mm up front and 50mm at the rear. It can also be run with a double chainset setup with 45mm clearance. Looks says it wanted to retain shorter chainstays and a snappier ride quality over a bigger rear clearance number. A front suspension fork can also be fitted for more technical terrain.

The G85 Cezal RS will be available as a frameset and in two full build options.

The frameset will retail at €3,290 and include a Token T47 bottom bracket, flat-mount brake hardware, and a Look LS1 27.2mm seatpost.

The complete builds centre around SRAM XPLR gravel-specific groupsets.

items.title: UEC European Championships: Italy triumph in junior mixed relay TTT
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Italy won the Junior Mixed Team Relay event at the UEC European Championships in Slovenia on Tuesday, riding the Polish team into second place, with Switzerland in third.

The team of Enrico Balliana, Brandon Fedrizzi, Patrik Pezzo Rosola, Azzurra Ballan, Eisa Bianchi and Matilde Rossignoli closked a time of 1:07:22 for the 44km race.

As with the other races in this week’s championships, the riders faced two laps of the 22km loop around the town of Šenčur, with the two kilometre climb to Možanca and its double digit gradients providing a stiff test. Each of the 11 participating nations started with their three-man teams riding the first circuit before the women took over for the second.

The set off in two tranches, with five teams in the first and the remaining six setting off 44 minutes afterwards. After fielding a team with only two women, Luxembourg emerged as the leaders from the first five nations, their result a surprising one after they fielded only two women for their second lap.

Italy were first off in the second tranche, setting the fastest time at the changeover, their women holding on to win by 23 seconds. The Swiss team were a further seven seconds back.

items.title: Tactics over watts? Surprise checkpoints and different route options as UCI revolutionises format for 2026 Esports World Championships
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
The UCI has announced changes to the format of the Esports World Championships intended to add a tactical element to the racing, where the winner will be the racer with most points, not necessarily the first rider across the finish line.

The UCI has also revealed the event will take place a week earlier than was originally advertised, in the Danish capital of Copenhagen on December 5, after the event was originally set to take place across separate locations.

Run in conjunction with the UCI’s race platform partner, MyWhoosh, the E-Sports World Championships will be split into two stages, the first with 'surge checkpoints', the second a more conventional points race, though with route options to add spice and decision making. Points will be combined from both stages and the rider with the highest total wins the title.

"They will need to demonstrate both physical strength and tactical acumen to be in with a chance of taking the ultimate honours and the prestigious rainbow jersey of UCI World Champion," said the UCI president, David Lapparient.

Held over 7.6km, the opening-stage surge checkpoints will be a surprise, announced to all riders in each race simultaneously, though only 500m in advance, with the first 10 across the line earning points. It’s hoped this will create a tactical dilemma for the riders who will need to position themselves carefully to ensure they are best placed to collect points, though not on the front in the virtual wind.

Perhaps the biggest innovation is the second stage. Held over four 5km laps, each lap includes two scoring lines where riders can earn points. For the first, riders will need to make a decision whether to pick a hilly route offering more points, or a flatter and faster one awarding fewer points.

The second scoring line will be a common checkpoint, coming after the hilly and flat routes have converged, requiring competitors to decide whether to choose the hilly route for more points, or the flatter route to prioritise recovery and the common sprint point. This format provides eight points-scoring opportunities throughout the second stage, with double points on the finish line.

"We wanted this year’s format to ask more of riders than simply producing the biggest numbers," said Matt Smithson, Director of Esports and Game Operations at MyWhoosh.

"The surprise checkpoints and route choices mean they have to read the race, make decisions under pressure and decide when it is worth spending energy for points. That should create a much more dynamic Championships and, crucially, a format that makes full use of what cycling esports can do rather than simply recreating a road race in a virtual environment."

Only 36 riders will compete in the event, 18 men and 18 women, all selected via a series of qualification events and a semi-final which took place on October 2.

The Copenhagen event replaces the two-venue championships originally slated, and will take place in a purpose built studio. The event will be broadcast live.

items.title: The 'weird' car theory sparked by F1 pecking order surprises
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Among the factors potentially behind a swing in Formula 1's recent pecking order in Malaysia is how an extreme track surface could have made some cars behave in a "weird way" aerodynamically. 

Mercedes and McLaren had claimed 14 of 15 pole positions between them prior to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and won 13 of the 15 races in 2026 so far. 

But they were comprehensively bested by Red Bull, and outqualified by Ferrari too, as Max Verstappen took advantage of F1's return to Sepang and its unique challenge to best the usual benchmarks. Even Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies admitted this was a "surprise". 

A prominent theme of the week was how the Sepang surface was unusually rough, ironically only matched by Bahrain's own Sakhir circuit, which this grand prix replaced. Mekies said the extreme heat, track roughness and layout of the track meant "most of the cars out there were out of their ideal operating window". 

An open, abrasive track surface combined with high temperatures is an established and well understood challenge, though. More interesting was a more intricate variable that hints at how that kind of surface disturbs a car's aerodynamic performance. 

Mercedes acknowledged its biggest issue was around parts of the lap where Sepang's track was its worst and most broken-up, with an emphasis on slower corners. 

Meanwhile, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella was "puzzled a little bit" why its prowess in high-speed corners from recent races in Madrid or Zandvoort - the latter also utilising older asphalt - was not evident in Malaysia. 

Stella offered an intriguing hint at why this could be the case when he said: "There's some conditions, even the Tarmac conditions, they make the car operate in a weird way, not only from a tyre's point of view."

He did not want to elaborate in much detail on a technical matter but when asked by The Race if it has an aero effect and he could point to the vague areas it has an impact on, Stella replied: "I think your pointing is not inaccurate."

This is understood to relate to how loose stones in such a rough surface generate disturbed airflow so it does not behave smoothly, or as expected, along the car's aerodynamic surfaces. 

So it may be that there were moments when some cars were more sensitive to this and did not have the real-world performance or aero consistency to match the actual load teams could see in the data.

Such a phenomenon was also prominent during the previous ground-effect era from 2022-25, as those cars generated huge amounts of downforce from the underfloor but at the same time were extremely sensitive to disruptions in that airflow. 

"We think that the car operated where it should have operated to extract the downforce and the mechanical grip," Stella said of McLaren's weekend. 

"If anything, it's more about the potential of the car and we actually increased the potential of the car with the upgrades - the information we have tells us that that's the case.

"It's more the competitiveness on track that tells us, 'Oh we seem to have lost some ground' relative to the others. 

"It's difficult to understand these things.

"We need to observe the car, the upgrades and the relative competitiveness in Singapore and then we'll go with the final races."

Mercedes did not allude to something quite so specific, but deputy team principal Bradley Lord did describe it as "a bit of a 3D problem that we need to work through". 

It was - in relative terms - a disappointing weekend for Mercedes as championship leader Kimi Antonelli was only second behind Verstappen and was unable to really challenge him for the win despite jumping into the lead at the start. 

"The combination potentially of updates, track temperature and track surface caused an interaction, a set of behaviours that meant the car was not in its usual happy state, that the drivers were having to turn the car on the throttle in the slow corners," said Lord. 

"That was further exacerbating the challenges of tyre temperatures. So that's not an easy thing to unpick."

items.title: Tre Valli Varesine Women's Race: Eleonora Gasparrini wins after last-gasp breakaway catch
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Eleonora Gasparrini (UAE Team L'IMAD) surged to her first win of the season in Varese, triumphing on the uphill finish to win Tre Valli Varesine Women's Race.

The Italian beat Sarah Van Dam (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Noemi Rüegg (EF Education-Oatly) to the line after a large chase group caught and passed a two-woman attack group on the final ramp to the finish line.

Karlijn Swinkels (UAE Team L'IMAD) and Nikola Nosková (Cofidis) had both been on the move off the front after attacking during the final laps of the hilly 133.9km race. The pair went clear of a group that included Aude Biannic (Movistar), Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek), Amber Kraak (FDJ United-SUEZ), Maud Oudeman (Visma-Lease a Bike), and Maud Rijnbeek (VolkerWessels) in the final 30km.

The move had initially gone clear 45km from the line, with the tough race going without a breakaway for a long time beforehand. Swinkels and Nosková proved the strongest of the group, though, pushing on together.

Despite the chase group behind them having greater strength in numbers, it looked as though the pair would stay away to contest the finish among themselves. There was little cooperation among the chase group, but the peloton was closing in behind.

But what was a 35-second gap eventually faded to nothing on the final hill of the race, just a few hundred metres from the finish line.

In a reversal of the final of last month's GP de Wallonie, where Gasparrini attacked late for Swinkels to follow wheels and sprint to victory, Gasparrini took advantage in the final, outsprinting her rivals to deliver the win for UAE after Silvia Persico's work to guide her to the front.

items.title: ALDS Game 2 Player of the Game: Ben Rice
items.author: Jeremy Nielsen
items.content:
The Yankees have lost an ugly game in the ALDS yet again. As a result of another contest in which they were played off the field by a division rival, they are once again compelled to win three straight games facing elimination to keep their season alive. The Yankees have never won a postseason series under Aaron Boone as the underdog—and through two games their lifeless, gormless play has proven immune to the best-laid pitching plans of one of the most dominant pitching staffs in franchise history.

If you’re looking for a hero in this 5-2 loss at Tropicana Field, you’re going to have to keep looking. At least unlike Saturday there was a number above zero on New York’s side of the scorecard. Ben Rice provided those two tallies with a pair of home runs to right, the first of which provided a brief spark of hope that the Yankees might not totally butcher this thing—before they totally butchered it just two innings later.

Rice hit a flyout in his first at-bat, precipitating a perfect first time through the order for Rays starter Freddy Peralta. But his second time up promised a better future for this game and this series. Fastball Freddy, as the broadcast referred to him roughly a dozen times throughout the night, started Rice off with said fastball before abandoning it in favor of his changeup. He made three successive attempts to lure Rice into chasing the pitch—and his third try was successful to bring the count to 2-2.

That whiff seemed to further convince Peralta to stick with his change, especially knowing that Rice is one of the league’s best fastball hitters. So for the fourth straight time, he went changeup away—but he left this one in the strike zone, along the outside corner. Rice capitalized, shooting it over the right field wall for a game-tying solo blast.

Rice did his job effectively again when he came up for a third time in the fifth inning. With two outs, Austin Wells doubled off Peralta to spark a rally. Ryan McMahon followed by working a walk after falling behind 0-2, which ended Peralta’s night. Rice was the first man to face lefty reliever Cam Booser, and got nothing good to swing at. The southpaw pitched around Ben, who refused to expand the zone. He worked his walk to load the bases for Cody Bellinger, known for his track record of success against left-handed pitching. Bellinger very nearly found the go-ahead hit he was looking for with a long fly ball to center field, but Jonny DeLuca ran it down on the warning track.

Of course, the Rays benefitted from a Yankee pratfall routine immediately afterward, destroying all positive momentum and building a 5-1 lead. But Rice, outcome be damned, was gonna turn in another good at-bat. Facing Ian Seymour to lead off the eighth inning, he took a first-pitch sweeper for a strike, then unleashed a lightning-fast swing on an inside changeup. His line drive down the right field line snuck over the wall for his second homer of the night.

Rice could not spark a greater rally. The Yankees went down in order against Seymour right after that second homer, and put up no resistance against closer Bryan Baker. The Yankees are on the verge on another ignominious end to a strong season, but at the very least we can give a tip of the hat to their best hitter all year, who never gave in even as the rest of the team kept making the same familiar mistakes that routinely send this team home emptyhanded in October.

If a miraculous and frankly uncharacteristic series victory from down 2-0 is in the offing, no doubt Ben Rice will be one of the key reasons. The Yankees will need more than just him to hit, but his exceptional talent must also continue to be front-and-center for the Bombers to save their season.

items.title: We rate the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 as some of our best headphones for cyclists, and they're now less than half price during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days

We ranked the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 as best for Android users in our recently updated best headphones for cycling buying guide. Right now, you can save up to 55% when you buy them at Amazon UK as part of its Big Deal Days sale.

There is a small catch, as only the pink-tipped earbuds are available at this price. I think they look very cool, but if they don't work for you, the black and grey-tipped options still have a decent £60 saving. Another money-saving option for those not swayed by the pink would be to buy official replacement tips for £19, or unofficial ones for £8.

The UK deal is not exclusive to Prime Members, but should you want to sign up, you can geta and cancel anytime before the £8.99 ($14.99 US) monthly fee kicks in.

Tester Will Jones gave the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 4.5 out of 5 stars in our best headphones for cycling guide, ranking them as best for Android. They have a best-in-class battery life of 12 hours and are comfortable when worn for long periods, making them ideal for all-day rides.View Deal

If you're in the US, the Pixel Buds Pro 2s are part of Amazon's Big Deal Days sale too, with a 22% saving, which drops the price to $179. There's no colour conundrum here though, as every hue is the same price.

As well as being super comfortable and being able to go 12 hours between charges, the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 have excellent gesture controls. There's also an iOS-like 'Find My' feature – which is invaluable if you can't remember which jacket pocket you last stuck them in, or if they should slip down the back of the couch.

Noise cancellation is decent, and there's transparency mode and conversation detection too. The Pro 2s are designed to cope with wet weather and come with an IP54 rating. The gesture controls can go haywire in the wet though, so Will suggests turning that function off when riding in the rain.

Overall audio performance is very good, but it's not quite up to the likes of Technics EAH-AZ100.

items.title: Canyon-SRAM strengthen sprint and Classics lineup with Georgia Baker signing
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Canyon-SRAM have announced the signing of former track world champion Georgia Baker from Liv-AlUla-Jayco, the team's third addition for 2027.

Baker joins Swiss duo Jasmin Liechti and Steffi Häberlin on the incoming list for the German team as Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, Maike van der Duin, and the retiring Tiffany Cromwell depart.

32-year-old Baker has experienced success on the track and road during a top-level career which stretches back more than a decade. In 2019, she was part of Australia's World Championship-winning team pursuit lineup, and she's also won two Commonwealth Games golds on the track.

"Georgia brings a very valuable combination of speed, power, versatility and tactical know-how. She has the physical qualities of a sprinter but is also capable of performing in the harder and more technical races," said Canyon-SRAM performance director Dan Fleeman.

He explained that Baker can work in a sprint lead-out train as well as excel in the Classics, where she's collected top-five finishes at Scheldeprijs, the Classic Brugge-De Panne, and Le Samyn over the years.

"She can play an important role in lead-out and positioning work during the final kilometres, putting sprinters in the best possible position, while in the classics, she has the ability to not just survive, but also contribute when the going gets tough.

"Georgia’s versatility is very valuable because it gives us different options depending on how a race develops, and there’s also the potential for her to take her own opportunities when the situation allows."

Baker said that she's excited to take on a new challenge, having spent the last five years at Liv.

"I think I’m most excited by the opportunity for a fresh start and a new challenge. Canyon-SRAM is a team that I’ve always respected from the outside, and I’m really looking forward to learning from a new group of people and hopefully bringing my own experience to the team as well," she said.

"I still love racing my bike, and I still feel like there’s more that I want to achieve. As I’ve gotten older, I think that my motivation has actually evolved. Of course, I still want to win and get the best out of myself, but I also really enjoy being part of a team, helping other riders succeed, and continuing to challenge myself in different ways."
