items.title: Fractured Neck, Broken Collarbone, Relegation: Coppa Bernocchi Crash Takes Heavy Toll
items.author: ahood
items.content: Raccagni could face surgery, Aranburu’s season is over, and Van den Berg loses third after a chaotic, crash-marred final 600 meters at Coppa Bernocchi. And that's not counting a delivery van that drove onto the course.
items.lbText:
Ben Swift, inset, finished with cuts and gashes after a big crash at the end of Coppa Bernocchi. (Photo: Getty Images)

Andrea Raccagni fractured a neck vertebra and Alex Aranburu broke his collarbone and part of his pelvis in a brutal, high-speed crash Monday at the Coppa Bernocchi .

Marijn van den Berg (EF Education-EasyPost) lost his podium place after the race jury relegated him in a messy finale to the Italian classic.

The pileup tore through the bunch about 600 meters from the finish in Legnano as riders were fighting for position ahead of a reduced bunch sprint.

Netcompany-Ineos riders Ben Swift and Filippo Ganna were among those gong down in the crash, and one rider smashed heavily into an unpadded light post.

Swift — who is retiring this season — crossed the line with cuts and gashes, but is still hoping to race Paris-Tours later this month.

Raccagni suffered a fracture of his third cervical vertebra, Soudal Quick-Step confirmed after hospital examinations that included a CT scan. The Italian was scheduled for assessment by surgeons Tuesday.

“He will be assessed by surgeons tomorrow to determine the most appropriate course of treatment and recovery,” the team said in its Monday statement.

Aranburu sustained fractures to his right collarbone and iliac wing, a part of the pelvis, Cofidis announced.

The race jury relegated Van den Berg, who crossed the line third, to 33rd to last in the finishing group after a wild race in the mid-week classic.

Race footage showed the EF Education-EasyPost rider making shoulder contact with eventual winner Noa Isidore (Decathlon-CMA CGM) while moving up on wide roads.

Isidore swerved and made contact with Swift, who fell at speed and brought down several riders behind him. Riders fell into a cement curb and one rider struck a light post at high speed.

Isidore stayed upright and won the ensuing sprint ahead of Tommaso Dati (Team UKYO). Van den Berg’s relegation moved Movistar’s Orluis Aular into third.

items.title: UEC defends accuracy of photo finish at European Championships in response to Giulio Ciccone questioning technology
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
The Italian pleaded to see more proof that he had fallen just millimetres short of the victory on Sunday, having led out the two-up sprint in Slovenia and only been caught on the line by Evenepoel's last-ditch bike throw. His disappointment in Šenčur turned to bewilderment 24 hours later, and he said that "in the filming where the finish line is visible, I keep seeing a dynamic that I cannot reconcile with that verdict."

In the two photo finishes that were released by the organisers, questions were raised due to the distortion of Ciccone's bike size, and the minuscule gap which had Evenepoel pipping him to the line. In information provided to EvoData, the company that did the timing for the Europeans, explained that the time difference was just 0.0002 seconds (0.2 milliseconds), an estimated gap of 2.8 to 3.3 millimetres when translated onto the road.

The UEC explained how the finish line technology works in a press release, stressing that neither a normal camera is used nor a normal photograph is produced at the line, and detailed why the visible distortions have no effect on the accuracy of the result given.

"The Union Européenne de Cyclisme (UEC) states that the photo-finish system used at the 2026 UEC Road European Championships (EtherLynx Vision PRO X) records the finish line thousands of times per second (13,000 in the specific case of the European Championship races), making it possible to determine the order of arrival with extreme precision, even in the event of minimal differences," read the press release.

"It is important to clarify that the photo-finish is not a traditional photograph. The final image is composed of the chronological sequence of recordings taken at the finish line. For this reason, the horizontal axis represents time and not distance.

"This can create apparent distortions of wheels, bicycles and riders, without affecting the accuracy of the result in any way."

Several social media users have tried to buy into Ciccone's theory by examining traditional photos of the finish line, but the gap from the line on the road and the part of the rider's front wheel which crosses the line first is too far apart to accurately determine who arrived first.

Again defending their thorough process, which positions photo finish cameras at either side of the line to verify their accuracy, the UEC looked to move on from the controversy as the Championships continue in Slovenia this week with the time trials.

"In cycling, the decisive reference point is the foremost part (tangent) of the front wheel at the exact moment it crosses the finish line," read the statement.

"At the European Championships, two independent photo-finish systems are used, which provide two separate images for verification of the result.

"The UEC will not issue any further statements on this matter."

items.title: An open field with no Evenepoel or Ganna – Analysing the European Championships elite men's time trial contenders
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Remco Evenepoel may have won the rainbow stripes in Canada to crown himself once again as the world's greatest time trialist, but the Belgian won't be present in Šenčur to go for the European title a third time.

Italian racer Filippo Ganna, who was top dog before Evenepoel came along, won't be present either, while the new cannibal Tadej Pogačar is also out. There's a wide-open field at the elite men's time trial at this year's UEC Road European Championships, then.

44 riders will tackle the 22.1km route in Šenčur, a challenging ride which features a two-in-one climb (2km at 10% and 900 metres at 4.7%) in the middle of the course – a feature which will have an outsized impact on the final result.

Last year's podium sitters Evenepoel, Ganna, and Dane Niklas Larsen aren't racing in Slovenia, so there'll be a trio of new faces atop the podium. There may very well be a first-time champion, too, with double champion Stefan Küng the only rider present to have won this title before.

So who's in the frame for the 2026 European title? Read on to find out.

With the biggest names on the time trial scene not taking part in Tuesday's race, Swiss specialist Stefan Küng looks likely to step into the role of the top favourite for the blue bands of European champion.

He has won the event twice before, in 2020 and 2021, and he has finished on the podium another two times, taking a heartbreaking second place by a single second behind countryman Stefan Bissegger in Fürstenfeldbruck in 2022 and missing out to Edoardo Affini by nine seconds in Hasselt two years later.

The 32-year-old has been in good form recently, having scored his second career Vuelta a España stage victory last month with a two-second victory over Callum Thornley in Jerez de la Frontera on stage 18.

He wasn't on the podium at the Road World Championships, though, finishing in seventh place in the time trial, 1:44 down on world champion Evenepoel, and he also finished 18 seconds behind fellow competitor here, Jakob Söderqvist.

With no Tadej Pogačar in the lineup, Primož Roglič heads into the race as Slovenia's great hope of a result.

The veteran racer has only taken part in one European Championships time trial in his career, finishing 16th at the 2016 Euros. He has fared better at the Worlds, meanwhile, scoring a silver medal the next year behind Tom Dumoulin.

36-year-old Roglič has certainly enjoyed an uptick in form in recent months, racing to second overall at the Vuelta a España, by far his best result of the season. His time trial effort in Jerez de la Frontera saw him place fourth in the 32.1km test, behind Küng and Thornley. He's certainly among the favourites for a medal on the hilly course in Šenčur.

Jakob Söderqvist may only be a neo-pro, but he signed his Lidl-Trek contract as one of the most promising young time trialists in the world. In his final two years before turning pro, the Swede triumphed against the clock at the Worlds under-23 TT, the Flèche du Sud, Giro Next Gen, and under-23 Chrono des Nations, as well as adding Worlds and European silver to his collection.

Söderqvist started his year with a third place in the Volta ao Algarve TT before going on to second places in prologues at the Tour de Romandie and Boucles de la Mayenne, winning the Swedish national title, and, most recently, coming away with fifth place in Montreal, 1:26 off Evenepoel.

At 23, Söderqvist is one of the youngest men in the race, but he's well in the running for a medal.

The first of the two Danish riders on our list, Mikkel Bjerg has twice come close to a medal in the European Championships, finishing 18 seconds adrift of bronze in 2022 and 26 seconds off the following year.

Bjerg hasn't been in the best form of his career this season, with eighth place in the 42km time trial to Massa at the Giro d'Italia his best TT result outside of the Danish Championships. Still, this race represents a better chance at a higher ranking for him, given the top contenders who won't be here.

As with some others on this list, the course isn't particularly to his advantage given the big hill which should be a deciding factor in the outcome of the medal placings. Still, he's a quality time triallist and should be there or thereabouts.

Bruno Armirail is France's main hope, though the 32-year-old is among the outsiders for a medal. His best result to date in three appearances at the Euros is ninth place on home ground last year.

He finished 26th at the recent Worlds time trial in Montreal, but impressed in the stage 16 TT at the Tour de France and in the stage 18 TT at the Vuelta, coming away with eighth and seventh places respectively.

That does suggest somewhat that his strength has been in recovering for those late-race efforts, something which obviously won't apply here in a one-off event.

The second Dane on our list is Kasper Asgreen, who can point to a strong record at this race, having finished in second, seventh, and eighth in three appearances dating back to 2019. His most recent outing came in Hasselt two years ago, where he finished eighth, 1:06 down on the champion Edoardo Affini.

Asgreen's form is looking up as he heads to Slovenia, too, with eighth place at the Montreal (where only Söderqvist and Küng from the Euros startlist finished ahead of him) his outstanding result of the past two seasons. He could be in with a shot at a medal here.

23-year-old Callum Thornley is another young hopeful on the list aiming for a high placing in Šenčur.

The Scottish rider enjoyed a great run of time trial results recently, including third at the Tour de Pologne and fourth and second places at the two Vuelta a España tests, with the second seeing him miss out on the win by just two seconds to Küng.

His most recent outing on the time trial bike saw him take 10th place in Montreal, just over two minutes behind world champion Remco Evenepoel and 18 seconds off Küng. Like Söderqvist, Thornley looks destined to be a top time trial contender for years to come – will either of the young hopefuls hit those heights well ahead of schedule here?

The Netherlands' best hope lies with , whose standout time trial result this season was third place in that 42km Giro time trial. The one-time Dutch TT champion will be competing at the Euros for the second time after finishing 10th in 2023.

With no Filippo Ganna, it's up to to lead Italian hopes. The 35-year-old was recently part of his nation's triumphant ride to mixed relay TTT success at the Worlds, while he finished the individual time trial in 16th place. His ride to sixth place in the hilly late time trial at the Tour de France also stands out in our memory.

is Spain's sole entrant in the time trial. The former national champion and under-23 world champion picked up silver here in the under-23 race three years ago, and he's in good form at the moment, having raced to fifth place in the road race.

Slovenia's second rider comes in the form of , one of eight riders at this race to have finished in the top 20 at Worlds. He was 17th in Montreal, ahead of Hayter and just behind Romeo and Cattaneo. Tratnik has been up there at the Euros before, finishing sixth at the 2020 time trial.

items.title: Brilliant Rays bats, brutal Yankees defense leave Bombers in 2-0 hole
items.author: Jake Devin
items.content:
It’s rare that a hitter feels in full control of a plate appearance. Hitting is an inherently reactive activity, with the pitcher in control of what pitch is thrown, how it’s thrown, where it’s thrown, even when and why it’s thrown. It’s even more difficult for the hitter to feel in control when facing a dominant pitcher, with elite arms attacking the opposition and making them feel as if they’re on the wrong side of an avalanche.

Which makes Monday’s offensive performance from the Rays all that more impressive. Facing the presumptive AL Cy Young Award winner, Tampa’s hitters were in control all night. They made Cam Schlittler sweat, they made him work, and in the end, they made him bleed. The end result was a 5-2 Rays victory, a commanding 2-0 series lead, and another Yankees season on life support.

Schlittler was coming off a stellar performance in a season consisting almost exclusively of stellar performances. He diced up the Red Sox in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, leaning on his curveball in a surprise manuever that left Boston gasping for air. Schlitter’s strategy wasn’t quite as curve heavy this time around, using it 18 percent of the time compared to 27 percent versus Boston, electing to go after Tampa with his trademark high-heat, three-fastball approach.

The Rays were ready. Tampa’s hitters have the flattest swings of any team in the league, which in theory should make them a tough matchup for Schlittler, with their swing paths putting the bat right on plane to make contact with Schlittler’s fastballs. In practice, Schlittler proved unable to overpower them.

Schlittler managed only seven swings and misses, a total he failed to reach just once during this magnificent season. The Rays struck out twice versus the right-hander, the lowest mark all year for Schlittler. Tampa’s hitters just never seemed uncomfortable facing the best pitcher in the American League. They never expanded the zone, rarely found themselves in unfavorable counts, and made hard contact in nearly every inning against Schlittler. The Rays’ swings always seemed to be on time, fair or foul:

And even their takes exuded confidence:

It was a remarkable feat, to stare down the most intimidating pitcher in the league and to force him to blink, not vice versa.

On a day where his defense or offense backed him up, Schlittler still might have been able to make it work, to grind through five or six innings and eek out a win. Instead, New York played one of its sloppiest games ever, tallying a staggering four (later changed by the official scorer from five) errors in the span of six innings, three in the first frame alone. You can thank the Rays’ fast, aggressive play style in part, forcing the Yankee fielders to speed up:

But the Yankees just failed to execute on defense in the most important game of the year, something that has happened before. Ryan McMahon booted the first batted ball of the game, Jazz Chisholm Jr. threw a ball away on an ill-fated attempt to turn two in the first, and in the fifth, George Lombard Jr. a committed a fielding error and also a throwing error that was later changed to a fielder’s choice, helping the Rays along to their four-run outburst that ultimately sealed the game.

Played under the haunting dome of Tropicana Field, it felt like the quintessential Rays game. They refused to strike out, put the ball into the field of play, and put pressure on the Yankees to make plays, pressure the Yankees wilted under. This strategy doesn’t work all the time (remember, the Yankees both scored more and allowed fewer runs than the Rays this year), but when it does work, it can make the opponent look silly for trying to win any other way. If you squint, the Yankees really have won their way; in a 1-1 ballgame with the bases loaded in the fifth, Cody Bellinger hit a ball 103 mph off the bat at a 27 degree angle, a combination that produced a home run 57 percent of the time in the regular season:

But Bellinger’s particular batted ball was to the deepest part of the park, and it settled into Jonny DeLuca’s glove a foot in front of the wall. If Bellinger could have pulled the ball just a little more, if he swung just barely harder, the Yankees could have been the team that surged ahead 5-1. Instead, Bellinger was left with nothing but a loud out, and the Yankees imploded in the next half-inning.

Outside of the continued brilliance of Ben Rice, there’s just not much to hang your hat on here. The Rays executed about as well as they possibly could given the circumstances, and the Yankees couldn’t have played much worse. New York returns to the Bronx deservedly trailing 2-0 in the ALDS for the second season in a row, having been undressed on the road by a division rival each time. As dire as it seems now, the season isn’t over; we all remember what happened in Game 3 last year. But we also remember what happened in Game 4, which underscores how deep of a hole the Yankees find themselves in yet again. They’ll need to find a minor miracle and pull out three in a row against Tampa Bay, or else find themselves trudging once more into the cold winter.

On the site today, Jeremy names the Yankees player of the game from Game 2, which had only one possible choice. Also, Madison recaps the White Sox/Guardians matchup from yesterday, Jonathan profiles Ruben Sierra for our Yankee Birthday series, and Peter delivers his At-bat of the Week, which features George Lombard Jr.

There are plenty of cycling deals, some better than others, but one of the best I've seen so far is on the Cycplus AS2 Electric Pump, which has dropped from £59.99 to under £50 for the first time – its best-ever price.

As deal-hunting expert and a long-time fan of the Cycplus range, the AS2 is easily one of the best electric pumps I've used. It even earned a spot in our buying guide as our top recommendation for hassle-free, non-manual inflation.

Below you'll find all the details, and I'd advise moving quickly, because when Prime Day ends at midnight on the 7th October, so will these deals.

The Cycplus AS2 offers game-changing electric pumping. Weighing just 97 grams, it's small enough to fit in a jersey pocket or saddle bag and eliminates the effort of manual mini-pumps. Capable of reaching up to 100 PSI and recharging via fast USB-C, it offers a fast, painless solution for fixing roadside punctures without adding unnecessary bulk to your ride setup.View Deal

The AS2 Pro takes electric tyre inflation a step further by adding a digital LED display for real-time pressure monitoring and customizable PSI target presets. Weighing 120 grams, it remains exceptionally compact while offering a higher maximum pressure of 120 PSI and a larger battery for faster inflation times. It also has an auto-shutoff function once the desired pressure is reached.View Deal

The AS2 Pro's headline feature is the large LED screen, with a pressure gauge function, allowing for easy reading of preset pressure values and real-time readings. For US Prime Day, it's available at one of its lowest-ever prices.View Deal

The main difference between the AS2 and the AS2 Pro lies in control and power: while the original Cycplus AS2 is an ultra-lightweight (97g) single-button inflator with no screen, the AS2 Pro adds a digital LED display that lets you set precise target pressures with a handy auto-shutoff. So if you require precise pressure, the Pro model is the way to go.

The Pro version also boosts maximum output from 100 to 120 PSI and inflates faster thanks to a larger battery.

There are a few drawbacks to be aware of when using any electric pumps. They can get quite hot when using them, so you need to be aware when using inner tubes with plastic valves, because they can melt. If you still use inner tubes, the AS2 range comes with a heat-protective extension hose to alleviate this, and a heat reducing protective sleeve, but be aware they don't get that hot when held in your hand.

They have to be charged too, so remember to do that before heading out.

In my opinion, the positives outweigh those negatives, and the convenience of use, precise pressure levels (especially with the Pro model and its LED screen), and the lack of effort when it's required are all box-tickers for me.

items.title: Want to go Strava-free? The Cateye Padrone is a brilliantly simple bike computer, and it's under £40 for Amazon Prime Day
items.author: Emily Tillett
items.content:
The best bike computers can do almost everything and are now packed with technology to track your ride data, offer maps for navigation, and even provide advanced features such as health monitoring, custom training plans and additional safety features.

Of course, there's nothing wrong with any of those things, but what about cyclists who want a low-tech option that skips the bells and whistles?

That's where the Cateye Padrone comes in, and it takes a very different approach to many modern bike computers. There's no GPS, no smartphone connectivity and no Strava integration - just an easy-to-read screen showing the basics, including speed, distance and ride time.

In our review, Immy Sykes gave it 4 out of 5 stars, praising its simplicity and the distraction-free riding experience it offers.

To access Amazon Prime deals, you'll need a Prime membership. You can sign up for a and cancel anytime before the $14.99 per month fee kicks in.

Cateye has been making bike computers since the early 1980s, so it knows a thing or two about what works. The Padrone is a great example, offering a simple but well-designed cycling computer.

At 67.5 x 43.0 x 14.5mm, it’s small enough to be discreet, but not so small that you’re having to squint from your position in the saddle. The easy-to-read screen remains clear even in bright sunlight.

The device detects movement and automatically starts and stops, so you don't even need to remember to switch it on. It's then easy to glance down and check your current or average speed, without getting drawn into a sea of data. Sometimes, that's all you really need.

If you’re a weight weenie, you’re in for a treat too. At only 31.6g, the Padrone is one of the lightest bike computers you’re likely to find.

As for battery life, the simplicity continues. The Padrone is powered by a small battery that lasts approximately a year with one hour of use per day, so there are no charging cables or extra accessories to worry about - or inevitably lose.

If you ride regularly in unfamiliar places, are heavily invested in training metrics or want seamless integration across multiple platforms, then you may want to look elsewhere. But if you want simple metrics for a distraction-free ride, great battery life and a reliable interface, all in a lightweight and affordable package, the Cateye Padrone is a great pick.

This UK-only deal saves you 31%, bringing the price down to just over £38.

items.title: Yankees news: Youth Movement in the Bronx
items.author: John Griffin
items.content:
MLB.com: Yesterday afternoon, Major League Baseball announced the finalists for this year’s Hank Aaron Award. Recognizing the two best offensive performances (one in each league), the award is conferred through a fan vote and a panel consisting of journalists and former players. Yankees first baseman/designated hitter Ben Rice finds himself as one of this year’s finalists, hoping to make it the three straight season (and fourth in five years) that a Yankees slugger takes home the award (Aaron Judge won it in 2022, 2024, and 2025). Other nominees include Baltimore’s Pete Alonso, Houston’s Yordan Alvarez (the likely favorite), and Kansas City’s Bobby Witt Jr.

The Athletic | Clark Gilmore: Clarke Gilmore, a current member of the Savannah Bananas and a former teammate of Ben Rice at Dartmouth, penned a guest article for ’s Peak newsletter, a series focusing on the mental side of sports. As you might have guessed based on the nature of the series, Gilmore spoke not about Rice’s physical prowess, but on his “consistency” that dated back to his college days — and could be seen not only on the diamond, but in much more mundane things, such as Mario Kart in the dorms.

FanGraphs | Matt Martell: Turning our attention from one Massachusetts boy to another, Cam Schlittler came out with a completely unexpected strategy against the Red Sox in Game 1 of the ALWC: the typically fastball-dominant youngster threw 32 curveballs — a whopping 27.4 percent of the time (during the regular season, he threw it just 9.8 percent of the time). The start was the culmination of a year-long process in which the Cy Young favorite working to turn his curveball into a veritable weapon, one that can can make him a dangerous pitcher not just now, but going forward.

items.title: The Kenda Velora Tire Review: Modern Endurance Road
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The new premium road offering from Kenda brings a lot more puncture protection and improved speed to its endurance platform.
items.lbText:
Kenda has launched the Velora Endurance, a new set of endurance road tires that offer a premium feel with a range of puncture-resistant long-haul options.

The Velora brings durability and low rolling resistance to the table, with Kenda claiming major improvements in puncture protection and watts saved over its previous models. The model also comes in three sizes: 28, 32, and 35 mm.

With Kenda’s re-entry into the premium endurance tire market—in addition to other tires like the Silca Protocol RCR —the 32-40 mm range for all-road tires is quickly filling out. Not too long ago, that range of tires was a quirky grey area between road and gravel, but now it serves as another area of the industry where there are scores of good options.

Read on to see how the Kenda Velora Endurance fits into the mix. Hint: it’s one of the better options available.

While the Velora Endurance brings new options to the endurance/all-road tire market, Kenda is taking a fairly traditional approach overall with this model. It’s built, first and foremost, for durability.

That durability is derived primarily from the puncture-resistant base layer of the tire casing. Instead of loading puncture-resistance features into the entire tread, the base layer runs just along the center of the tread. This keeps the tire weight low and the tire relatively thin, despite the 35 percent improvement in the center tread’s ability to withstand debris and detritus.

While the Velora prioritizes the same puncture resistance as previous endurance tires, it is still a big evolution from the heavy, plodding endurance tires of years past. Kenda pairs the endurance-oriented puncture-resistant base layer with a premium rubber compound that is much more pitched towards speed.

To find this speed, the Velora uses the new K-Series rubber compound that has been slowly rolled out across several of Kenda’s recent new releases. That new rubber compound has been specifically formulated for performance on tarmac and yields a significant 12-watt reduction in rolling resistance compared to the previous Kenda endurance tire.

While Kenda also claims better rolling resistance compared to unnamed competitors, there is no third-party data yet for the tire’s overall rolling efficiency.

That being said, that compound is built to be both fast and durable. Kenda claims that the Velora Endurance is very wear-resistant, with a 27 percent reduction in tread degradation compared to the brand’s previous endurance tires. You could say the Velora is built for endurance in more ways than just long rides.

Lastly, while the tire is firmly a road tire, it does have prominent shoulder “siping” that runs in clusters along the tire. Those sipes, which are thin grooves cut into the shoulder of the tire, are specifically designed to help boost traction in wet environments. The grooves help funnel water away from the broad, slick center tread, which boosts traction especially on slick corners. The siping also helps add a bit of traction in dry conditions when riding on light, loose-over-hard conditions.

Over the last month, I have been able to put a few hundred miles on the 32 and 35mm versions of the Velora Endurance tires, and I have been very pleased with how the tires feel and perform in the right circumstances.

Personally, I felt more of a draw to the 35mm option as there are just fewer great options at that width. Additionally, as tires have gotten bigger, 30-32 mm is the range of width I use for race tires, so testing the 32mm—let alone the 28mm—just didn’t feel like it made much sense. Instead, having a nice 35mm endurance tire was the perfect pair for some adventures on the new Trek Domane, a modern endurance bike with clearance up to 40mm.

Would I have loved to try the Velora in 38-40 mm? Absolutely, but unfortunately, Kenda cut things off at 35mm. Nevertheless, I found the 35s had a great balance of versatility, reliability, and speed that really surprised me.

Out of the box, the Velora Endurance tires do look and feel like endurance tires. They have more structure, they feel on the heavier side, and the center tread is notably a bit thicker and more rigid than a pure road racing tire. But even with those attributes, the sidewalls felt fairly flexible. When I was mounting it onto the rim, the tire also felt more similar to a good racing tire than a rigid, heavier endurance tire.

Speaking of weight, the Velora is certainly no featherweight, but it holds its own. At 370g for the 35mm, the tire is about middle of the pack—similar to the Specialized Mondo, lighter than the Pirelli P-Zero, and heavier than the Silca RCR.

After the installation, I found that the tire felt alive straight away. There wasn’t any of the stiffness you might get from a tire with thick, new rubber. Instead, it rolled pretty fast and handled well, with the tire holding its structure even at a relatively low 50 PSI of pressure. One of my nitpicks with mid-width slicks is how inconsistent they can feel. The heavier, thicker tires can be too rigid and can be harsh and bouncy, neither of which inspires much confidence during cornering or at speed. Others are too light, and those can feel muddled and squishy at “all-road” pressure—even worse for confidence.

The Velora Endurance has a good balance between rigidity and suppleness. My guess is that comes from the tire’s split personality, with a fast rubber compound and strong-but-narrow puncture protection creating an effective pairing for that balanced handling.

The out-and-out speed of the tire is where things are less clear. The big test for the tire’s speed was a long Saturday group ride that functions a bit like a segmented race. The first two efforts are both uphill drags, a perfect scenario to feel a tire’s overall speed, before I would set off on my own up a gravel road and a long, steep gravel climb to test the all-road chops of the tire.…

items.title: Aleix Espargaro back to MotoGP in latest Honda shuffle
items.author: Simon Patterson
items.content:
Honda test rider Aleix Espargaro will return to MotoGP action at this weekend’s Indonesian Grand Prix, replacing fellow test rider Taka Nakagami as stand-in for the unwell Joan Mir.

Espargaro has been drafted in because Nakagami crashed out on his very first lap of the weekend last time out at Motegi and broke his collarbone.

Espargaro’s return to action doesn’t just mark his first time racing since last year’s season finale at Valencia, but it's one of the few times he'll ride a MotoGP machine since a private test crash at Sepang in April left the three-time race winner with a career-threatening shattered back.

He fell during a private outing alongside Nakagami at the Malaysian circuit earlier this year, breaking four vertebrae and needing to be medically evacuated back to Spain before requiring multiple surgeries to stabilise the fractures. 

“It is always a great honour to join the factory Honda team in MotoGP,” said Espargaro in a team statement. "I want to say thank you to them for trusting me to ride while Joan and Taka recover. 

“After the crash at the start of the year and my injury, I have not had as much time on the bike as I would like, and we travel to Mandalika with realistic expectations as I’ve had only a small number of laps and it’s a really physical track before we even speak about the weather. 

“Let’s understand how we can best help the team and Honda this weekend and focus on that.”

The former Aprilia racer spent the opening months of the year focused on Honda’s current RC213V machine, splitting duties with Nakagami while the Japanese rider concentrated on their new 2027-spec 850cc Pirelli-mounted machine until he was forced to take on double duty as test rider for both machines.

That saw him joining the factory team at the Austrian Grand Prix to replace Mir before heading to Japan as a scheduled wildcard on the current 1000cc machine, with Somkiat Chantra deputising for Mir before returning to his regular Honda World Superbike duties this weekend.

However, with Nakagami now out of action thanks to the broken collarbone he sustained at Motegi one week ago during that wildcard outing with Honda’s test team, it may well mean that Espargaro has been briefed to take it easy this weekend at Mandalika.

Another crash would leave Honda in dire straits in the final few months of development for the new bike before handing it over to their 2027 race team.

There has been no further update from Honda on Mir’s condition, with the team reporting before the Japanese Grand Prix that he continued to recuperate at home under the care of his medical team as he undergoes "a series of tests" with "the goal to uncover the root cause of a variety of symptoms the Honda HRC Castrol rider has been suffering from for several months".

items.title: Wet races and why future of F1 engines appears to be V8 turbos - Q&A
items.content: <article>BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.</article>
items.lbText:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won his first race of the season in a dramatic rain-affected Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Kimi Antonelli finished second in the Mercedes and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who fought his way back to the front after an incorrect tyre choice at the start, completed the podium.

Antonelli extended his lead in the championship to 84 points, after team-mate George Russell retired with an engine failure.

This weekend, it's the Singapore Grand Prix - Formula 1's original night race.

Before the race at Marina Bay, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Do we miss out on exciting wet-weather racing because an overly cautious approach is applied when rain occurs prior to the start of the race? We are watching the best drivers in the world, who have wet tyres, but it seems when it rains prior to the start of a race, the action gets under way too late. - Sam

This question comes up a lot whenever there is a wet race, but in this specific situation the delay in starting the race was not caused by any conservatism when it comes to wet running.

The cars were sent out on formation laps when the track was still pretty wet on Sunday in Malaysia, but then a bug in the wet-weather engine settings provided to the teams by the FIA affected a number of cars, including those of Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton on the front row.

That meant the formation laps had to be aborted, and a new code written and given to the teams to upload to ensure that did not happen again.

It just so happened that in the intervening 25 minutes, there had been no more rain, so the track was pretty dry by the time the race started. Although it has to be said that it took a safety car on lap nine before the drivers who had started on treaded intermediate tyres came in for slicks.

On a generic level, there is no fundamental objection in F1 to racing in the wet - most of the drivers enjoy it. But there is now a collective agreement that they will not race when they can't see where they are going.

So races are not started when that is the case - as it was at the original start time in Malaysia.

But if you cast your mind back to Brazil in 2024, and Verstappen's brilliant drive from 17th on the grid to victory, that was run in wet conditions.

F1 needs to have hard look at itself - Sainz

After the Bahrain Grand Prix, Lewis Hamilton said that, had he started on the intermediate tyres, he could have won the race. Given the race data and his pace, do you think that's a realistic claim had Ferrari put him on the inters at the start? - Michael

The truth is that Hamilton - and anyone else - will never know, because there was no direct comparison between his pace and Max Verstappen's in similar conditions.

In the first few laps, Hamilton was on slicks and Verstappen on intermediates. When Verstappen switched to slicks, Hamilton's tyres were much older.

On the very few laps when Hamilton was in clear air before he caught Isack Hadjar, his pace when generally nowhere near Verstappen's but then his tyres were nine laps older, so you would not expect it to be.

And then once he finally passed Hadjar, there were only three laps to go.

On one of them, Hamilton was within 0.1secs of Verstappen, on the other two he was 0.5secs and 1.2secs off. But how much were either of them pushing?

What we can say is that Verstappen looked imperious all weekend, and it was probably going to be difficult for anyone to beat him - even Hamilton, who, it's worth saying, on Saturday was not sounding that confident of challenging him.

But it's just a whole load of ifs, buts and maybes, isn't it?

Malaysia, true to form, brought a great race, chaos and weather. It was sold out. Fans have loved it, missed it, drivers liked the track. We know why it dropped off the calendar but what would it take to come back permanently? - Nick

Malaysia dropped off the calendar because the government there was no longer willing to pay the rights fee, feeling that the expense did not justify the return.

It returned only because the Crown Prince of Bahrain was keen to stage his race, F1 was happy to accommodate him, and he managed to strike a deal with the Malaysian government.

There's no doubt the race was a success. It had a record crowd of 261,000 this year, more than double the previous largest weekend attendance of 126,690, reflecting F1's growth around the world.

If Malaysia was keen on returning to the calendar on a more permanent basis, there is no reason why F1 would not listen to them.

But whether that led to a deal would depend on whether one could be struck that satisfied both parties.

With Red Bull running their own powertrains, what part does Ford play? - John

Max Verstappen's victory in Malaysia on Sunday was not only a landmark because it was Red Bull's first of the season - it was also their first as a power-unit manufacturer.

Red Bull Powertrains was set up specifically to make an engine for the new 2026 regulations, so the team could be in control of their own destiny following Honda's official withdrawal from F1 at the end of 2021.

Ford came on board as a partner early on, and this is much more than simply a badging deal in return for finance/sponsorship money.

Team principal Laurent Mekies said on Monday: "Ford has been with us on this project since pretty much the very beginning.

"They are a key strategic partner for us on these operations. They are helping us on a number of topics.

"Specifically, to give you a few examples, they are manufacturing some of the key elements of the engines.

"So, some of these key elements are manufactured in Milton Keynes (at the Red Bull campus), some of these key elements are manufactured at Ford. And they are a 200,000-people company. And therefore, also in terms of engineering, if and when we need specific support on some topics, we are able to get access to some very good specialists they have.…

items.title: The action Mercedes can take over confusing F1 upgrade
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Mercedes is keeping all options on the table, including running a potential back-to-back test with its old package in Singapore, to try to understand why its latest Formula 1 upgrade did not deliver the step forward hoped for.

However, rather than unleashing a predicted 0.3-second gain in laptime, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff wondered if it had actually resulted in a step back of up to 0.5 seconds as rival Red Bull took its first victory of the season with Max Verstappen.

Mercedes was at a loss to explain why improvements being shown on the data in terms of extra downforce were not manifesting themselves in the laptimes.

And it was particularly perplexed about why the gains it had made in high-speed corners had come at the cost of low-speed performance, and had appeared to impact its straightline speed as well.

The key answer Mercedes needs from what happened in Malaysia is how much of its performance deficit was down to the new package and how much of it was down to the unique circumstances of the Sepang event - with high temperatures and a rough track surface.

As world championship leader Kimi Antonelli said: "That's the question we need to answer because we don't really know if it made us go faster or worse.

"It's fair to say, this season that whenever we went on really old Tarmacs, we've struggled.

"For example, in Zandvoort, McLaren was much quicker than us, especially on the older Tarmac. So, I think maybe it's just a question that the Tarmac is just very old and that for the tyres it's very, very hard, and maybe we just struggle on this kind of Tarmac."

While the track surface could explain its problems in slow corners, it would not have impacted its top speed.

But deputy team principal Bradley Lord thought this was probably mostly related to extra downforce added to the car having resulted in more drag.

"That's probably one of the lesser question marks," he said. "We know that adding downforce that brings with it drag, and the calculation is that what you gain in the corners will outweigh what you lose down the straights.

"We've seen what we're expecting there, we're seeing the benefit in the high-speed corners and the medium-speed - and the drivers say they can feel it as well. 

"But there's no doubt that we've struggled in certain corners all weekend, particularly the slower ones."

Lord later said in Mercedes' post-weekend debrief: "The combination potentially of updates, track temperature and track surface caused an interaction, a set of behaviours that meant the car was not in its usual happy state, that the drivers were having to turn the car on the throttle in the slow corners. That was further exacerbating the challenges of tyre temperatures.

"So that's not an easy thing to unpick. It's a bit of a 3D problem that we need to work through, and then figure out exactly what steps we take going forward to make sure that we've got the base understanding we need to understand that the update is working well and that we're heading in the right direction in our development, not just for this year's car, but for next year as well."

Mercedes is set for some intense engineering debriefs over the next few days to try to get to the bottom of what happened in Malaysia, and work out how best to get answers for this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.

It is understood that the squad is open-minded about how best to tackle the issue and that nothing is off the table right now.

One possibility to fast-track an answer about what has happened could be to run the Mercedes cars in different configurations in practice in Singapore so it can gather real-world data about the gains and losses from the new upgrade.

If it concludes that the upgrade has not worked, then it is not ruling out rolling back on it long term despite the logistical complications that would cause.

Equally, Mercedes could ultimately conclude that the Malaysia showing was a one-off caused by the heat and track surface, and it sticks to pushing on with the new parts on both cars.

What Mercedes does for Singapore depends on what conclusions are found early this week. There's also the added complication of Singapore being a sprint event with only one practice session on Friday.

Lord said: "There are many things to unpick. We've seen some teams without upgrades take a step forward this weekend.

"Other upgraded teams have taken a step forward, while [some other] teams that have upgrades have performed less well than we might have expected.

"We're not the only people with some questions to answer as we leave the weekend. But certainly we've got to unpick what is down to what and understand if that has any implications on how we head into Singapore and the remaining six races after that."

items.title: Yankees make a million errors, drop Game 2 of the ALDS to Tampa
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
I hate Tropicana Field. I know many of you do too. If you are not a Yankees fan and are doing what I am also guilty of doing—reading the reactions of salty fans after playoff losses—grab your popcorn. This is the good stuff you’re probably looking for.

It blows my mind that baseball games in 2026 are played at places like this. It honestly blows my mind even more that this place was destroyed by an act of God two years ago, was rebuilt despite plans to replace it in the near future, and is being used for big playoff games. The roof is baseball-colored; there is statistical proof that teams other than the Rays struggle defensively here due to a lack of experience; the turf leads to weird hops that cause more errors to be committed against Tampa Bay than any other team in baseball. It’s the strangest home-field advantage in baseball, and one that the Rays ran roughshod over to take advantage of a Yankees team that was just not focused from the jump tonight—and one that, to be clear, absolutely deserved this atrocious loss, even if it was played in the baseball version of Elysian Fields.

Alright, enough of my anger-filled soapbox. The Yanks set the tone for this one with three brutal first-inning errors, played shoddy defense the rest of the night, and just got Rays’d. Any opportunity they had to use their speed or slap hitting, they used it. The Yankees were not prepared. Aside from two home runs from Ben Rice and an oh-so-close deep fly out from Cody Bellinger with the bases juiced, the offense was dead again in a 5-2 loss that puts the season on the brink.

When you get no-hit for nearly eight innings the game before, you desperately want to get the monkey off your back early the next night. The quality of contact was good in that first inning against Freddy Peralta, with a warning-track fly out from Rice and a scorched Bellinger lineout, but the Yankees went quietly in the first before the utter chaos of the bottom half.

On just Cam Schlittler’s second pitch of the game, Yandy Díaz hit a soft Trop chopper to Ryan McMahon, which he promptly booted after misreading the hop. Jonathan Aranda then lined a single up the middle for the one real hit in the inning. Needing a double play, Schlittler got Junior Caminero to spike a ball into the turf that was snared by George Lombard Jr. for a brilliant flip for a forceout. Unfortunately, Jazz Chisholm Jr. decided to throw the ball into the dugout with no chance to turn two, giving the Rays the early lead.

The defensive inning from hell continued when a three-pitch strikeout from Liam Hicks was overturned into a catcher’s interference error on Austin Wells. Awarding a batter a base for a check-swing catcher’s interference is dumb, and I will forever believe that. The speedy Chandler Simpson ripped a ball to second for what looked like a tailor-made double play, but an awful throw from Chisholm pulled Lombard off the bag. The rookie shortstop somehow managed to tap the bag after to avoid a fourth error in the inning, and Cam survived the inning from hell with only one run allowed.

We got more Trop shenanigans when Spencer Jones hit a ball a mile high off the B-ring in center field, which was caught by Victor Mesa Jr. Objectively, almost every other team drops that ball because of their lack of experience reading fly balls here, but the Rays caught it, naturally. Two more quick outs had Peralta rolling through two.

Jonny DeLuca golfed an 0-2 curveball in the dirt for a leadoff double in the second, but was stranded on a trio of groundouts surrounding a two-out walk. The bottom of the order went down quietly as well, giving Peralta a perfect game through three innings just one night after Rasmussen’s brilliance. At this point, I’m not sure the vibes could get much worse.

Schlittler continued to grind through the third, allowing singles to Caminero and Simpson, but got out of a jam after a 108.5 mph scorched grounder from DeLuca was fielded cleanly by Lombard to end the threat. Just one batter later, with the Yankees entering their 13th inning of the series with just one hit, Rice allowed everyone on the team and in the fanbase to breathe for a second, smashing a leadoff home run in the fourth to tie the game at one.

Bellinger followed with a single, but was stranded by the next three hitters. Schlittler responded to the desperate gasp for a shutdown inning, retiring the Rays in order with help from a surprisingly solid play by Trent Grisham in center field. Peralta seemed to be cruising again after retiring the first two in the fifth, but things got interesting after a bullet double by Austin Wells and a gritty walk by Ryan McMahon. The ever-aggressive Kevin Cash pulled him for Cam Booser, betting on his lefty specialist to neutralize the best hitters on the team.

He walked Rice on five pitches to bring up Bellinger with the bases loaded. This was the moment. This was where the Yankees could show who they were. For a brief second, it seemed like they would. The All-Star left fielder absolutely pummeled a bad 0-2 fastball to deep center field. 102.9 mph, 405 feet. In 12 ballparks, it’s a grand slam. In some others, it’s off the wall. Unfortunately, as has happened all too many times in the postseason in the Judge era, the big hit fell just a few inches short, landing harmlessly in the glove of DeLuca.

It’s the type of gut punch that takes the air out of a fan, and maybe it took the air out of the team. It’s not how baseball works, but maybe it is. Schlittler allowed a bullet single (that Jones maybe should’ve caught?) and a bullet double from Caminero to set up second and third with nobody out. Usually, a team’s cleanup and five-hole hitters wouldn’t be conducive to 55 and 65 mph choppers that bounce two feet in front of home plate in RBI opportunities, but these are the Rays. Both runs scored on back-to-back Baltimore chops that the Yankees had no chance of getting an out at the plate on, even if Lombard had defended the latter cleanly. That gave the Rays a 3-1 lead.

The frustration didn’t end there. After Brent Headrick entered and struck out Mesa, we got another Trop chop grounder to Lombard. Due to the bounce the ball took and the speed of DeLuca, he had to rush the throw, which forced a long stretch from Luis García Jr. If the play was made cleanly, DeLuca would’ve been out by an eyelash, which tells you how perfect they had to be, but García couldn’t squeeze the throw, and everyone was safe. Another error. One batter later, Richie Palacios hit a two-run single to effectively ice this one, making it 5-1 Rays.

We then hit a weird point in the game. Ian Seymour came in for the Rays as a lefty bulk reliever, but Aaron Boone elected to keep his righties in the dugout. As a fan who was resigned to the outcome after the Palacios single, it seems like nothing, but damn, that’s pretty rough of your manager to be so apathetic in this spot. The lineup had no pulse against him in some rough matchups.

Playing out the string, John Schreiber tossed a scoreless sixth, Ryan Weathers and Paul Blackburn combined for the seventh, and Blackburn and David Bednar combined for the ninth. For the offense, all they had left was another home run for Rice, who continues to have a postseason to remember while his teammates give him no help, like 2018 LeBron.

Bryan Baker got the save in the ninth, 1-2-3, to solidify Game 2 for the Rays. If the Yankees want to win this series and get to the ALCS, they must win three straight against a team they’ve struggled against all year and win a game at Tropicana Field on Saturday after going 2-7 there to start this season. We’re essentially right back where we were a year ago with the Yankees down 0-2 and leaving Toronto. Bleak, I know.

There will be baseball played on Wednesday. After that, it’s up to the Yankees to decide. Game 3 will be at Yankee Stadium at 8 pm EDT. It’s Max Fried (pending the birth of his child) against a pitcher to be determined, but it will likely be Nick Martinez.

items.title: True grit specialists primed to challenge the run of road pro rainbow jerseys – Analysing the Gravel World Championships contenders
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
The 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships casts a spotlight on Western Australia this weekend, the first time the race for rainbows has ventured outside Europe. The rugged territory around Nannup is quite opposite, geographically and literally, of Classics-style races held across four previous editions.

There was a buzz among the dedicated off-road riders when organisers announced a course that would be dictated by wide, hard-paced dirt roads and cross rugged forests. Maybe this was the year most suited to a gravel rider, rather than another ride for WorldTour pros. The table was set, now who would commit to long-distance travel to enjoy the feast?

The cost and time to travel to Western Australia has kept some away this year and the quantity of riders will be lower this year in the elite fields but that also means that those who are making the trip are doing so with intent, rather than making a last minute decision to work it into their schedule for a day.

There's also nearly triple the amount of climbing as compared to last year in the Netherlands, the women's 125.5km contest going from 1,190 metres of elevation gain to 3,179 metres. The elite men will cover 144km with a similar bump in climbing that now totals 3,713 metres. And don't forget about the technical descents.

However, there is no lack of quality for the elite fields, most of the riders well versed in the unpredictable off-road races provided by UCI Gravel World Series, Gravel Earth Series and Life Time Grand Prix, among the leading collectives.

Two of the top riders from the Life Time Grand Prix return to the Worlds for gravel - Keegan Swenson (USA) and Sofia Gomez Villafane (Argentina) - having passed on races in Belgium and the Netherlands the last two years. Mountain bike and gravel specialist Matt Beers (South Africa) returns for the first time since 2022. The overall winners of the Gravel Earth Series are also in the lineups, Geerike Schreurs for the Netherlands, and Mads Wurtz Schmidt (Denmark).

Also back in action are last year's winner Florian Vermeersch (Belgium), and 2024 gravel world champion Marianne Vos (Netherlands), both who have been on the podium multiple times.

The home charge of six Australian women will include Oceania gravel champion Nicole Frain and gravel national champion Tiffany Cromwell, kicking up the gravel on Saturday morning. There are 11 Aussie men for their Sunday race, led by gravel national champion Cameron Scott, and 2025 national champion and SEVEN winner Mark O'Brien.

Here's a look at some of the versatile riders who are expected to make the right moves and turn the dirt roads into gold.

From the moment the name Sofia Gomez Villafañe popped up as a confirmed starter, it was hard to imagine that anyone who would enter could knock her far from the top of the favourites list. It's not that she has a stunning history at this event specifically – although she did finish a more-than-respectable 12th at the first edition in 2022 and came 34th when she last raced in 2023 – but her record outside the UCI-sanctioned domain is something to behold. The Argentinian-born rider has won Unbound Gravel 200 and The Traka 200 twice and claimed the Life Time Grand Prix series three times. It took more than half a season for her gravel winning streak to be disrupted this season.

It's understandable, however, that the UCI Gravel World Championships hasn't been high on her priority list in recent years between a Life Time Grand Prix Series clash, terrain that certainly didn't play into her hands, and a field packed with road riders that would be positioned near the front of the grid. Villafañe's haul of non-UCI wins may be heavy in gravel prestige but only gave her minimal UCI points and therefore poor positioning. Still, she did gather 200 points this year some from her win at Castellón, which is part of the UCI Gravel World Series.

Even with only a small number of points to soften the start situation it looks to be a World Gravel Championships that will play to the strengths of the top gravel specialists, with more gravel than ever before and an unrelenting series of challenging climbs. She may not start at the front of the field, but there is every chance in Nannup that is where she will end up. (SG)

A former champion on the start line of a World Championship always deserves respect, but that goes tenfold for one named Marianne Vos.

With 13 other world titles to her name, a second at this event last year along with her win in 2024, there is no question that the Dutch rider heads to the start line in Western Australia with a considerable claim on a favourite slot. What's more, her talent across the disciplines is a real asset when it comes to the large gravel World Championships fields, where road tactics can come into play as well as the skills to handle the sometimes tricky terrain. Vos has both the bike-handling skills, knowledge, experience and comfort in the field to conserve energy when she needs it most. What's more, she is one of the few international riders that will also be in familiar territory, having once been a regular at the Tour of Margaret River which ran in the area.

Add to that the unrelentingly competitive nature of the Dutch superstar in the discipline, and you can be sure she is hankering for a win after a season where they have been thin on the ground. If she comes to the finish line in a reduced group, she'll be hard to beat so her rivals are bound to work hard to drop her on the climbs before. (SG)

Since totally committing to gravel at the start of last season, Nicole Frain has made clear just how capable she is in the off-road discipline. The 2022 Australian road champion has combined her skills developed in the peloton with an ability to ride in the 'grey zone' and keep pushing hard through the race to find ample success. In fact she finished at the very top of the UCI Gravel World Series overall in 2025 and this year has captured the Oceania Championships and four UCI Gravel World Series race wins. She was 26th in the Gravel World Championships last year but it wasn't really a course that played to her strengths.

This year's addition of more gravel and climbing will suit Frain, however the extent of it could push her to the limits of her ascending abilities. Still, not surprisingly – given it is a home World Championships for Frain – she has put a target on the event and has been tracking along well in training towards it, despite a nasty bout of the flu along the way. Plus she is well aware of what she is in for having carved out the time to do a course reconnaissance earlier this year.

Her road background works in her favour to help her manage the ebb and flow of the more peloton-driven dynamic that is usually surfaces more heavily at the race than many other gravel events, but despite that her emphasis on developing the technical skills and gravel focus will give her another advantage. On top of that, she will be lining up right near the front, given she's sitting just one spot away from the top of the UCI Gravel World Series standings. (SG)

One of the most versatile riders among elite women in Nannup is Rosa Klöser. The Canyon-SRAM WorldTour road rider competed at the Tour de France Femmes this year, supporting runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma, and framed the road stage race with gravel wins at The Traka 360 and Sea Otter Europe. Her lead into her fourth Gravel World Championships saw her win a climbing-heavy Pyrénées Catalanes Gravel Tour, and outdistance runner-up Nicole Frain by 15 minutes.

She has competed in three Unbound Gravel 200 races and finished fifth or better, with the victory in 2024. This year she earned points on a debut in the invitation-only Life Time Grand Prix. However, she failed to finish Leadville Trail 100 MTB in August, riding in fifth position when she flatted with 14km to go and eight plugs later could not continue. She pulled out of the Grand Prix knowing that she could not compete at other races.

Germany brings a strong squad to Australia, with proven gravel riders Romy Kasper, Nele Laing, Jade Treffeisen and another Unbound Gravel 200 winner, Carolin Schiff, alongside the 30-year-old Canyon rider. If the squad can form an alliance and work for an in-form Klöser, then she has a good chance for redemption ride in Nannup to heal any Grand Prix wounds. (JT)

'Gee' Schreurs has had her most successful season yet in off-road racing in 2026, winning a trio of Gravel Earth Series events for the series overall title. She also rode to a second career win at the Gralloch and took hard-fought podiums at Unbound Gravel 200 and The Traka 360. She has the endurance and power to conquer the Nannup course with more than 3,000 metres of climbing, nearly triple last year's race, but will she be allowed the freedom to do so?

The tall Dutch rider competes on the powerhouse Specialized Off-road squad, and has often supported her teammate Sofia Gomez Villafañe when the two lined up together, notably at The Mid South and Unbound 200 where they went one-two, Schreurs runner-up both times. They switched roles at Lauf Gravel Worlds where Schreurs earned the win and Villafane took fourth.

While Villafañe is the only representative for Argentina on Saturday for elite women, it probably it might be a little tricky for Schreurs to ride for a trade teammate while in Dutch orange. The very capable Schreurs is a threat in her own right among the seven-rider Dutch squad, but the stacked team may be out to give Marianne Vos a second gravel World title. Then again, racing in the Netherlands last year the home team landed 12 riders in the top 20, including Schreurs, and there was no organised support that led Vos and eventual winner Lorena Wiebes catching, and passing a breakaway ride of teammate Shirin Van Anrooij. Look for Schreurs to be at the front of the race in any regard, and land on the podium. (JT)

Look over the podiums of the last three years at the UCI Gravel World Championships and there is one name you will see a lot of, and that's Florian Vermeersch. The UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider hasn't spent a lot of time on the gravel, with road commitments coming first, but he has certainty made his mark when lining up at the rainbow jersey race right from 2023 when he came second on debut. It was a position he then repeated in 2024, continuing a pattern for the rider that had developed on the road of being up there on big target events, like Paris-Roubaix where he came second in 2021, but never quite having the fortune to have his powerful efforts end in a victory celebration.

That, however, all changed in 2025 in the Netherlands with a solo effort of about 20km that left him claiming a world title. That means Vermeersch will line up as both the defending champion and also as the rider who has been the most regular visitor to the elite men's podium at the race, however there is no doubt he'll be facing a different style of challenge this October, with more gravel, more climbing and more travel plus a strong field to contend with when he gets there. "It would be awesome to be the first two-time winner but I'm aware that it’s not going to be easy," acknowledged Vermeersch when his attendance was announced.

However, with the number 1 on his back and two runner-up spots as well he has proven that he is a rider not to be underestimated when he gets a chance to race for his own results. Indeed, he has already visited the lower steps of the podium at Omloop Het Nieuwsblad, E3 Saxo Classic and the Tour of Britain so far this year, and he is bound to do whatever he can to keep his Gravel World Championships podium run rolling too. (SG)

At this point there is only one more result that could add any real lustre to the trophy case and that's the gold medal at the UCI Gravel World Championships.

The Danish rider hasn't had the best experience at the event so far, with a flat tyre and side cut ruining his race. This year, however, the event has been a focus for the second half of the season, with Würtz Schmidt seeing the Australian event as a key opportunity. He certainly has shown what a formidable foe he is this season, and its hard to go past him as a key favourite even in a field with a number of road ring ins.

However, it will be interesting to see where he is on the start grid and whether that works against him, as while his European Championships delivers UCI points, Unbound 200 and The Traka are both outside the UCI domain so they may be high on prestige but count for nothing when it comes to points. Additionally, at The Traka and Unbound Würtz Schmidt benefited from being part of top gravel team, Specialized-Off Road, who took advantage of their strong trio with Keegan Swenson and Matt Beers, but – in theory at least – they will all be racing for their separate countries at the Gravel World Championships. (SG)

It's been three years since Keegan Swenson last competed at the UCI Gravel World Championships, where he finished fifth in Italy. Since then, Cobe Freeburn has been the only US men's elite rider to crack the top 55. Swenson brings strength and swagger to Team USA as he is a dominant force across any off-road race, from six consecutive wins at Leadville Trail 100 MTB to four victories at SBT GRVL, plus a win and three other top 10s at Unbound Gravel 200, all climbing-heavy courses in the US. This past year won his first rainbow stripes in Switzerland as the 2025 UCI Mountain Bike Marathon World Champion.

The first half of 2026 was delayed by an out-of-competition crash where he suffered a fractured pelvis, but he returned to form with podiums at Sea Otter Classic Gravel, Lauf Gravel Worlds, and the win at SBT GRVL. The Utah native was again the top US finisher at MTB Marathon Worlds, but this time seventh. His effort in the Italian Dolomites provided the only UCI points, as he focused on the US-based Life Time Grand Prix events, where he is at the top of the leaderboard and looking for a fourth title in five years.

With a wildcard entry from Team USA, Swenson has confirmed he will take the start in Nannup by squeezing in the travel between rounds of the Grand Prix. Like a few others, he'll have to miss Little Sugar MTB on October 11, but he'll use that as his one throwaway race in the series. The wide roads with 80% mix of dirt, loose rocks and clay combined with relentless climbing of 3,713 metres of elevation gain are similar to US courses, sure to reward an endurance specialist like Swenson. (JT)

Matt Beers lined up at the very first edition of the UCI Gravel World Championships, but like a large proportion of the gravel world that regularly races in the traditional stronghold of the US, he has been absent since. This, however, is an edition that is hard to pass up for a number of the big names, with a course that plays to the strengths of the discipline specialists and a location that makes it harder for the strong road nations to swamp the front of the grid with a large contingent that can effectively control the race. The South African has won Cape Epic four times, finished second at Unbound this year, won Big Sugar, Belgian Waffle Ride California and Lauf Gravel Worlds last year, plus has been on the podium of The Traka the past two years, in the 200 and 360.

Beers is the type of rider who can hold his own on the climbs, push powerfully in a break and also deliver a solid sprint at the end of it, with a good example being his winning effort against Keegan Swenson at the long-running and unofficial Gravel Worlds last year. They are all skills that could be put to good use on the gravel-heavy course from Nannup, which for the UCI Gravel World Series event this year split the field early. (SG)

There were a long list of riders who we went back and forth on for this fifth and final spot in the men's elite contenders list but in the end it was hard to go past Lukas Pöstlberger. The former road professional, with a Giro d'Italia stage win to his name, has really hit his straps on the gravel this year. He has won a UCI Gravel World Series race, The Gralloch, reclaimed his Austrian Champion's title and celebrated on the line of Europe's biggest gravel event, The Traka. The Traka 200 victory was hard to forget, a tight and well played battle to the line, which he charged toward with Braydn Lange (Canyon x DT Swiss All-Terrain Racing) and the Buff BH duo of Martin Stošek and Wout Alleman chasing as well as having MTB legend Nino Schurter not far behind.

That win has offered clear proof of what he is capable of, and he's also made the trip out to Australia early enough that he has a decent amount of time out on the gravel roads around Nannup to explore the course and acclimatise. We saw what happened in Spain earlier this year when he put a clear target on an event and everything runs to plan.

Subscribers get unlimited access to exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

items.title: 76ers 120, Knicks 97: Scenes from a sleepy scrimmage
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Real fans watch preseason games, these half-hearted scrimmages in which stars tend to lollygag, and the guys fighting for roster or rotation consideration tend to play as you’d expect—like guys trying to secure seats at the southern reach of the bench. Bandwagoners and parade crashers don’t tune in for this slop. Real fans do, cuz a Knicks game is a Knicks game. We even watch summer league!

After a short summer respite, the World Champion Knickerbockers and your loyal P&T blogger were all feeling rusty. From the start of tonight’s 120-97 loss to the Sixers, the champs continued to show their penchant for the long ball, heaving more than half their shots from the outfield. Both teams converted 33% from deep through the first 12 minutes, and here’s some good news: Finals MVP Jalen Brunson’s surgically repaired wrist had a familiar sweet snap as he drilled two three-pointers.

The guests took an early lead, but Philly answered with a 14-3 stretch through the heart of the quarter. Seeing former Celtic Jaylen Brown in Philadelphia blue boggled the brain for a moment. He carried his unit with LeBron James, Joel Embiid, and Tyrese Maxey taking the night off (chickens), and the new Sixer collected 13 early points. Meanwhile, Brunson and OG () Anunoby scored eight points apiece for our heroes.

Former Knick Ariel Hukporti started the game, but exited early with an injury after facing up with Karl-Anthony Towns. He was assisted to the locker room, and it had the hallmarks of an Achilles tear. If that turns out to be the case, it’s a devastating blow to a likable guy who stood to get significant playing time this season.

On the subject of Towns, he attacked the paint and looked not a bit sour about his contract situation. Behind him, Andre Drummond played his first (unofficial) game as a Knick and was exactly the same Drummond he’s always been.

As the quarter went on, Tyler Kolek (with longer locks) assumed ball-handling duties. He seemed to have a mandate to score and forced it a little. Due to an absence of defense on either side, the teams swapped buckets like high-schoolers on layup lines. One welcome exception was the dependable Landry Shamet, who drained a pair of triples.

After 13 lead changes, the Knicks finished the quarter trailing just 33-32, despite the Sixers out-shooting them 54% to 48%.

To start the second quarter, Jaylen Brown returned for a short stint, as did Brunson and Towns for the Knicks.

But, true to his word, Coach Mike Brown doled out minutes to as many players as he could. The spotlight in these early days is squarely on sophomore Mohamed Diawara. He attacked the rim with mixed results and coughed up the ball twice. Not a great sign after a crummy summer league. Alongside him, Jordan Clarkson logged his allotment of minutes, picking up where he left off.

Veteran James Wiseman took a turn at center, hoping to convince Brown to award him the team’s final roster spot. He scored two buckets but seemed a step slow on defense. Speaking of which, Pacome Dadiet guarded with more aggression than I remember. His offense, however, was pretty much exactly as I remembered—he and Miles McBride combined to shoot 0-of-4 from downtown in the half.

The second quarter belonged to the 76ers, who reached a 14-point lead late in the period and went into intermission ahead 72-58. They shot 53% from the field and 46% from deep, converting 11 dingers to the Knicks’ five. After missing a bunch of shots in the second quarter, our guys had shot 23% from deep. Brown led all first-half scorers with 22, while Anunoby logged 12 for the good guys.

Kolek and Shamet started the third, as did Walker, who answered their buckets with a trey of his own. Diawara turned on the charm with consecutive finger-rolls, a putback, and a steal. From there, the teams traded inefficient offensive blows.

Drummond swatted three blocks, and his layup fueled a nice push during that run, but Clarkson committed two travel violations and whiffed on multiple shots. Wiseman hit from the line and dunked a tip-in, while Ochai Agbaji went scoreless with some misses, and Dadiet’s fouls sent the Sixers to the stripe. By the end of this sludgefest, both teams had scored 21 points. The Knicks were still down, now 93-79.

Drew Eubanks and Bruce Brown started the fourth quarter for the Knicks, and we saw cameos by Kevin McCullar, Jr., Tyler Nickel, Tony Bradley, and Jaden Akins. By the buzzer, Brown had played 20 players (and it would’ve been 21, but Jose Alvarado is nursing a bruised knee). Aikins and Dadiet both hit from deep, which were rare sights on a night when the Knicks shot 8-of-41 from yard.

For the home team, rookie forward Saint Thomas impressed with a double-double. Thanks to his efforts, the Liberty Bells inflated their lead to 23. Caleb Love continued to have a nice game for them (15 points, 3-of-6 from deep). When the cutting was done, our heroes had fallen, 120-97. Big deal. We’ll give these bums the business on banner night.

The Knicks host the Wizards on Thursday. Safe travels, Knickerbockers, and get well soon, Huk.
