items.title: Preseason Game Thread: Knicks at 76ers, October 5, 2026
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Knicks travel to Xfinity Mobile Arena tonight for their inaugural preseason game and their first appearance on the court since beating the Spurs for the NBA Championship (yes, that really happened).

The 76ers are not the same team that New York swept in round two of the playoffs. This offseason, Philly bulked up with additions of Jaylen Brown and LeBron James. Paired with fellow starters Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid, and V.J. Edgecombe, this squad is built to challenge the throne. Temper your excitement for tonight’s tilt, though: James, Embiid, and Maxey, Anfernee Simons, Dominick Barlow, Adem Bona, and Tacko Fall are all OUT tonight.

We expect limited minutes for New York’s starters—Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart, O.G. () Anunoby, and Karl-Anthony Towns—as they continue to get back online after a short summer break. Meanwhile, Coach Mike Brown is eager to see what Mohamed Diawara brings to the table in year two, and who stands out among the centers competing for the third-string spot. Jose Alvarado (knee contusion) is the only Knick on the injury report.

Game time is at 7 p.m. EST on MSG. This is your game thread. This is Liberty Ballers. Please don’t post large photos, GIFs, or links to illegal streams in the thread. Be excellent humans. And go Knicks!
items.lbText:
The new-look Phillies hope rattle the champs in the preseason opener.

The Knicks travel to Xfinity Mobile Arena tonight for their inaugural preseason game and their first appearance on the court since beating the Spurs for the NBA Championship (yes, that really happened).

The 76ers are not the same team that New York swept in round two of the playoffs. This offseason, Philly bulked up with additions of Jaylen Brown and LeBron James. Paired with fellow starters Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid, and V.J. Edgecombe, this squad is built to challenge the throne. Temper your excitement for tonight’s tilt, though: James, Embiid, and Maxey, Anfernee Simons, Dominick Barlow, Adem Bona, and Tacko Fall are all OUT tonight.

We expect limited minutes for New York’s starters—Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart, O.G. ( The Big Tipper ) Anunoby, and Karl-Anthony Towns—as they continue to get back online after a short summer break. Meanwhile, Coach Mike Brown is eager to see what Mohamed Diawara brings to the table in year two, and who stands out among the centers competing for the third-string spot. Jose Alvarado (knee contusion) is the only Knick on the injury report.

Game time is at 7 p.m. EST on MSG. This is your game thread. This is Liberty Ballers . Please don’t post large photos, GIFs, or links to illegal streams in the thread. Be excellent humans. And go Knicks!

items.title: Charm City Cross Day 2: Manon Bakker and Tofik Beshir sweep weekend with C2 victories on muddy Baltimore course
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Manon Bakker (Alpe d'Huzes) and Tofik Beshir (CXD Trek Bikes) conquered the mud and won the C2 elite races at Charm City Cross, sweeping both days of UCI races in Baltimore, Maryland. The pair also secured overall titles in the six-race US Cyclocross Series (USCX).

Even with overnight rain and continued drizzle on Sunday on the twisting Druid Hill Park course, Bakker did not make a switch to mud tyres to start the race and used the speed to gain an early advantage. Sidney McGill (Materiaal-Lastig) matched her pace on the first pass of Mansion Hill, but then put a foot down and disconnected from the Dutch rider for the rest of the race. Bakker would solo the rest of the way, despite slipping several times and having to make pit stops, and score her fifth victory in the series.

"These 3 weeks have shown me why I love 'cross so much. The competition during the games and the fun outside. Feels good to be back on track," Bakker posted on Instagram a day later.

McGill, who won the C2 race at Virginia's Blue Ridge Go Cross a week ago, rolled across the muddy finish line in second place, 34 seconds back. Mia Aseltine (Competitive Edge Racing) took third, another 14 seconds later. With fifth place, Aseltine's teammate Kaya Musgrave locked in third overall in the USCX.

Bakker finished second in the series each of the last two seasons, but was nothing but dominant this year, saying "Finally, I got it".

She announced on social media last month that she did not have a team for her cyclo-cross season, so would compete in a blue kit to promote a cancer foundation. "Alpe d'Huzes is a charity that is very close to me, the mountain I've been climbing since I was young. The slogan 'Giving up is not an option' fits me perfectly now," she wrote on Instagram.

In the men's race, it was a showdown between Beshir and Pan American champion Andrew Strohmeyer. Now with Competitive Edge Racing, Strohmeyer took the hole shot and then rode in tandem with his Comp Edge teammate Ryan Drummond. However, on the second lap, Strohmeyer was on his own against the CXD Trek Bikes duo of Beshir and Miles Mattern.

Beshir and Strohmeyer then locked horns for the back half of the race, each trying to find any grip on the slippery course. They tangled with three laps to go in the pits, Strohmeyer hitting the deck, and then again on an off-camber section on the final lap, Beshir taking an outside line that interrupted the momentum of Strohmeyer, who again went down.

“I was trying to hold back a little bit and save energy for the later part of the race,” Strohmeyer said. “The separation came naturally. No one really accelerated. People just make mistakes and the people who stay consistent start riding away.”

The 19-year-old Ethiopian stayed away to the finish, his fifth victory in the series. Tyler Clark (Caledon Hills Cycling Armada) would slot into second place by 18 seconds, while Competitive Edge put Dylan Zakrajsek into the final podium spot, followed by Drummond in fourth and Strohmeyer in fifth. Clark would finish second overall in the USCX, while Calvin Conaway, eighth on Sunday, finished third overall.

"It was definitely hard, but I was just trying to have fun and trying to follow Strohmeyer and learn from him,” Beshir said to organisers. “I saw my opportunity and I chopped him a little bit. I really felt bad because I respect this guy.

"You improve every year that you come here, but you don't really know how much [you’ve improved] until you go out and you do it."

He noted that the wet conditions made the pit stops dangerous. “I immediately regretted it once I came out of the pit and saw he crashed. Yes, it is racing, but I have so much respect for this guy.”

USCX included three consecutive weekends of C1 and C2 races in 2026, with openers at Rochester Cyclocross in New York and the second round at Virginia's Blue Ridge GO Cross in Virginia, both in September. Charm City Cross concluded the series.

items.title: Giulio Ciccone Questions European Championships Photo Finish Against Remco Evenepoel
items.author: ahood
items.content: ‘I’ve watched the available footage hundreds of times’: The Italian wants to see the decisive image after missing European gold by 0.0028 seconds.
items.lbText:
Ciccone reacts after losing the European Championships in a photo finish. (Photo: Getty Images)

Giulio Ciccone wants to see the image that decided the European road title for himself, because he still has doubts about Sunday’s razor-thin defeat .

The Italian said he still cannot come to terms with the photo finish verdict and footage of his dramatic loss against Remco Evenepoel .

“The title was awarded by a margin of 0.0028 seconds, or 2.8 thousandths of a second,” Ciccone wrote on Instagram.

“I’ve watched the available footage hundreds of times and, in the shots where the finish line is visible, I keep seeing something that I cannot reconcile with that verdict.”

Evenepoel snagged gold Sunday with a spectacular bike throw in Slovenia to edge out the Italian in a two-up sprint so tight that it took a photo finish to call the winner.

On Monday, Ciccone praised the Belgian’s performance and defended his racing tactics, but said he wanted to see the evidence for himself.

“Remco was the strongest rider yesterday,” he wrote. “I’m asking for something very simple: to see the photo finish at the actual finish line.”

Ciccone said commissaires and federation technical staff explained Monday morning how the photo finish works and the criteria used to interpret it.

But that’s not enough for the 31-year-old Lidl-Trek star to accept the outcome.

“So I’m not asking for another explanation,” he wrote. “I’m asking to see the photo finish that corresponds exactly to the actual finish line.”

Ciccone’s questions followed a brutally close finish to Sunday’s wild and wide-open European Championship.

Ciccone and Evenepoel dueled to the end, with the Italian looking to have the winning edge after out-positioning the Belgian on the final corner. Evenepoel opened up a desperate burst in the closing meters and timed his bike throw perfectly at the line.

After a long and tense wait, the race jury eventually awarded the victory to Evenepoel.

In a lengthy public post on Monday, the Italian said he wants to see the photo of both wheels crossing the line.

“Because if a European title is decided by 2.8 thousandths of a second, I believe it is legitimate to ask for that crossing to be shown with the same precision used to determine the result,” he wrote.

“If that image confirms the verdict, there will be nothing more to add,” he wrote. “But until I’m shown that correspondence, a question remains for me that has yet to be answered.”

On Monday evening, the Union Européenne de Cyclisme — which runs and organizes the European championships — issued the following statement:

“The Union Européenne de Cyclisme (UEC) informs that the photo-finish system used at the 2026 UEC Road European Championships (EtherLynx Vision PRO X) records the finish line thousands of times per second (13,000 in the specific case of the European Championship races), making it possible to determine the finishing order with extreme precision, even when the differences are minimal,” a media note read.

“It is important to clarify that a photo finish is not a traditional photograph. The final image is composed of the chronological sequence of recordings made at the finish line; for this reason, the horizontal axis represents time, not distance. This can create apparent distortions of wheels, bicycles and riders, without any impact on the accuracy of the result.

“In cycling, the determining reference is the most advanced part (tangent) of the front wheel at the moment it reaches the finish line. At the European Championships, two independent photo-finish systems were used, providing two separate images to verify the result.”

items.title: Gabriel in Man Utd team photo but no hint of reconciliation
items.content: <article>As he prepares to celebrate his 16th birthday, the rift between Manchester United and JJ Gabriel shows no sign of being healed.</article>
items.lbText:
JJ Gabriel has been included in Manchester United's official team photo for this season but there remains no hint of a reconciliation with the club as new details of his efforts to leave Old Trafford emerge.

The teenage forward - who turns 16 on Tuesday - features in the photographs that were released on Monday.

It is understood the pictures were taken on 8 September - two days before he played his final game for the club and informed them of his intention to leave.

It is virtually certain his next involvement in a United game will be as an opposition player.

United still hold his registration and, according to sources close to Old Trafford, the club have made multiple attempts to reconcile the situation as part of their duty of care to the teenager. So far, it has been to no avail.

Gabriel is now a target for several of Europe's top clubs, with Real Madrid and Barcelona among those taking a keen interest. He now has a European Union passport, which is thought could smooth his passage to the continent.

However, while no clubs have approached United so far, they would consider legal action if any evidence of an illegal inducement by a club or agent - that would contravene regulations in relation to young players - was to emerge.

While tensions between Gabriel's camp and United had been simmering for a number of months, sources have told BBC Sport the player's decision to seek a move away was ultimately triggered by his non-inclusion in Michael Carrick’s side for the Champions League encounter with Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK on 10 September.

The youngster's camp had expressed a desire for Gabriel to be used as a substitute against Sabah - which, on paper, was the easiest of United's league-phase games.

Sources say the prospect of the Londoner coming on against Brighton in the EFL Cup on 16 September was also discussed, with United officials subsequently insistent that was the plan.

Had he played in either match, Gabriel would have become United's youngest ever player.

However, by the time the encounter with Fabian Hurzeler's side arrived, the striker had already told the club of his intention to quit and had left the country.

Gabriel could not play against Sabah because he had not been registered on United's Uefa A list of players when it was announced on 3 September. The precise reasons for this have not been made clear.

It did not prevent him scoring a hat-trick in a Uefa Youth League game against them at Leigh Sports Village earlier on 10 September. While he has not been back to United since, it is not clear whether anything significant happened after that game.

For their part, United believe they made it clear they view Gabriel as immensely important to their first-team future, even though sources have indicated the player did not report for the start of the academy's pre-season training schedule at the beginning of July - a week earlier than the senior squad - despite being asked to do so.

Sources also say they lobbied the Premier League to allow the forward to use "JJ Gabriel" on the back of his shirt - which they believe underlined their commitment to the academy prospect.

Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - but he is reported to have changed his name for commercial purposes.

In addition, United say they have provided Gabriel with first-team care and services - included regular meetings with senior coaches and nutritionists.

That he was included in the senior team photo is also viewed as further evidence of their commitment to his development and transition into first-team football.

When Gabriel committed himself to United in the summer of 2025, the lure of breaking through at United, and the targets he could aim for, was strong.

He was only 14 at the time but already he was looking towards the first team. Within a couple of months, Gabriel was called into senior training sessions by Ruben Amorim.

Expectation grew to such an extent that interim boss Darren Fletcher was asked if it was possible the forward could make his competitive bow in the FA Cup third-round tie with Brighton in January.

Fletcher - then Gabriel's coach at under-18 level - said no, believing the youngster wasn't physically ready.

However, as he continued to excel at under-18 level, it seemed a case of when, not if, Gabriel would be given his chance.

He ended the 2025-26 campaign as the Premier League's Under-18 player of the year and picked up the same award at United. It seemed certain he would be involved at the start of pre-season, when the majority of United's senior players would be absent after their World Cup exertions.

What happened instead solidified existing doubts of those close to Gabriel that United were the right club for him.

First, he was not part of Carrick's squad for the trip to Helsinki to face Wrexham in a friendly. On 24 July, he was an unused substitute against Rosenborg in Trondheim, a match in which Carrick made 10 outfield changes. Five of those players have since been sold or loaned out.

Gabriel finally got his chance against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm on 1 August, when he replaced Bryan Mbeumo for the final eight minutes.

That turned out to be it. He was on the bench for the final two games against Leeds and AC Milan, but did not get on. Against Leeds, former FA Youth Cup team-mate Dan Armer and 18-year-old newcomer Tynan Thompson were both introduced.

Doubts over Gabriel's physicality persisted, but his performances at under-21 level made a compelling argument he was ready.

Brighton was mentioned as a potential senior debut, but the perils around that made, for those close to Gabriel, the Champions League encounter with Sabah a better option.

The theory was correct. United beat them 4-0 and Carrick had used all five substitutes by the 72nd minute. The following week, United threw away a 2-0 lead and lost against Brighton.…

items.title: Bottas cycling from Malaysia to Singapore Grand Prix
items.content: <article>Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas switches four wheels for two and opts to travel to the Singapore Grand Prix by bike.</article>
items.lbText:
Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas has opted for an unusual route to this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, avoiding a short flight and instead cycling the 350km (217 miles) from Malaysia.

His journey began just hours after spinning out of Sunday's chaotic Bahrain Grand Prix , which was held at Sepang outside the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur as a one-off.

The Finnish driver is making the journey - much of which is off-road and on gravel - alongside his partner, professional cyclist Tiffany Cromwell, and will need to be in Singapore for his media commitments on Thursday.

On Monday, stage two of his journey, he spent nearly six hours on his bike, covering 161.91km.

Swapping the driver's seat for the saddle before reaching the heat and humidity of Marina Bay this weekend is just another in a series of cycling-related endeavours for Bottas.

The 37-year-old earned a spot at the Gravel World Championships following a fifth-placed finish in his age group as an off-road qualifying event in the Czech Republic during Formula 1's summer hiatus.

But the World Championships take place on the same weekend as the Singapore Grand Prix, so he will be unable to use his place.

Bottas is closely involved with FNLD GRVL, a race held each summer in his native Finland, and, when the Emilia Romagna Grand Prix was cancelled in 2023, he decided to use the time to compete in a gravel race in Scotland .

Cycling has become one of Bottas' main pursuits away from F1, frequently sharing training rides and races with Cromwell.

Bottas has endured a difficult return to Formula 1 with new team Cadillac this season. He is 22nd in the drivers' standings, is yet to score a point after 16 Grands Prix and has failed to finish eight races.

items.title: Lidl-Trek and Gaia Realini agree to end contract a year early
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
One season before her current contract was due to expire at the end of 2027, Lidl-Trek and Italian rider Gaia Realini have mutually agreed to part ways at the end of 2026, the German team announced on Monday.

"After four years together - four precious years that have contributed so much to my personal growth and brought so many great emotions - we have decided that the time has come to go our separate ways," said Realini in the announcement.

"Thank you, Lidl-Trek, for everything we have shared and experienced together."

Lidl-Trek signed the diminutive climber in 2023, after she had impressed racing for Continental team Isolmant-Premac-Vittoria, notably at the Giro d'Italia Women. She found immediate success in her first race, taking second on the queen stage and overall at the UAE Tour Women behind teammate at the time and compatriot Elisa Longo Borghini.

From there, Realini only kicked on to become one of the top climbers in the world, taking third at La Flèche Wallonne, seventh at Liège-Bastogne-Liège, and winning Trofeo Oro in Euro in her first spring as a professional.

As the summer of stage racing rolled around, Realini proved to be a revelation, finishing third overall and winning a stage at La Vuelta a Femenina, then matching that GC result of third at the Giro d'Italia Women and Tour de l'Avenir.

This decision was vindicated by her highlight result of fifth overall at her maiden Tour de France Femmes, which she backed up with third on GC at the Tour de Romandie; by this point, Realini was an established GC leader, built for the most vicious, steep climbs.

However, a fractured elbow in training ruined her start to the 2025 season, and she's struggled to return to her previous best ever since, failing to finish in the top 15 of any race she started in her third season on Lidl-Trek.

While still not at her 2023-2024 peak level, Realini has started to find better results in this ongoing season, taking eighth and 12th on the two key climbing stages at the Vuelta, and finishing 10th overall at the Faun Tour Femmes. Her most recent result was 14th at the Giro dell'Emilia Donne, with Tre Valli Varesine the only remaining race on her confirmed schedule for 2026.

Realini is the third confirmed Lidl-Trek women's departure for 2027, with Felicity Wilson-Haffenden joining Fenix-Premier Tech, Shirin van Anrooij heading for Canyon-SRAM, and Amanda Spratt retiring.

Whether Realini will continue in 2027, and where that may be, is yet to be confirmed.

items.title: Silca Protocol RCR 29 Review: Go Bigger
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Silca built a 29mm tire with great ride feel, but that fails to stand out in any strong way. If you want to beat the competition, you have to look at a different size.
items.lbText:
Comfortable ride feel Excellent dry cornering grip High puncture resistance for a race tire Competitive weight-to-width ratio Aerodynamically optimized width Excellent choice in 38mm size

Silca recently launched a new series of tires. The lineup covers both road and gravel, and everything offered is focused on high volume and ride feel. Of course, they launched without much of a bang, and there definitely weren’t any major claims made… No, I am obviously kidding. This is Silca, and these tires launched to so much hype it hurt. The claim was that they were head and shoulders above the rest of the field.

Then Bicycle Rolling Resistance put the RCR 29 through its testing regime, and the results were… a bit lackluster. Big claims have now been made on the other side of the fence, but not that many people have actually ridden these tires. I’ve now got a few hundred miles on them, and I think there’s more to these tires than a drum test—but I don’t love everything. Let’s look at the good and the bad when it comes to the Silca RCR 29 road tires.

What I do on a bike—almost always a race bike—is ride it longer than anyone expects. I want a tire that soaks up rough pavement, but I’m not running 34mm tires because I also want aerodynamics in a straight line, and I’m not interested in increasing wheel width (meaning weight) to optimize for a wider tire. In other words, I want to have my cake and eat it too.

I’ve been running the Silca 29mm tires at 52 psi on a 22.5mm internal width rim, and to me, they pull this balance off. A 29mm width matches well with modern rims in terms of the Rule of 105 and aerodynamics. That 29mm also means if you are a stickler for following ETRTO recommendations, you can run a 25mm internal width rim, but that’s not something I worry about.

Where I find the Silca tires really shining is cornering in the dry. Bicycle Rolling Resistance doesn’t test dry cornering because it’s universally quite high, but these tires have tested high in wet grip. Personally, I don’t care a ton about wet grip because these are on a bike that won’t see much rain, but I do think there’s nuance in dry pavement cornering grip, and these land in my “good bucket.”

Lean the bike, stand on the outside pedal, and you can feel the bite. Over and over, I surprised myself by cutting tight switchbacks a little tighter than I normally would, while still feeling confident and in control. A big part of this feeling goes back to a tire that does a great job soaking up bumps. Even on a stiff race bike, I don’t find the front wheel coming off the line over small cracks.

That means the real advantage again goes back to that ride feel, but sometimes that is accompanied by the puncture protection of an overinflated water balloon. That’s not the case here. Even before the BRR testing, I had a guess that it was decent based on the 2.1mm tread thickness. That matches the GP5000 thickness, and while thickness isn’t an exact 1:1 for puncture protection, it’s a decent way of setting expectations. BRR confirmed exactly what I expected, although it is a bit lower than the P Zero Race RS (which is also thicker). My own experience here is that all of the popular race tires are pretty close in puncture protection, and it’s good enough. Silca falls in line.

Basically, the Silca tire falls into the “good enough” bucket. I told you it has good ride feel, cornering grip, and puncture protection, and that should be enough, right? It is enough, but why are you choosing the Silca tire?

The Continental GP5000, Schwalbe Pro One, Pirelli P Zero Race RS, Goodyear Eagle F1 R Z29 Aero, and Vittoria Corsa Pro are all good tires with slight advantages and disadvantages. Maybe one leans a little this way and another a little that way, but it’s incredibly close. I doubt I can convince dedicated Vittoria fans to switch to the Zipp/Goodyear tire, and equally, for what reason would you switch from your favorite tire to the Silca? What is the unique selling proposition for Silca?

Given that Silca is all about marginal gains, I really wanted to see these come out as an aero-optimized tire. I’ve talked to Josh Poertner about aero tires plenty this year, and I know he believes in them, but the RCR is not an aero tire. When I asked for clarification, the answer was that, at this point, he doesn’t have a way to add aero gains without losing rolling resistance.

It’s a fair answer and it makes a lot of sense, but it would also make you think the Silca tires excel at rolling resistance. Now that Bicycle Rolling Resistance has tested that they are mid-pack, that’s a tough argument to make, too. Silca claims that the RCR is faster than the Vittoria Corsa Pro Control, and BRR confirmed that it’s 3.6 watts faster at 72 psi. That’s a win, but the same testing shows the GP5000 as 1.8 watts faster than the RCR.

I won’t argue that 1.8 watts is worth choosing the GP5000, but is anyone going to argue that the GP5000 is a tire that lacks cornering grip or that the ride feel isn’t good? I might even say the Silca tire has better ride feel, but it’s about as subtle as 1.8 watts. It’s worth noting that Silca also has better puncture protection, but I’m still not convinced any of this is quite enough to get people jumping brands.

The main negative I see here is the lack of a compelling reason for people to switch brands. The Silca RCR 29 is another good tire, but it’s not doing anything special. I, for one, can’t wait for Poertner to crack the aero nut without harming puncture protection or rolling resistance.

This could be the place where the Silca RCR tires gain some converts. The product description has a section that covers “Carbon BeadLock technology,” which is a technology Silca is using to swap the normal Kevlar bead “with non-stretching carbon fiber to eliminate moisture absorption, stretch, and tire wobble for a precise rim fit over the entire lifespan of the tire.”…

items.title: Monday Posted & Toasted Notes: KAT sounds off, yearning Mike, basketball time!
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Last time I checked, we were celebrating. Turns out, we’re now back to watching games take place again! Not , but hey, the boys can only play when they tell them to, and I won’t complain. Links and things today, quotes (probably) tomorrow.

  • Karl-Anthony Towns made it very clear on Monday morning that he and the New York Knicks aren’t even remotely close to agreeing to a contract extension at this point.

“Simply put, I want to do something to keep the team together and can work with the Knicks and also values me. And none of those things are close to happening.

“(Reaching an agreement before the start of the regular season) doesn’t look good.

“No s–t Sherlock (an extension shouldn’t be understood as a reward for last season). I just won a championship. You’d think it was pretty easy. Unless you guys (reporters) think I have something else to prove.”

  • More on that inside the newsletter, but here’s a summary for the lazy: the Knicks enter the season with the highest preseason over/under win total in the Eastern Conference for the first time since 1993, with sportsbooks setting them around 52.5 to 53.5 wins, but New York has finished with the East’s No. 1 seed only four times in franchise history and hasn’t done it since 1993. Something has to give, doesn’t it?
  • Nitty-gritty breakdown of KAT’s contract situation by The Athletic’s Fred Katz and how it could eventually have major implications for Miles McBride’s future in New York.
  • Carmelo Anthony believes neither LeBron James, Joel Embiid or Jaylen Brown should remain the central figure in Philadelphia after the Sixers’ blockbuster offseason.
  • Giannis Antetokounmpo made it clear he still has “five, six good years” remaining in his career, all of which would probably go for nothing while the Heat remain in cap hell without a strong-enough roster around the Greek. Hooray!
  • Dillon Brooks hopes he has another decade of NBA basketball ahead of him and doesn’t want his “great year” (?) to make him complacent.
  • Old-man-yelling-at-a-cloud Cedric Ceballos argued last year that Stephen Curry wouldn’t have been given the same freedom to launch extremely deep 3-pointers in his era and would never have become a great hooper, let alone the man who changed basketball, and recently explained his take. Not sure it convinces me.

items.title: Noa Isidore sprints to Coppa Bernocchi victory to claim another Italian win for Decathlon CMA CGM
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Noa Isidore (Decathlon CMA CGM) emerged victorious from a messy sprint at the 107th Coppa Bernocchi, taking victory from the bunch with a powerful kick in Legnano ahead of Tommaso Dati (Team UKYO).

The final run to the line was marred by a nasty crash with 700 metres to go, several riders including Ben Swift (Netcompany Ineos) coming down before the sprint was opened up.

As the split bunch ramped up in pace, Dorian Godon (Netcompany Ineos) and Matteo Trentin (Tudor) tried to storm into the slipstream of late attacker Gil Gelders (Soudal-QuickStep), only to be overhauled by those charging quickly behind them.

Isidore speared his way through the middle and past the fast-finishing Dati for the win, with Marijn van den Berg (EF Education EasyPost) taking third on Monday.

"It's a good finish for me. The goal today was to win, so I came here in Italy for that and I'm very happy," said Isidore after the finish, taking his third victory as a professional in his second year on Decathlon's WorldTour squad.

"I'm really happy this year I can be a leader sometimes with my team, and I proved I can win, so I'm happy for me and my teammates who worked for me.

"In the sprint, I just saw the guy from [UKYO], and I thought, 'Just push, push, push, push, you can do it', and I won, so it's good."

Three riders from the early breakaway survived all the way until 1.6k to go, with the charging bunch also bringing back a powerful chasing group that contained Jhonatan Narváez (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and Neilson Powless (EF Education - EasyPost) inside 10km to go.

It was Samuele Zoccarato (MBH Bank CSB Telecom Fort), Sergio Samitier (Cofidis), and Ben Granger (Solution Tech NIPPO Rali) who had made it into the finale from the break, but even with the Spaniard's undying efforts, they were unable to hold off the chase led mostly by Ineos, EF and Uno-X Mobility.

No team really had full control in the finale, though, which was true of the majority of the action near Milan, leading to several teams accelerating their leaders to the front, which played a role in the crash of Ben Swift and several others.

In fact, the race winner came dangerously close to being involved in the high-speed incident, as the rider who inadvertently caused Swift to lose balance, as he was squeezed by an EF rider, which caused a ripple effect in the bunch and saw more than six riders hit the deck hard next to the pavement.

"I think it's Filippo Ganna next to me," said Isidore, but it was actually Swift, wearing the number four dossard for Ineos, "and the guy from EF just pushed me and I couldn't do anything, so I hope Filippo is good now. But it's like that,"

Racing at the Italian Autum Classics will continue on Tuesday at Tre Valli Varesine, as the build up to Il Lombardia and the final Monument of the 2026 season this Saturday continues.

items.title: 'I've looked at the images hundreds of times' – Giulio Ciccone pleads for transparency as he questions controversial photo finish loss to Evenepoel at European Championships
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
After missing out on the European title by the narrowest of margins, just 0.0028 seconds, Giulio Ciccone (Italy) has pleaded for clarity when it comes to the photo finish that confirmed Remco Evenepoel (Belgium) as the champion from a tight two-up sprint in Slovenia.

Taking to Instagram almost 24 hours after the elite men's road race, the now controversial photo finish was still on Ciccone's mind, after the images showed what looked close to a dead heat, with Evenepoel only snatching the win by a matter of millimetres.

He never questioned that Evenepoel was the strongest rider in the race, but Ciccone struggled to accept the photo finish result without further proof, insisting that he just wanted to "see the photo finish on the real finish line."

"It's hard to control my emotions after yesterday's race. But I want to start from something that is out of the question for me," wrote Ciccone on Monday. "Remco was the strongest rider yesterday. He rode like a champion, he could interpret and manage a complex race and offered an extraordinary performance.

"Then there's the photo finish. The title was awarded with a difference of 0.0028 seconds, i.e. 2.8 thousandths. I've looked at the available images hundreds of times and, in the filming where the finish line is visible, I keep seeing a dynamic that I cannot reconcile with that verdict.

"This morning the commissioners, together with the federal technicians, explained to me how it works and the criteria with which the photo finish was interpreted. So I'm not asking for another explanation.

"I am asking to see the photo finish that corresponds exactly to the actual finish line. I would like to be able to see, unmistakably, the passing of our two wheels at the exact point where, according to the regulations, arrival is determined. Because if a European title is decided by 2.8 thousandths of a second, I think it’s legitimate to ask that that very passage can be shown with the same precision with which the result was determined.

"I'm not asking that a television shot will replace [the] photo finish. I'm not questioning the value of Remco nor the amazing race he ran. I am asking a very simple question: see the photo finish on the real finish line. If that picture confirms the verdict, there is nothing else to add. But until that correspondence is shown to me, for me it remains a question to which I have not yet received an answer."

The UEC, which organises the European Championships, told that they have two photo-finish systems, one on either side of the road, and that images from both of these systems were shown to Ciccone and the Italian federation, along with an explanation of how the technology works.

Ciccone was able to hang onto Evenepoel's accelerations on the final lap, and after mostly sitting on his wheel in the final run to the line, opened up his sprint early around the final corner. He looked as though he had it won, getting the jump on the Belgian, but Evenepoel came back with enough speed to catch him on the line with an elite bike throw.

After a long wait, Evenepoel was announced as the winner, leaving Ciccone banging his handlebars before the frustration turned to disappointment, and he was left hunched over a barrier with his agent, Alex Carera, there to console him.

In cycling, photo finishes are not taken by a regular camera, meaning that questions were raised as soon as the images appeared on screen, with Ciccone's bike appearing smaller than reality in the picture, and Evenepoel's longer.

What's actually happening is that a single vertical strip at the finish line is continuously being scanned every millisecond, resulting in the photo finish, and the X axis being a representation of time – in this case 0.0028 seconds – not of distance.

This is what causes the distortion of both riders and their bikes, as explained by Belgian broadcaster : "The end result looks like a two-dimensional image of a single moment, but in reality, they are photos of lines placed one after another." Italian publication further explained the process, with 15,000 images being produced of the strip in the last second, with Evenepoel arriving first by three millimetres.

Similar photo finish controversy is not unusual in cycling, with Wout van Aert's victory ahead of Tom Pidcock at the Amstel Gold Race in 2021 also raising the same questions. On that occasion, it was just six millimetres in favour of the Belgian that landed him the victory.

items.title: Six champions crowned, new winners and lap records fall at Castle Combe
'In terms of potential he has everything, absolutely everything' – From late call-up to first race with pro team, Matthew Peace looks right at home
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
It was unexpected, but Peace was ready and prepared for what was to come, after all this was a path his older brother Oliver had taken last year, which perhaps gave the 19-year-old confidence to follow his brother into the Picnic PostNL development programme.

But, as he said of this pathway, "knowing what to expect and also doing it is two different things". This was especially true when this late season race was "a bit of a surprise" and there certainly hadn't been time to get set for the conditions, which proved a formidable foe.

"It took me a couple days to get used to the heat and the humidity. It was completely different here because I was just in the UK and it was a bit cooler there," Peace told on the sidelines of the race on stage 6, where even walking to sign-on was enough to work up a sweat.

"I didn't have pressure or expectation coming into the race. It was just learning, so it's just been a really nice experience."

Peace may not have gone into the race with any pressure but he certainly wasn't there to make up numbers, with the plan being that he would support their main GC option Mattia Gaffuri. The Italian, however, had a brutal run at the event, first having to grapple with stomach problems on the first climbing stage on day two and then, when he was starting to feel better, crashing early and finding out afterwards that he had ridden much of the stage with a broken hand.

These days were certainly not ones that followed the plan but Peace was playing his part regardless, finishing 22nd on stage 2 to Gunung Jerai and 13th in the Cameron Highands, while there was than also a 21st in the Genting Highlands.

"I'm quite happy with how it's been going. I've just been like holding on for as long as I can each day, and I seem to be performing quite well. And I was here to support Mattia, and he was hurt. So it was a bit unfortunate we lost him, but then I just did what I could," said Peace, with his efforts not ending in the mountains as there were also digs for the breaks in the later stages.

In the end he finished 19th overall, the youngest rider by far in the top 20. Importantly, it also gave him a one up in the sibling rivalry with his older brother Oliver, who came 42nd overall at the race in 2025, because, he joked, one of his targets was "trying to do better than he [Oliver] did last year".

Even though this was Peace's very first race with the top-tier team, and indeed his first ProTour level race, such are the hopes for the talented British rider that when we spoke to his sports director Melvin Rulliere mid-way through the race, he seemed pleased, and not in the least surprised by the performance of the youngest member of the squad.

"A year ago he was fifth in the World Championship Junior, and we know now how the young kids are ready to race. So he is in a role where he is here to support a leader and learn from from that. But yeah, in terms of potential, he has everything, absolutely everything," Rulliere said.

"For sure, he will be a good rider. Physically, he climbs really well, but also he has a really good aptitude in riding a flat stage."

items.title: Russell at risk of 'double whammy' grid penalty
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
George Russell could face a further “double whammy” hit following his Malaysia retirement if his Mercedes Formula 1 power unit cannot be fixed.

The Mercedes driver had looked on course to take a podium finish at Sepang before he was forced to stop his car five laps from the chequered flag with a suspected engine problem.

The stoppage was a big blow to his already slim world championship hopes, as it meant the gap between himself and team-mate Kimi Antonelli has opened up to 84 points with just seven races remaining.

But worse than the setback in the standings is that the failure could further hurt his chances of beating Antonelli in the next races.

Russell is on the edge in terms of mileage with his current pool of engines, and he had been holding out for a switch to a fresh version until an expected upgraded Mercedes specification appears at the United States Grand Prix.

Mercedes is set to make use of opportunities under F1’s ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) rules to bring a new power unit homologation to Austin for all its cars.

But if Russell’s Malaysia engine is broken and cannot be fixed, then it will mean he would face the possibility of back-to-back engine penalties if he did not want to finish the season with a power deficit to Antonelli.

That is because he would need to take a fresh power unit in Singapore to get through this weekend, which will incur penalties, and then take a further hit in the following event in the United States for the ADUO step.

Mercedes still needs to properly analyse Russell’s power unit to find out the cause of his problem, but deputy team principal Bradley Lord admitted there could be some longer-term consequences.

“Yes, there may be a double whammy effect there after such a gut-wrenching blow,” he said. “It was devastating to see him have to pull off as he did.”

Lord said that there was no immediate answer as to what had triggered the issue, but he hoped it would not take long to understand.

“He came on the radio behind the safety car and said the PU started to sound funny,” he said. "We saw sensors then misbehaving and it was clear we had to pull the car over and we'd had a failure of some sort.

“We still need to understand what it means for his pool because he's not rich in low-mileage power units either. So that may mean we need to alter what had been our previous plan."

Russell described what he experienced as a “sudden failure” as he acknowledged that this had been a season where things were getting away from him.

Asked about any remaining title hopes, Russell said: “I knew that if I wanted to come back in the championship, I needed luck on my side, it wouldn't just be good performances.

“But here we are. Not only do I not have luck on my side, I've got bad luck on my side. I'll just keep fighting weekend by weekend, but of course it's exceptionally unlikely.”

items.title: ‘Speak With Data’: UAE Boss Slams Skeptics Fueling Del Toro-McNulty Conspiracy Theories
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: McNulty and Del Toro's trade team manager defends Mexican amid talk of illegal collusion with USA at world championships: 'He was strongest, even if McNulty won.'
items.lbText:
Did Isaac del Toro help his UAE trade teammate Brandon McNulty win the road world title?

That’s the debate that’s doing the rounds after McNulty brought the U.S. its first rainbow jersey in 33 years at the UCI road world championships last weekend.

“Del Toro was obviously working for McNulty,” gnashed Tom Pidcock in the aftermath of a wild race in Montréal.

Michael Matthews insinuated similar as Team USA’s losing rivals picked apart what went wrong last Sunday.

The Tin Foil Hat Brigade has been picking over race replays and sparking conspiracy theories ever since.

Was there a nefarious trade team alliance in this race of nations?

Speaking to QuiBici Sport , McNulty and Del Toro’s manager at UAE Emirates-XRG dismissed the doubters.

If the Mexican Del Toro somehow colluded with Team USA after McNulty slipped away with his decisive attack, Joxean Fernández Matxin wants to see proof.

“To anyone who insinuates this, I urge you to speak with data and not with opinions,” Matxin told Qui Bici Sport . “How long was Del Toro on the front? And the others who are talking, how long were they on the front trying to close it down?

“If you bring me evidence with numbers showing that he pulled less than the others, then I can agree with you,” Matxin said. “But if they are just words, with all due respect, it remains an opinion we can all form.”

Matxin’s words of defense are hardly a surprise.

He’s in the upper tier of management at UAE, the super team boasting Del Toro, McNulty, and Tadej Pogačar on the books and now a third straight year hosting the reigning world champion.

Of course he’ll say McNulty won fair and square.

But even without any possible supporting data, the evidence was all over the TV screens.

Del Toro was the most active rider in the race, despite representing one of cycling’s minnow nations.

“He wanted to win worlds,” Matxin said. “He defends the colors of Mexico because he is proud to be Mexican. He wants to make history for his country.”

Matxin went as far as to say that his Tour de France podium-finisher was the best rider in Montréal.

“In my opinion, Del Toro was the strongest, even if Brandon won. You could see that in how the other riders marked him,” Matxin told QuiBici . “The course may not have been the best for him, but in terms of condition, he was superior to everyone.”

With Pogačar on the sidelines and Remco Evenepoel on an off-day, it was a rainbow opportunity Del Toro would never throw away.

Speaking to Velo last week, Team USA sport director Mike Creed and cult favorite road captain Larry Warbasse also dismissed the collusion conspiracy .

The theory that Del Toro switched passports in the final of road worlds was, according to Warbasse, “ridiculous.”

“You don’t pull all day and then just give the race to McNulty,” Creed told Velo . “If you just finished 270km and you’re frustrated, and your name is Tom Pidcock, that’s understandable.

“For everyone else, it’s just stirring the pot,” Creed continued. “I don’t know anyone who would give away the world championships.”

So why didn’t Del Toro pull the chasers when McNulty launched his winning raid?

One, he was probably gassed. He’d just been riding the front for the best part of 40km.

Two, he was isolated and caught at the opposite end of the spectrum from USA, who flooded the zone with McNulty, Matteo Jorgenson, and Quinn Simmons.

Del Toro wasn’t shy when he debriefed the race to ESPN MX last week.

His rivals exploited Mexico’s collective weakness, and he couldn’t do more when his race started to unravel.

“The peloton raced a little against us or used the fact we didn’t have the best team,” Del Toro told ESPN MX .

“I didn’t want the gold medal to get away from me,” he added. “Finally, though, it was very difficult for me to keep going, and I ran fifth, unfortunately. It’s a bittersweet taste.”

If Team USA paid Del Toro for his role in McNulty’s world title, the Mexican clearly invested in some good acting classes.

Speculation aside, McNulty now owns the rainbow jersey for the next 12 months.

Despite the background debate, the consensus is that the 28-year-old earned the stripes courtesy of individual strength and the smarts of U.S. nationals.

McNulty hasn’t publicly spoken out about the Del Toro drama, and it’s hard to imagine he ever will.

However, the shy Arizonan could barely hide his delight after he debuted his new striped top this weekend in Italy.

McNulty hit 10th at the Giro dell’Emila on Saturday and narrowly missed the win Sunday at Coppa Agostoni.

“For sure it is still settling in, with the jersey and everything,” McNulty said Sunday after he finished second in the six-rider sprint.

“It is super special [being the world champion],” McNulty said Sunday. “I feel like the races pass faster; I don’t really think about kilometers to go anymore. Hopefully that continues. Perhaps it will wear off, and I will go back to suffering, but the last two days have been so special.”

McNulty gets two more shots at winning in rainbows before he shuts down his 2026 season.

The hilly circuits of Tre Valle Varesine await on Wednesday.

Three days later, McNulty teams up at UAE Emirates-XRG with – guess who – Del Toro for a monument brawl with Evenepoel and Paul Seixas at Il Lombardia.

That’s a race where the American and Mexican will race together.

items.title: Eight things we learned from F1's Malaysia weekend
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
From another Red Bull milestone to multiple teams being confused about why they were struggling, to a new flaw in the 2026 regulations being exposed, Formula 1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia taught us plenty.

Here's everything we learned from the first F1 weekend at Sepang in nine years...

F1's wet-weather problem is only getting worse

F1 has long looked allergic to racing in the rain over the last decade and the 2026 regulations seem to have made that allergy even worse.

The exact "software bug" that sent things haywire at Sepang wasn't a specific allergy to rain - the cars didn't break down directly because of the water on track. But it was the uniquely low-speed conditions created by the wet Sepang circuit that exposed the bug in the electronic control units fitted to the cars.

And it came after some already glum predictions of how the 2026 F1 cars would cope with a rain-soaked track. Isack Hadjar, who tested at a wet Suzuka earlier this year, said: "The only thing I remember from Japan is that the tyres have zero grip. It would make the racing very dangerous with a lot of water".

The delays needed for the FIA to send updated software to the teams meant we didn't see racing with lots of water - robbing everyone watching of a fascinating spectacle - and it leaves a big question: what will actually happen when these cars finally do race in the rain?

As FIA single seater director Nikolas Tombazis said: "Can I guarantee it will never happen again? This specific problem, yes. A problem? No, but we will do our best to avoid it."

Who knows if a first proper wet race would expose yet more problems with F1's most complicated power units ever.

Another great Red Bull F1 story achieved 

Red Bull has rattled off some astonishing F1 achievements in its journey to being one of grand prix racing’s most influential and successful entities. And it has now added another stellar chapter to its story: becoming a race-winning engine manufacturer. 

A decade or so ago, Red Bull’s engine situation was the butt of a few jokes. Not just because its partner Renault was floundering in the V6 turbo-hybrid era, but because that relationship deteriorated so badly Red Bull struck a deal to run those same engines as a customer while officially branding them as TAG Heuers. 

On the surface, we were expected to pretend there was an engine on the grid from a watch company. Well, it’s not quite the same, but now we can say (much more legitimately) there’s an engine from an energy drinks company. And it has won a race. 

Do not underestimate the scale of this challenge and success. Ford-sponsored Red Bull Powertrains has achieved something enormous by taking on, competing against, and now beating established F1 engine builders.

The investment has been immense, and the quality of the personnel sky-high, but all the right ingredients in the world guarantee nothing. Just ask Aston Martin. 

And it has also ensured Max Verstappen keeps his run going of winning a race in every single season he has competed with Red Bull. Which is not bad in itself.

Mercedes upgrade has an urgent question mark

A gain of three tenths was the internal expectation for Mercedes' major upgrade going into the Sepang weekend, but it's left it wondering whether it needs to trial it against the old package in Singapore.

Mercedes hadn't brought a major upgrade since the Canadian Grand Prix in May and it probably had a car capable of winning both titles this year even without a further upgrade.

But a step forward at Sepang would have made that title run-in a lot more comfortable and provided a good platform for 2027. But that hasn't happened; instead, it's wondering if its car has actually gone backwards.

Mercedes will have some intense engineering debriefs before Singapore to understand why it underperformed in Malaysia and whether it was simply a one-off because of the Sepang circuit's particular characteristics.

The Race understands Mercedes hasn't ruled out testing its upgrade versus its old-spec car in Singapore, though that would be tricky given Singapore is a sprint weekend.

McLaren needs to understand if it’s been left behind 

Not for the first time this year, McLaren was left to rue gambling on the wrong starting tyre. But at least, unlike in Canada, it was not alone in such a misjudgement. 

The bigger concern for McLaren is that it simply lacked competitiveness at Sepang. Its point-less return in Azerbaijan was exaggerated by incidents in the race, but that was still a muted weekend and so it was again in Malaysia, where neither Oscar Piastri nor Lando Norris had the pace to do much more in their recoveries. 

McLaren was simply fourth-best behind Red Bull, Mercedes and Ferrari, and that run just a few races ago - where it was scoring poles and even wins - has ended abruptly. 

“We have to acknowledge that potentially some competitors have developed their car with bigger steps that we did,” team boss Andrea Stella admitted. 

The only silver lining is that it finished with both cars in the points at all. That could have been very different after Norris got away with a huge misjudgement behind the safety car, and only narrowly avoided taking out himself and Piastri. 

Given Norris wrongly called for Franco Colapinto to be banned for a lapse in judgement a week ago, this was a major let-off for the world champion. 

Alpine needs help to be best of the rest now

While Red Bull’s main F1 team is now a race-winning force again, sleeping on the achievements of Racing Bulls this season would be a mistake. 

Holding fifth in the constructors’ championship means the former Toro Rosso and AlphaTauri team is on course for its best-ever season across any of its identities since Red Bull bought the ailing Minardi outfit. 

In Malaysia, Racing Bulls bagged another double points finish - despite neither of its cars starting in the top 10 - while chief rival Alpine let another opportunity to score slip. 

These two teams have quite often traded having the fifth-fastest car, but Alpine has been troublingly inconsistent and inefficient of late, failing to score in three of the past six events. 

As Racing Bulls is now 22 points ahead, Alpine needs help to finish best of the rest. With the top four teams having a clear advantage, if everything goes as it should the midfielders are fighting over ninth and 10th - or three points per round. There are only seven races left and in sprints, only the top eight cars score. 

It won’t play out exactly like this, but even if Alpine beats Racing Bulls with both cars every time from now until the end of the season, it could only gain 21 points unless there’s some outside assistance.  

No team is entirely consistent through the year, as circuit characteristics vary against the strengths and weaknesses of a car and engine package, but Aston Martin and Honda have just enjoyed another wild swing.

This embattled team went from detached at the back of the grid one weekend to respectably competitive the next when a big car upgrade arrived in Hungary earlier this season. 

But a miserable - truly miserable - Azerbaijan weekend has just given way to Aston Martin’s best result of the year with Fernando Alonso finishing eighth in Malaysia. And no car or engine changes can explain that. 

Evidently the Sepang circuit, while still reasonably power sensitive, did not expose the worst of Honda’s lingering deficiencies like Baku did - in fact Honda says it even learned driveability lessons it can use running with the wet weather engine map that limits battery power to 250kW.

And the Aston Martin chassis was clearly working much better last weekend as well. The team just doesn’t fully understand why.

It also nearly fumbled its big opportunity. Aston Martin was among the teams to gamble on slicks when the race finally started, and if safety cars had not bailed it out by resetting the order, Alonso would not have had a chance to take advantage of others having messy races to steal a very unlikely eighth place. 

Now it’s on to Singapore - where Honda’s engine issues will be less of a burden once more, so if Aston Martin can really get to the bottom of how to get its car in such a sweet spot again, another opportunity surely awaits. 

Regret and confusion over Haas no-score

Haas earned its first double points finish of the season in Baku, but Sepang was a much trickier weekend - even though Esteban Ocon briefly ran as high as sixth early in the race.

That's because Ocon was on the right tyres (intermediates) while team-mate Ollie Bearman was spiralling backwards on softs.

"I ended up on slicks, and that was the wrong choice. It wasn't my choice. I was adamant that we start on inters, and there was 0% chance that we put the slick," Bearman explained after the race.

"But the team decided to put me on the slick at the last minute, which I didn't know about. Obviously, the decision was made to split the strategy. I didn't agree with it, and in hindsight, I still don't agree with it."

Bearman admitted the team "would have looked like heroes" if the strategy had paid off, but felt "a bit hard done by" to be given what he felt was the "risky strategy" when he was the lead car within the team on the starting grid.

"It was just a shame because I felt like that decision to start me on the soft totally screwed my race," Bearman added. "I lost so much race time. I couldn't do anything about it.

"I don't blame anyone. I just want to understand what we could have done better".

Team boss Ayao Komatsu said Haas decided to "split the risk" but he "regrets" not pitting Bearman as soon as the team realised how much laptime he was losing.

The subsequent safety car closed a lot of that gap back up and Ocon lost hold of his strong points position, with Komatsu explaining, "on pit entry [Ocon] went wide and our pitstop wasn’t the best [3.6 seconds], so we lost position to one of the Racing Bulls and then pushed the new tyres too hard, and from there, Esteban’s race got destroyed."

He ended up finishing behind Bearman as they came home a distant 14th and 15th, bringing Haas's recent run of strong form to a painful end.

F1 can't wait another nine years to return to Sepang

Sepang fell off the F1 calendar just before its Netflix-fuelled popularity boom, so this weekend would have been the first taste of the circuit for a lot of the fanbase - and for over 50% of the drivers.

And it did a lot right on its unexpected return. Challenging track for qualifying? Tick. Overtaking opportunities? Tick. Strategic variation? Tick. Variable weather? Tick (even if the 2026 power units couldn't handle it).

On a calendar dominated by so many new city-centre circuits, it showed the value of an old-school track. No gimmicky corners or awkward constraints to fit your circuit around, just a well-designed, old-school track that makes use of natural elevation.

There were complaints from drivers about the "character" of the aged track surface, but does every circuit need to be a polished, completely flat runway?

The one clear improvement for any Sepang return would be fan management. There were plenty of reports on social media of fans with lengthy journeys out of the circuit, even though shuttling did improve as the weekend went on.

There are no formal plans to return to Sepang beyond 2026, but it's certainly proved itself as an 'F1 supersub', ready to jump in and host whichever country's race has been cancelled.

items.title: Ángel Arroyo, 'a legend of Spanish cycling', dies aged 70
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Ángel Arroyo, the 1983 Tour de France runner-up who is widely credited with sparking a revival in Spanish cycling, died on Sunday at the age of 70.

Tributes have since flooded in from Spain any beyond for a rider whose palmarès might have ended up fairly modest in proportion but who nevertheless is seen as making a much bigger contribution to the sport in Spain and the decades of success that followed his career.

Spain had celebrated Tour de France victories thanks to Federico Bahamontes in 1959 and Luis Ocaña in 1973, but there had been a slump in the years that followed the latter’s success. Arroyo led the line for the Reynolds team when they started as a professional outfit in 1980, and his success was swiftly followed by Pedro Delgado, who won the Tour in 1988, and Miguel Indurain, who won it five times in the 1990s when the squad was known as Banesto.

It’s now known as Movistar, in what is the longest-running team in the sport, and they have just celebrated a Spanish Vuelta a España winner in Enric Mas after years of success thanks to, among others, the former world champion Alejandro Valverde.

Valverde, who now works for the Spanish Cycling Federation, was among those to pay tribute to Arroyo on Monday, writing: “Rest in peace Ángel Arroyo. One of the great names of Spanish cycling in the 1980s.”

The Movistar team added: "Ángel Arroyo has died, a legend of Spanish cycling and one of the great riders of our team. With him, in 1983, we stepped on the podium of the Tour de France for the first time. He was a fabulous rider and one of the best climbers of his time."

As is common in professional cycling, Arroyo’s legacy is a complicated one. He was stripped of the overall title of the 1982 Vuelta a España after testing positive for the banned stimulant methylphenidate. The news came out a few days after Arroyo had celebrated what appeared to be a breakthrough achievement. Arroyo didn't deny the offense but described the use of such substances as widespread and has described himself as the 'moral winner' of the race.

In any case, Arroyo went on to make the podium of the Tour de France the following year, finishing runner-up behind the young Laurent Fignon. He did so after taking his most famous victory on the stage 15 time trial up the Puy de Dome volcano. The following year, he won the brutal mountain stage into Morzine and finished in sixth place overall.

"They were the seasons in which Spanish cycling recovered its pride and understood that it could once again compete with the French, Belgians, and Italians in the biggest races," writes Nacho Labarga in Monday’s edition of the Spanish newspaper .

"Arroyo was the link that connected two eras: that of the drought years and the generation that would go on to turn the Tour de France into familiar territory for Spanish cycling."

Arroyo’s success waned in the following years, and he retired in 1989 at the age of 32, but not before he’d been part of the Reynolds team that delivered Pedro Delgado to Tour de France glory in 1988.

"He was a cornerstone in building up cycling in our country," Delgado wrote back then.

Arroyo’s legacy is further underlined by the cycling club that was created in his name by his neighbor, Victor Sastre, which gave rise to the likes of José María Jiménez, Pablo Lastras, and a certain Carlos Sastre – Victor’s son and the winner of the 2006 Tour de France.

After retiring from professional cycling, Arroyo, who had little in the way of savings, went on to run a carwash business for many years. "I’m at the age to retire, but I cannot do so," he said in an interview with in 2023. "If I stop, I wouldn’t be able to pay for heating in the winter or air conditioning in the summer. I live hand to mouth."

"Some might see my work as a humiliation, but for me it is not. I like it and I enjoy what I do. I have the life of any other worker.”

items.title: 'Perhaps it will wear off and I will go back to suffering' – World Champion Brandon McNulty still riding high as he makes impressive start to rainbow jersey reign
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Brandon McNulty opened up his time as World Champion this past weekend in Italy with two impressive races at the Giro dell'Emilia and Coppa Agostoni, where he was 10th and second, respectively, but also on the immediate attack in his new rainbow jersey.

He, of course, started as one of the heavy favourites for the former, and did light up the decisive San Luca climb on the third of five ascents, but McNulty was unable to go with the winning move led by Visma-Lease a Bike's Matteo Jorgenson and eventual winner Davide Piganzoli, who played things perfectly in the finale.

As for reasons for not being at your best, though, none can be better than the one McNulty gave on his Instagram, detailing how the superhuman 35km solo effort – which so nearly came unstuck – he put in to claim the rainbow jersey in Montreal was still taking its toll.

"I enjoyed every single second of my first race in rainbows today," said McNulty. "It’s safe to say I left every single bit of my legs, and probably some pieces of my soul on roads last weekend so I’m still missing a bit, but there’s still a lot of opportunities to come!"

That next opportunity came on the subsequent afternoon in Lissone, and after his UAE team did much of the early work, McNulty found himself off the front in the eventual race-winning move of seven riders with 40km to go.

Six made it into the final sprint after no one was able to get away solo, leaving McNulty to try and get his first win in rainbows from a small group kick. His punch was solid, but not enough to come around Frenchman Paul Lapeira (Decathlon CMA CGM), ending his first weekend as World Champion with a second place.

Still riding the wave of what will become a career-defining victory, McNulty has begun his year-long reign with two impressive performances. Yes, when Tadej Pogačar returns next season and they race together, the US rider will still play second fiddle as a super domestique, but that win in Canada could yet propel him to new heights.

"For sure it is still settling in, with the jersey and everything. [Sunday] was good, I am still a bit fatigued from last week and also [on Saturday] I went super hard. It was a really hard race and I was happy to be there in the final, and then sprints can go one way or the other, so I am happy with the efforts today," said McNulty on UAE's team website.

"It is super special [being the World Champion]. I feel like the races pass faster, I don’t really think about kilometres to go anymore. Hopefully that continues! Perhaps it will wear off and I will go back to suffering, but the last two days have been so special. Everybody has been very supportive and I have had so many people come up to me to congratulate me, so I want to say thank you to everybody."

McNulty will next be in action at Tuesday's Tre Valli Varesine, again taking on the role of leader in Pogačar's absence at these Italian Autumn Classics, before he will likely do the same at the final Monument of the 2026 season on Sunday: Il Lombardia.

items.title: This Amazon Prime Day deal drops the Hammerhead Karoo bike computer by $85
items.author: paul.brett@futurenet.com (Paul Brett)
items.content:
Amazon Prime Big Deals Days are here, and run for 48 hours from October 6th to 7th.

As deal-hunting guru, one early discount I've spotted is on one of the best bike computers and our recommendation when it comes to serious navigation performance.

For UK Prime Day shoppers, the Karoo 3 is even cheaper away from Amazon. Sigma Sports are also getting involved in the big discounts and have dropped the Hammerhead Karoo 3 to just £359, almost £100 off the usual £450.

To access Amazon Prime deals, you'll need a Prime membership. You can sign up for a and cancel anytime before the $14.99 per month fee kicks in.

UK shoppers can grab a huge £91 off the Karoo 3 at Sigma. As one of the biggest cycling retailers in the UK, Sigma Sports has its alternative to Amazon Prime Day Sales, and there are plenty of worthwhile reductions, including the Karoo 3. They also offer Amazon-matching free delivery on orders over £50.View Deal

When we put the Hammerhead Karoo through its paces, it earned an outstanding 4.5-star score. In fact, tech expert Tom Wieckowski noted during testing that it came close to snatching the crown as the best overall cycling computer on the market. Just missing out to the Garmin Edge 1050, but the 1050, with its incredible array of features, just got the nod. However, at $700, it does cost significantly more.

We found the navigation performance to be a real highlight on the Karoo, and it delivered impressive precision. Karoo's multi-band GNSS technology ensured accurate tracking in any environment, from city streets to rugged trails.

Another new mapping feature is its ability to send a pin from Google or Apple Maps to the Karoo on the fly. Simply share the selected pin from the maps app to the computer map screen, and the Hammerhead will create your route, which makes finding a coffee stop, shop or any other landmark a breeze, especially when you don't know where you are.

Alongside navigation, a cycling computer is judged on battery life. In our original review, Tom noted that battery life was claimed to be 15 hours, which at that time was more than enough for most people.

Hammerhead has recently dropped software updates for the Karoo, and it now stretches the battery life even further, with a claimed up to 35+ hours in Battery Saver mode. So if you have multi-day bike adventures planned, or just a forgetful charger, then these updates further boost the attractive features on the Karoo device.

Elsewhere, Tom highlighted that the Karoo "brought an awful lot to the table" and built on the class-leading touchscreen and resolution that the previous model was well-known for.

The Karoo might not match up to our best overall choice, the Garmin Edge 1050, but it's not far behind. Especially when you consider the Garmin device will cost you at full price $699 in the US. In the UK, the Garmin Edge 1050 is discounted on Amazon by a not very impressive 3%, to £603.70.

We reckon the Karoo can easily hold its own against the Garmin, and offers an appealing smartphone-like user experience of the Karoo, and at this price, the Karoo is a very appealing purchase.

items.title: 'The last jersey I still wanted and needed' – Champion of championships Remco Evenepoel completes the set with eighth elite title out of eight
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Remco Evenepoel is undeniably one of the greatest riders of this ongoing generation, but as he added the UEC European Championships road race title to his already illustrious palmarès in Slovenia, the Belgian completed the set of winning all eight championship titles available to him.

Across the two disciplines of the road race and individual time trial, at just 26, Evenepoel has now won both at the Belgian National Championships, European Championships, World Championships, and the Olympic Games, in a run spanning back seven years, with 24 medals won at the elite level.

In an era mostly dominated by one rider, Tadej Pogačar, Evenepoel's talents as a time trial expert and elite one-day racer, long known since he burst onto the scene as a junior, have seen him go on to achieve a level of completion the Slovenian has only managed half of.

And looking back to 2018, just 18 months after he had become a cyclist, is it any real surprise? At the Europeans Championships, he did the double in the junior road race and time trial in Zlín, Czechia, before netting an unprecedented double double as he achieved the same feat at the World Championships in Innsbruck, winning both junior rainbow jerseys by more than 1:20.

Even as an inexperienced teenager, Evenepoel was the master of championships, and this latest feat and completion of the championship bingo only adds to his legacy as a rider for the big occasion.

"This jersey is added to my list of achievements, but you played a big part in that. A huge thank you for that," he added that evening, in his speech to the Belgian team and staff. "The same goes for the staff. Everything was well organised again. Thanks to everyone who contributed even a little bit.

"And I think I'm not riding championships anymore now, right?" he joked. "No, that's not true."

His first major elite title came at the Europeans a year after his junior dominance, vindicating his early step up to the professional level as he beat specialists Kasper Asgreen, Edoardo Affini, Stefan Küng, Alex Dowsett and Filippo Ganna to the title in Alkmaar at just 19.

Evenepoel's next gold medal came at the Belgian Championships, but not until 2022, with his major crash at Il Lombardia in 2020 stunting some of his inevitable progress. He beat then-teammate Yves Lampaert convincingly to the time trial title in Gavere.

Fast forward three months and Evenepoel became road race World Champion in Wollongong, claiming the rainbow jersey by more than two minutes after he went solo in the last 25km.

In 2023, he added two more major titles, winning the Belgian national road race title ahead of Alec Segaert in Izegem, before going on to win the first of his four World titles in the elite time trial, scorching to victory in Stirling after finishing on the podium in his first three attempts.

He made history a season later, becoming the first male rider to do the double at the Olympic Games in Paris, dominating the race against the clock, before claiming an iconic solo win in the road race. With the help of Wout van Aert marking Mathieu van der Poel up the Montmartre climb, Evenepoel was able to time his attack to perfection, surviving despite a late bike change, and celebrating in front of the Eiffel Tower.

With this feat achieved, Evenepoel's tally of championship wins was already at seven, with just the European road race remaining on his hit list. Before the race in Ljubljana, Evenepoel had gone close twice to completing the eight, losing out to Sonny Colbrelli in a two-up sprint in Trento in 2021, and only being beaten by Pogačar in France a season ago.

Lining up at the start with Pogačar still out injured, Evenepoel was the heavy favourite to claim the iconic European jersey, but as is typical of the Belgians' entire career, it was never going to be as simple as him riding off solo into the sunset.

The Italian team mounted a major challenge, upping the pace for their big leaders Giulio Ciccone and Christian Scaroni, and just as the race started to really heat up and Evenepoel began his move on the Možjanca climb, with Ciccone following him, the Belgian crashed.

A week after the disappointment of failing to deliver at the World Championships, Evenepoel's hope of the eighth was looking like it might go up in smoke, but with luck on his side, his bike wasn't badly broken, and his teammates were just coming up to help dig him out of the hole.

Maxim van Gils and Ramses Debruyne brought him back to the front, and the next time up, he was able to put the hammer down again. But still, the race wasn't done, with Ciccone able to follow and then staying – for the vast majority of the run for home – in the stronger rider's wheel.

Not only did it take a two-up sprint to decide the day, but one of the closest photo finishes in recent memory confirmed Evenepoel was the champion, narrowly pipping Ciccone with an expert bike throw by the barest of margins in Šenčur. Not only did he complete the set, but Evenepoel had righted the wrongs of Montreal.

"I might not have really shown it, but I was still very disappointed in myself and my performance. I also felt like I had disappointed the whole country with my performance," he said. "I still hope that everyone is proud now that we are back. And sorry again for last week's World Championship. Now I'm going to celebrate this one big time."

Evenepoel travelled back to Belgium today, but will be on the road once again on Wednesday, "Because there is another important race on Saturday," as he heads for Italy to take on Il Lombardia. Second in the past two seasons behind Pogačar, Evenepoel will be the favourite for the Monument and will look to close out a successful 2026 season with a bang.
