items.title: Formula 1 Superstar Valtteri Bottas Is Cycling From Malaysia to Singapore for His Next Grand Prix
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Some drivers would take a private jet for the long journey from Sepang to Singapore – but not Bottas, the F1 racer-turned gravel aficionado.
items.lbText:
Valtteri Bottas is decompressing from a disappointing DNF at Sunday’s Grand Prix in Malaysia by cycling some 350km to his next race.

It’s not the usual way Formula 1 drivers choose to recover from the mind-zapping fatigue and furnace-like conditions of a 300kph race in stormy Southeast Asia.

But it’s the way that F1’s elite gravel cycling convert has decided will work for him.

On Sunday night, Bottas completed “Leg 1” of a multi-day adventure ride toward this coming weekend’s Singapore Grand Prix.

The 37-year-old Cadillac driver had spun out on lap nine of a wet and wild race on the Sepang International Circuit on Sunday, which was being used as a substitute venue for the originally planned race in Bahrain.

Not long after stripping out of his overalls, Bottas clocked 56km in little more than two hours of night-time riding heading southeast toward Si Rusa.

The veteran car driver and Canyon bikes ambassador posted a video to Instagram showing him bumping his way across gravelly trails, followed by a #foodporn photo of a boutique dinner upon arrival in the popular tourist spot on the Malaysian coast.

With a base salary of around $5 million USD, Bottas hardly needs to “dirtbag” his journey, after all.

Bottas is famed for his off-the-racetrack exploits.

He’s been riding bikes for years and more recently integrated into the gravel racing scene through his partner, Tiffany Cromwell. He’s scored podium finishes at SBT Gravel and the Belgium Waffle Ride, and helped establish the FNLD GRVL event.

Bottas told his sponsors at Canyon earlier this year that he sees the bike as good for both his body and his mind.

“When I’m on my bike, I gain cardio, but I also use the bike almost like a stress release, you know? In a way, it’s a great way to clear my head if I have a bit of stress, and a chance to explore,” he said.

“It’s also a way for me to challenge myself when I’m not racing in my car. And when I miss racing, then I race on my bicycle.”

And while Bottas hasn’t spoken publicly about his trans-Grands Prix adventure this week, he must see it as a timely pressure release.

The long-time bike lover qualified for the UCI Gravel World Championships in Australia on October 11 after he finished fifth in his age group at the gravel world series event in Hlinsko, Czech Republic.

However, the champs had to go on ice for Bottas.

They clash directly with the approaching Singapore GP, where he and his Cadillac teammate Sergio Pérez will chase some much-needed points to claw their way out of the bottom of the F1 drivers’ championship.

items.title: Gary Anderson: F1 got lucky Malaysia chaos wasn't worse
items.author: Gary Anderson
items.content:
When the Formula 1 cars headed off on their formation lap for the Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang, I didn't know whether to laugh or cry.

I simply couldn't believe what I was seeing and felt that a few million other people and I were just about to be robbed of what should have turned out to be a great race. Old sparring partners Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton sitting side by side on the front row was going to be epic.

The weather conditions changing at the last minute always spices things up, but cars were basically stopping everywhere.

It was all through no fault of the drivers or the teams; their hands are tied with these stupid 2026 regulations.

I'm just about fed up with complaining about them. They are so far away from what I would call racing or what a racing driver wants that it just makes a mockery of what is supposed to be the crème de la crème of motorsport.

I'm not going to go into the fact that these cars can't or aren't allowed even to venture out on the track in the wet - that's all for another day!

Today's gripe is simply about how these stupid power unit regulations and how they are implemented are basically dangerous.

How many times this year, after seeing a driver make what we thought was an error, does that driver come on the radio and say ‘I have no idea what just happened there'? We only have to go back to Baku when Valtteri Bottas went into the safety barrier on the final lap of the race. This happened because he went down the escape road at Turn 1, the car “got confused” about where it was on the track, so instead of slowing down when he pressed the brake pedal as he wanted to, it went straight on into the barriers.

If we look at the sporting regulations; Article B1.8.1 states: “The driver must drive the F1 car alone and unaided.”

Now I completely understand why the paddle-shift gear-change system complies with that requirement, as the driver has to instigate the gear change by operating the paddle. However, I am confused that if the driver is pressing the brake pedal and the car ‘decides' it doesn't want to slow down, how does that comply with Article B1.8.1?

Moving that onto what happened on the formation lap for the Bahrain GP, we have the following rules being severely tested;

Article B1.8.5 states: “At no time may an F1 car be driven unnecessarily slowly, erratically or in a manner which could be deemed potentially dangerous to other drivers or any other person.”

And Article B1.8.7 states ”Any driver whose car has a significant failure or fault which means it cannot reasonably return to the pitlane without unnecessarily impeding another competitor or otherwise hindering the competition must leave the track as soon as it is safe to do so.”

In the technical regulations, Article C1.4 states: “The stewards may prohibit the participation of a vehicle whose construction is deemed to be dangerous.

“Should the relevant information become apparent during a session, such a decision may apply with immediate effect.”

And Article C1.5 states: “F1 cars must comply with these regulations in their entirety at all times during a competition,” and Article C1.7 says “It is the duty of each competitor to satisfy the FIA and the stewards that its Formula 1 car complies with these regulations in their entirety at all times during a competition.

“With regard to power units used on a Formula 1 car, this duty and responsibility also extends to the PU manufacturer.”

If you sum those up, the driver, the teams and the power unit manufacturer's hands are tied by an inadequate understanding and, from that lack of understanding, an inadequate set of regulations.

If we just take the startline chaos we saw in pre-season testing, where the cars couldn't manage a practice start, the FIA changed the start procedure to incorporate a five-second turbo spool-up time prior to the lights coming on. This was because of the lack of understanding of how much the teams would struggle after the removal of the MGU-H.

Being the governing body, the FIA could change that and any regulation it wanted by deeming it as a safety change. Stranded cars on the grid are dangerous but it never needed to get to that point in the first place.

And back to these power units as they are now, how long do we have to wait before someone gets hurt? Just imagine the chaos that was just around the corner if the race at Sepang had actually started in dry conditions and that thunderstorm came in around lap five.

We would have had cars littered all around the track with the drivers playing with the steering wheel buttons a bit like Elton John on his piano keys; the only difference would be they would be hitting control-alt-delete.

While they were doing that, they wouldn't have been complying with either the no erratic driving rule of Article B1.8.5 or the don't unnecessarily impede others with an ailing car mentioned in Article B1.8.7.

I'm not going to go into the rights and wrongs of what happened at Sepang because, in reality, it doesn't really matter what the details of the reason it happened were. It shouldn't have happened.

However, what worries me more is that the regulation setter, the FIA, was able to come up with a software fix in a very short amount of time and install it in all cars without any depth of real-world testing. Then what other software gremlins are lurking in there, waiting to rear their ugly head?

Now's the time to act with maturity and responsibility and react to the situation we saw at Sepang. Yes the FIA say it covered that problem with a software fix, but did it fully eradicate it or is the next problem lurking just around the corner?

This was race 16 of this season. Yes, it was the first wet event, but even still, the problems we have should not be happening.

I have been saying for a long time that the driver needs to be given control of the car through their two pedals and the steering wheel. Pull or push the upshift paddle for an upshift, pull or push the downshift paddle for a downshift, turn it to the left if you want to go left, turn it to the right if you want to go right, press the brake pedal if you want to slow down; the harder you press, the more you slow; press the torque (throttle) pedal if you want to go faster; the further you press it, the more torque you get.

As far as the harvesting and deployment is concerned it is very easy to fix. You need to put the cart before the horse instead of someone inventing this 50/50% internal combustion engine to electrical torque usage. And that 50/50 split is - other than for a very short snapshot in time per lap - basically impossible when you have cars that over an average lap are requesting positive torque from say 20% through to 100% (with this the driver is basically saying ‘I want to go faster') for roughly 60% of the lap with a negative torque request (I.e. less than 10% positive torque and brake pressure) from say 20% to 100% of the maximum brake pressure seen on a lap (the driver is basically saying ‘I want to go slower') of the brake pressure for only 20% of a lap.

If you simply take those numbers you get 80% of the lap either accelerating or braking significantly, the other 20% is down to part throttle usage. If they are anywhere near correct then you either need three times the harvesting capability you have relative to deployment, or you go to a 75% internal combustion engine and a 25% electrical torque balance.

Yes, it will mean that this mythical 1000bhp and speeds in excess of 350km/h (218mph) on the straights that F1 seems to be chasing will be reduced to probably 850bhp and 320km/h (199mph), but do we really care? I remember when that 200mph in old money was seen as a great threshold to shoot at. This ratio could be optimised pre-event for each circuit by simply averaging out the balance request from the five power unit manufacturers.

After everything settled down, we still had a very good race, but we need to remember that one of the cars that stopped on that initial formation lap was Hamilton, before his Ferrari eventually restarted. After a dubious tyre choice of slicks for the restart, which basically left him over a minute behind the leader, with a little help from the VSC and then the safety car, he ended up on the podium. However, through no fault of his own or his team, his Ferrari could have ended up not even starting.

items.title: Key figure in Honda's F1 return to be replaced in 2027
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Honda will get a new racing boss next year after the retirement of current president and CEO Koji Watanabe, who helped manage the manufacturer’s official return to Formula 1.

Watanabe will be replaced as the head of Honda Racing Corporation by Keiichi Yasuda on January 1, slightly earlier than executive-level changes would typically happen in April to align with the motorsport season.

Yasuda is currently HRC’s executive vice president and representative director.

Like Watanabe, he is a company man who has been with Honda since 1990. Prior to his HRC leadership role, which included overseeing Honda’s official F1 return under the new 2026 engine regulations, Watanabe rose to be a senior figure on the communications and marketing side within Honda.

He assumed the HRC job as part of Honda’s restructuring of its motorsport efforts in 2022 when it unified its motorcycle and car racing programmes under the same entity.

That made Watanabe a senior figure and spokesperson for Honda’s enduring relationship with Red Bull to the end of 2025 and then its new engine project with Aston Martin this year.

Honda has had a dismal formal return to F1, though, suffering a lack of performance even since the chronic reliability problems that caused an embarrassing start to the season across testing and the early races.

This has at least in part been caused by Honda’s shaky commitment to F1 and its damaging decision to withdraw officially at the end of 2021 - only continuing as effectively a service partner to Red Bull, managing the engines that were frozen in homologation from 2022 to 2025.

Honda’s board then decided to re-commit to F1 for the new rules in 2026 after all, which meant attempting to revive a project that had been gutted to redistribute engineers to other programmes - thus leaving Honda on the back foot for the new regulations.

One of the consequences of this was Aston Martin claiming it only discovered late last year just how different the Honda project was to its previous, more successful era with Red Bull.

The key decision for this was made before Watanabe was put in charge of HRC, though his role inevitably made him an important figure thereafter even if his influence over the state of the project this year is hard to discern.

Honda says the change for 2027 is being made “as part of a planned periodic personnel rotation designed to strengthen the management structure in response to global transformation and to accelerate business expansion for the next generation”.

Yasuda comes from the human resources side of Honda, with an interest in its motorcycle activities, and rose to the top position in Honda's HR division prior to joining HRC in 2026.

items.title: Honda HRC to get new boss with Watanabe set to retire
£800m in, £800m out - why Man City scandal shines light on Man Utd finances
items.content: <article>Manchester City's owners have been found guilty of injecting money into the club. At Manchester United, fans are frustrated at how much has been taken out.</article>
items.lbText:
The Premier League's statement laid it out in black and white.

'A total of £830.69m, payable and paid by Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) to the club'.

In other words, Manchester City 's owners circumvented the league's financial regulations by pumping money into the club.

The damning judgement landed less than five days after Manchester United 's extended filing to the New York Stock Exchange which detailed their end of year accounts to 30 June 2026.

Contained within it was an interest payment of £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year.

And respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble now estimates that United's net interest payments since the leveraged Glazer takeover of the club in 2005 have risen to a total of £852m.

Without excusing City's owners in any way, it has not escaped the attentions of many fans from both Manchester clubs that while the arrival of one ownership group in the city has resulted in money being ploughed in, with the other, it has meant a similar significant sum being taken out.

United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."

This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence.

Record revenues of £677.6m, projected to go as high as £760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate.

Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths.

In confirming they had spent £191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional £90m. It took their overall debt to £1.15bn.

To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was £667m.

Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was £375m. Of that, £218m must be paid before 30 June 2027. United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another £122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets – although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this.

When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said £63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined.

Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad.

Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that.

In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at £313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to £302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season.

While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance.

Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer – their £148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others – their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear.

When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated £47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less.

Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for £74m in 2019, United have only generated more than £25m for a player on four occasions – for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho.

It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales.

In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020.

Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late.

The negativity around Manchester City 's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford.

Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium – all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch.

In 2017-18, United made £80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got £31m for reaching the Europa League final. In their recently negotiated shirt deal with Adidas, a £10m annual reduction is applied if the club miss out on reaching the Champions League.

When Carrick sends his team out against bottom-club Tottenham at Old Trafford on 10 October, they will be attempting to drag themselves up from 12th place in the table.…

items.title: What’s behind Marquez becoming so serious
Most aero socks are a waste of money: Here's the wind tunnel verified proof
items.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
items.content:
Even though aerodynamics has become priority number one for most competitive cyclists buying new kit, aero socks are perhaps the most ridiculed upgrade of the past decade.

Speaking generally, the promise of 'free' (albeit often very expensive) speed is hard to ignore, compounded by the fact that pro cyclists – who rarely need to worry about the accompanying expense – place extreme importance on the matter as their careers can be made or lost by it.

Yet while most aero products are embraced quickly and without second thought, aero socks took a good while to gain acceptance. They didn't pass the fashion test, and the old guard dismissed them as a gimmick or a marginal gain too far. But when comparative tests started showing measurable benefits, more and more teams started wearing them, and nowadays, they're a staple in the pro peloton. You'll spot amateurs in them too, especially on race day.

We've now hit a point where some aero socks are so highly technical and researched that they regularly fetch up to £50+ per pair, and some even stretch as far as £100, and that's before we get into custom territory. The thing is, others can be had for just £3 if you know where to shop.

So do you actually stand to save more watts by buying the more expensive - or name brand - socks?

To find out, we collated 26 pairs of socks and headed to the wind tunnel.

Our cohort included 22 pairs from named cycling brands, including Velotoze, Rule28, Aero Cycling Gear, NoPinz, Rapha, Castelli, Assos and more.

It also included a pair of comparatively cheap 'Rock Bros' socks that we bought from Amazon, an extremely cheap pair of 'West Biking' socks from Temu, a pair of cotton everyday socks from the British high-street clothing store Next, as well as some technical hiking socks from another high-street store.

The full list, in alphabetical order, is as follows:

  • Aero Cycling gear v5 Hexaflow
  • Mountain Warehouse Hiking Socks
  • Next everyday cotton socks
  • Rule 28 Neo Aero Sock (Double Layer)

So are expensive aero socks any faster than cheap aero socks? Does a pair of aero socks beat a pair of nominally 'standard' cycling socks? What about compared to a pair of everyday or hiking socks?

The title of this article has probably already given you a clue as to the answers to some of these questions, but scroll down to find out the details.

Unlike previous CN Labs tests, where you're forced to read through (or scroll past) 3000 words explaining the protocols, caveats and standardisations, I'm going to dive straight into the results and do the nerdy stuff later. Please do take time to read the nerdy bits below, though, as that'll help you understand how we landed on the data and what caveats apply.

It's also important to state up front that the data is subject to an error margin of 0.2w at the lower speed, and 1.17w at the higher speed.

The biggest thing of note here is that there are very small differences between all the pairs of aero socks on test. There's just 1.85 watts between the fastest and slowest, and the difference between many of the socks in between is smaller than our error margin.

The Aero Cycling Gear V5 was fastest, but both NoPinz's Sonic and Rule 28's One Aero Sock can lay claim to victory too, with the error margin taken into account.

According to Rule 28, its more expensive Neo Aero Sock, with its double-layer finish, was designed for speeds over 55km/h for time trialling and track riding, so its mid-table result isn't a surprise here. It's also a lesson in choosing the right product for your needs, as spending more money doesn't automatically equal better performance across the board.

Just off the podium, the NoPinz Hypersonic Mk2, Sockeloen FSOTP 468 and Santini Madss are close behind, with Castelli's Fast Feet 4 sitting just behind those.

And then the next dozen are all pretty much indistinguishable, despite the price bracket ranging from £3.68 for the 'West Biking' brand of socks we bought from Temu, to £50 for the Rapha and Assos options.

Behind this, there are small steps down, before a bigger jump to the two pairs of non-cycling socks.

The error margin here is around 50% bigger than that of the 30km/h test, meaning even more potential for crossover between results. The results show that the Rule 28 One Aero Sock banked the best result, but it was a bit of a lottery as to which actually came out on top. Any of the top 17 - yes, seventeen - can claim the top spot, because they were all within 1.17 watts (our error margin) of the winner.

And to clarify, this is a pretty tight error margin at such a high speed, just ten counts (or 0.0010) in terms of CdA. So while it looks like we've just performed a bad test that shows all socks as being about the same, that's because all the socks are… about the same.

When you get into the bottom third of the table, we do start to see some differences, but most of those still sit within the error margin of five places either above or below.

Notably, the Velotoze Aero Pro is a step behind the others, despite being a high-priced aero product. Having shared the data with Velotoze, we're at a loss as to what caused this. It could be that the material was overstretched when fitted, or it could have been a glitch. It doesn't concur with Velotoze's own data, which showed them to be 6 watts faster than Velotoze' baseline coolmax socks at 40km/h in its own internal testing.

And the Veto 1.0 is a standard cycling sock by design, with none of your typical aero fabrics or trip strips, nor the common papery thin fragility, but the brand does claim to have tested them in a wind tunnel with good results.

We're looking at a gap of 4.9 watts (+/- 1.17w) between the fastest and slowest cycling socks on test, which is still better than a kick in the teeth, but given the £14.99 pair of Rock Bros socks from Amazon are just as fast as the £30-50 pairs from all the big brands, it's a damning outcome for anyone charging big money promising aero gains.

And like the 30km/h data above, the distant duo at the bottom of the table (in the form of the hiking socks and the everyday cotton socks) are the exception that proves the rule. There's a further five watts between the slowest aero socks and the slowest non-cycling socks.

I guess my main regret here is not taking more 'normal' cycling socks along to see how they compare, but I'm quite confident they'd sit within the error margin too.

While there's no clear trend that we can see, it's interesting to see how the order differs at the two speeds.

The consistent position of the two non-cycling socks – the hiking socks and the cotton everyday socks – at the bottom of the table is reassurance that the wind tunnel was spitting out accurate numbers. If a pair of woolly socks from my local hiking store outperformed dedicated aero socks, I'd be concerned we'd done something wrong.

While it's fair to say the difference between each pair of socks is minimal, can we at least spot a trend with taller generally being faster than shorter?

That's long been the general train of thought. It's why we see time triallists in knee-high socks, and partly why the UCI banned socks over a certain height (although that was mainly because they look weird too).

To find out, I've grouped the socks by their height to see if taller does indeed equal faster.

There's a slight bias towards better performance at the taller heights, but it's far from clearcut. We had socks here ranging from 20cm to 26cm tall, but some of the socks in the 20cm category are just as fast as those up at 24 and 26cm.

This one's so clear-cut that it doesn't even need a graph to prove it. The £3 socks are mid-table, the £14.99 socks are on the podium, and more than one near-£50 pair sits in the bottom third of our test.

There's no clear correlation between price and aerodynamic performance.

On the day, we decided that next time, we'd try to work with a brand like Sockeloen or Vorteq to create a custom-fitted pair to see if that makes any difference. Sockeloen offers a €1000 option that involves aero consultancy, for example.

Of course, cheaper items - socks and otherwise - could cut corners in other areas. They might be faster in a one-minute wind tunnel test, but if they lose their stick and fall down halfway through a ride, or if they lose their stretch and become baggy after three washes, or they fall apart entirely, you're giving away all the aero gains and more.

The contrary to that, though, is that many aero socks from big-name brands are incredibly fragile. Some are much better than others, but the papery finish you get on some is easy to damage. I've ripped three pairs in the past year alone. And the lack of stretch in the material on others means you really need to fight to get them on, which in turn increases the risk of damage.

That's not the subject of today's test, so we will be putting the various socks through their real-world paces to see how they fare in longer-term use.

But even so, when there's no aero performance guarantee, and the risk of damage means they could last just as long as something made less well, why buy something at 3x - or, in the case of the Temu socks, 14x - the price?

There are clearly watts to be saved between the non-cycling socks (everyday cotton and the hiking socks) and the cycling socks, of which the best example is the Veto 1.0.

There is then another small uptick to the nominally 'aero' socks, but the difference between that Veto 1.0 and an 'aero' cycling sock could range anywhere from negative three watts (ie, worse) to a maximum of around six watts (both at 45km/h).

But given our data shows small differences between the aero socks, there's no single winner in today's test. Rule 28 will enjoy the results of the 45km/h test, and likewise Aero Cycling Gear in the 30km/h test, but the reality is the socks are all so close to one another that you, as a consumer, should probably just buy the cheapest, or the ones you like the look of most.

At £3.68, the 'West Biking' socks I bought from Temu promise incredible aero performance in terms of watts saved vs money spent. They did feel pretty basic in their materials, though, as can be expected at a price that would allow you to buy FOURTEEN pairs for the same cost as the most expensive on test.

The feel and quality of the £14.99 'Rock Bros Grid' socks from Amazon were just as good as most of the 'big brand' products, though, so I'd be very tempted to buy those; and that's still between half and a third of the price of most others here. The only downside to those is the big 'Rock' on one leg and 'Bros' on the other, but they make them in dozens of various colours and designs. If they made them in pure white, I expect they'd sell incredibly well.

Assuming you do want to buy something that promises to be aero, there's very little way to know which is the best one for you.

There's no obvious correlation between aero performance and cuff height, price, or brand. They're also all designed to work at varying speeds, and the optimal pair for you will probably depend on what sort of riding you're doing, whether it's windy, how many people you're riding with, and the shape and size of your legs.

Therefore, unless you're going to hire a wind tunnel and a team of data scientists to run simulations on your upcoming race, you're probably best off just buying the cheap ones and spending the rest of the money on carbs.

To find out how aerodynamic they were, we took all the socks to the wind tunnel at the Silverstone Sports Engineering Hub.

The wind tunnel measures CdA (Coefficient of Drag x Area), which quantifies how easily something passes through the air. The 'Coefficient of Drag' is a measure of how easily air passes over something's surface, while the 'Area' is a simple measure of its size. Reducing the size of something isn't always possible (although there is a size difference between a hiking sock and a paper-thin aero sock), so helping the air flow over it neatly is where the aerodynamicist's skill comes in, with things like ribbed fabrics and trip strips.

As you'll have seen above, we tested each pair at two wind speeds: 30km/h and 45km/h, to try to see if any of the socks performed better at one speed over the other. We used a powered roller to spin the wheels at the same speed as the wind, to add a little more realism to the test.

We tested each pair of socks on a static-leg mannequin. While a pedalling leg mannequin is more realistic, it's not something we currently have access to. Fortunately, the repeatability of a static leg mannequin is generally better, so we'd have less accuracy and fewer conclusions. The repeatability of a real rider is much lower, and would have led to an error margin approximately 3x the size of what we had.

We tested at three different yaw angles: -5°, 0°, and +5°. This is a narrower sweep than our bike tests, but it still covered the angles that riders will experience a vast majority of the time, and it still allowed us to calculate a single wind-averaged drag figure representative of real-world conditions. We could have stopped at zero degrees – a direct headwind – since most socks are largely symmetrical, but we opted to test both sides to be more confident in the data we were seeing.

Each measurement was captured for 15 seconds. This is approximately twice as long as needed to see a steady CdA figure and get a result that we can confidently call accurate – a mannequin doesn't move, so there's no unwanted wobbles or head tilts that need to be smoothed out by a longer exposure – but shortening the sample time would have only saved us around five minutes across the whole test, so not really worth it. Better to have extra confidence in the data.

Aside from the socks, everything was kept exactly the same for each test. That includes the bike, the mannequin, its position on the bike, its clothing, its helmet, the shoes, and so on.

We didn't standardise the sock height across all socks, because some are designed to be around 20cm tall, whereas others sat at 26cm. Trying to run everything at 23cm would have meant some being overly stretched, and others being baggy and wrinkled.

Instead, we fitted each one in a way that felt natural – not too stretched, but not loose or baggy – and we measured the height (ensuring it was equal on both legs too). Then we adjusted it to the nearest centimetre, so as to standardise socks somewhat against similar-height competitors.

Those heights were then correlated against performance to see if we could spot a trend between height and aero.

To quantify the error margin, we tested the same pair of socks at three points throughout the test and then worked out the maximum gap between them. That difference was then used as the error margin.

That equated to an error margin of 0.2 watts at 30km/h, and was slightly bigger at 45km/h, coming in at 1.17w. Those margins are outlined in the graphs above.

It's important to note that this error margin is around 3x better than the last time we tested aero socks - which was done with a real rider - and resulted in an error margin of over 3 watts. Even so, the error is still big enough to encompass around half the socks we tested, and thus prove that although some are faster than others, the differences are quite minuscule.

As ever, our data is representative of our day of testing and is far from the final word on the aerodynamic performance of these products, especially as it might pertain to each individual using them.

We're proud to say the test is completely impartial, and we believe it is the biggest of its kind in terms of the number of products tested, but we don't pretend it's the be-all and end-all.

We simply hope that it provides an extra stream of comparison data for our readers, to help them choose which one to buy in the broader context of other similar aero comparisons, as well as the various other metrics that govern a good or bad purchase (ie price, comfort, aesthetics, and so on).

With that in mind, there are some unexpected results that are worth highlighting. The Velotoze Pro Aero is perhaps the biggest outlier in the 45km/h test. It doesn't align with the 30km/h test, nor Velotoze's own measurements, and we've been back and forth with them to try to understand it. Theories include possibly overstretching the sock on fitting, but we've been unable to pinpoint an obvious error.

Another includes the Sockeloen FSOTP 468. Despite being designed to excel at 46.8km/h (hence the name), it dropped down the order at the nearby 45km/h speed. This is closer to the others and thus could just be a fault of the error margin, but still it's surprising to see it perform worse than its peers at a speed it was designed to excel at. These socks weren't brand new out of the box; they'd been worn a few times since we received them for our prior aero sock test. They hadn't stretched to any noticeable extent, but my strongest theory here is that they've lost some of their performance in age.

The Assos socks were also used, held over from our previous round of sock testing in 2024, and despite performing really well in our previous test, they were mid-table this time. It's possibly a coincidence, but it could add weight to the above.

When making calculations for speed (and in turn, time to complete a 40km TT), we aren't accounting for gradients, corners, drivetrain loss or any other variable. We're looking for the difference between each product here, not an absolute forecast.

And finally, this test wasn't in any way sponsored. We paid for the wind tunnel hire at the normal rate, and this test, like all of our CN Labs projects, is made possible solely and entirely by the paying subscribers. Without your support, these tests wouldn't happen, so thank you.

items.title: ‘He Felt Really Guilty’: Worlds Defeat Had Bigger Impact than Believed on Evenepoel
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Remco Evenepoel grabs victory in Euro road championships by the tiniest margin, then renounces TT defense.
items.lbText:
Remco Evenepoel (r) celebrates winning the European road race championship in Ljubljana, Slovenia (Photo: David Pintens / Belga Mag via AFP) (Photo: DAVID PINTENS)

The huge roar Remco Evenepoel let out when the photo finish result was confirmed said it all: winning the European road race championship was a massive release.

Second in the Tour de France, first in the GP Cycliste de Quebec and first in the world TT championships saw Evenepoel line out in the worlds road race as a big favorite. That hope unraveled with a curiously subdued performance and a distant 12th place.

Missing out on the win hurt, but so too letting down the national team and the Belgian supporters. He was billed beforehand as one of the main contenders and his compatriots worked very hard to put him in the position to win.

Not delivering on that was hard to take but, until Sunday, it was something he had played down.

“It was honestly a really tough week for me after the deception [disappointment] of the worlds,” Evenepoel said shortly after being confirmed as the new European champion. “It was playing more in my head than I have been showing, so it is a big relief to be back on a good level today and to complete my championship jerseys. It feels amazing.”

Indeed, the 26-year-old looked to have the weight of the world lift off his mind, something his wife Oumi confirmed.

“He likes to pretend to be tougher than he is, but he felt very guilty towards his teammates, the federation and the Belgian fans,” she told VTM News on Sunday afternoon.

“I’m extra happy that he can take home that jersey, the only one he missed.”

Evenepoel didn’t have it easy in the race. The Belgian team did incredible work to set things up for him and paved the way for a huge attack the penultimate time up the climb.

He blasted clear with Giulio Ciccone for company, but then hit the deck on a tight uphill curve.

“I went a bit too fast in the corner and I just slipped away,” he said Sunday afternoon, referring to his front wheel. “I think there I could have gone, but in the end we stayed calm and we came back to the plan. Then I put in an attack just before the descent and then I was with Cicco in the front.”

Getting back to Ciccone was crucial but, in the end, the Italian did very little of the work. He had learned his teammate Christian Scaroni was chasing alone and that meant he further pulled back on any collaboration. However he did finally do a turn close to the finish after both the Belgian and the Italian team cars pulled alongside to advise their riders.

There were no race radios allowed and so speaking directly to the team managers had extra importance.

Belgian team chief Serge Pauwels did communicate Evenepoel; what did he say to him?

“That the gap with Scaroni was 50 seconds, that he should try and back off a little bit in the last kilometer, that it was safe to do the sprint,” he answered. “Because we knew of course that Ciccone wasn’t working any more.

“I hoped that even if it worked a little bit then it was maybe enough, because the difference in the end wasn’t that big.”

That’s certainly the case: Ciccone rounded the final bend in a much better way and got the jump on his rival, with Evenepoel approximately three lengths back and chasing desperately.

He closed and closed, and won the race with a much better lunge for the line. The difference?

According to HLN , it was just .00028 of a second.

The official result came through soon afterward and the explosion of sound from Evenepoel and his team showed what it meant.

“Honestly, I felt I was really coming over him,” said Evenepoel. “I thought that I was going to win it, but you never know. I think the images were really clear, the big relief that I felt and how proud I am to take the victory today.

“Like I said, it was a really tough week mentally to recover from the deception and to put a deception for my country on the world championships. I hope that I made everyone proud today.”

He did, but his fans are going to have to make do with the road race as his sole European title this time around. He had never won that particular contest, other than as a junior, but he does have two past Euro TT titles to his credit.

A third would be almost guaranteed if he competed, given his form in winning the world championship TT.

Evenepoel is fast approaching the end of his season. He’s never won Il Lombardia , with big rival Tadej Pogačar taking the past five editions. He was however second in 2024 and 2025 and, with Pogačar absent due to injury, will fancy his chances.

Because of that, he has taken the big decision to give up the chance of winning another TT title.

“No, no, I am going to focus on Lombardia now,” he said, when asked if he’d be lining out in the time trial on Wednesday.

It’s a brave and somewhat risky decision to make but taking the road race title for the first time has given him the result he was really chasing.

It’s also a huge reassurance following his dejection in the Canadian worlds.

“I am going to celebrate tonight because it is a special one,” he smiled.

“Like I said, now I won all the championships in pro cycling, so I think this one we can celebrate big time.”

It is, and even more so after last weekend didn’t go to plan.

“I’m happy for him, because otherwise I had to comfort him again,” his wife said, smiling.

items.title: Preseason Game Preview: Knicks at 76ers, October 5, 2026
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Is there really a game already? Oy vey. We are still getting used to how brief the summer break is when the basketball team you cover is actually successful in the postseason.

Indeed, the NBA champion New York Knicks open their preseason schedule tonight. They’ll travel to face a Philadelphia 76ers club that has bolstered its own championship aspirations this summer. What was a solid but flawed Eastern Conference contender now features LeBron James and Jaylen Brown alongside Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, and sophomore VJ Edgecombe, assembling one of the most star-studliest lineups in the league.

For the defending champions, this scrimmage will be the first peek at what Mike Brown hopes to tweak for the upcoming season. The second-year coach has already stressed that he intends to ease his core into the exhibition slate. They had a short summer recess, after all. Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart, OG () Anunoby, and Karl-Anthony Towns will not shoulder heavy workloads right away, which should open the door for extended looks at the players still fighting for roster security and rotation minutes. Additionally, sophomore Mohamed Diawara will be challenged to prove that he’s ready for a leap after a promising first season and fizzling out in summer league.

We’ll be focused on the center position where the coaching staff is still sorting out depth behind Towns and former Sixer Andre Drummond. Journeymen James Wiseman, Tony Bradley, and Drew Eubanks are all competing in camp for the third-string spot, and Monday’s game affords them a chance to show how they stack up against Embiid and ex-Knick Ariel Hukporti.

As for the health of New York’s starters, Hart continues to play with a damaged digit, and Brunson has reportedly looked sharp in camp after recovering from wrist surgery. Meanwhile, there’s an undercurrent of unresolved contracts, with Towns, Hart, and Miles McBride all eligible for veteran extensions. Because they are in (or effectively in) the final year of their deals—McBride on an expiring contract, Towns with a $61M player option for 2027-28, and Hart with a $22.4M team option for 2027-28—they can negotiate and sign extensions at any point until June 30, 2027. All three have expressed interest in buttoning up their paperwork sooner than that, but this seems like the storyline that will hang over the entire season.

For the Fightin’ Cheesesteaks, our curiosity centers around how coach Nick Nurse will get James, Brown, Embiid, and Maxey to share the ball and defend consistently. We expect their early games to have some of the confusion of an All-Star game, when the alphas try to figure out who will be less-alpha on any given play.

Really, the primary goal of a preseason game is “Don’t break nothin.” You won’t see Captain Brunson take a charge tonight, or Hart do anything that could make his finger fall off. New York swept the Liberty Bells in the second round of the playoffs, as part of a 13-game win streak, and while tonight’s opponent has improved, neither club wants to reveal its tricks in a meaningless contest. They’ll save the good stuff for opening night, when they clash on banner night at Madison Square Garden. Still, it will be fun to see our champs take the floor again. And so soon. Prediction: Knicks by six.

Who: New York Knicks (0-0) at Philadelphia 76ers (0-0)Date: Monday, October 5, 2026Place: Xfinity Mobile Arena (formerly Wells Fargo Center), Philadelphia, PAFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

Journeymen James Wiseman, Tony Bradley, and Drew Eubanks are all competing in camp for the third-string spot, and Monday’s game affords them a chance to show how they stack up against Embiid and ex-Knick Ariel Hukporti.

As for the health of New York’s starters, Hart continues to play with a damaged digit, and Brunson has reportedly looked sharp in camp after recovering from wrist surgery. Meanwhile, there’s an undercurrent of unresolved contracts, with Towns, Hart, and Miles McBride all eligible for veteran extensions. Because they are in (or effectively in) the final year of their deals—McBride on an expiring contract, Towns with a $61M player option for 2027-28, and Hart with a $22.4M team option for 2027-28—they can negotiate and sign extensions at any point until June 30, 2027. All three have expressed interest in buttoning up their paperwork sooner than that, but this seems like the storyline that will hang over the entire season.

For the Fightin’ Cheesesteaks, our curiosity centers around how coach Nick Nurse will get James, Brown, Embiid, and Maxey to share the ball and defend consistently. We expect their early games to have some of the confusion of an All-Star game, when the alphas try to figure out who will be less-alpha on any given play.

Really, the primary goal of a preseason game is “Don’t break nothin.” You won’t see Captain Brunson take a charge tonight, or Hart do anything that could make his finger fall off. New York swept the Liberty Bells in the second round of the playoffs, as part of a 13-game win streak, and while tonight’s opponent has improved, neither club wants to reveal its tricks in a meaningless contest. They’ll save the good stuff for opening night, when they clash on banner night at Madison Square Garden. Still, it will be fun to see our champs take the floor again. And so soon. Prediction: Knicks by six.

Who: New York Knicks (0-0) at Philadelphia 76ers (0-0) Date: Monday, October 5, 2026 Time: 7:00 PM ET Place: Xfinity Mobile Arena (formerly Wells Fargo Center), Philadelphia, PA TV: MSG Follow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

items.title: ‘In one moment I was really believing it’ - disappointed Giulio Ciccone reflects on agonising second place at European Championships
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Giulio Ciccone raced a near-perfect race at the UEC European Road Championships on Sunday, not only being the only rider able to follow Remco Evenepoel’s attacks but also able to capitalise on the fact that his teammate was chasing. He stayed with the Belgian all the way to the finish, setting up a two-up sprint for the title.

Unsure who had won, the pair waited past the finish line until the result was announced. Ciccone bowed his head while Evenepoel, nearby, let out a joyful scream.

He could not hide his disappointment on the podium and while talking to the media afterwards.

“I feel really really disappointed. But first I want to say congrats to Remco, super strong ride,” Ciccone told .

Letting the Belgian squad control the front of the pack, Ciccone waited, and then covered Evenepoel’s first attack on the Možjanca climb with 36 kilometres to go. When the Belgian overcooked a corner and slid out, Ciccone eased off and waited for the peloton.

But he was ready for the next attack, coming only four kilometres later. The pair pulled away from the pack, gaining time, and then Ciccone refused to work when he found out that his teammate was chasing behind with 14 kilometres to go.

“I also was lucky with the situation in the race with [Christian] Scaroni alone behind us. So I also played on the situation to stay on the wheel. I understand that for him was not a nice situation in the front, but this is the race situation.”

Racing a total of five times around the circuit, Ciccone had time to plan his approach the final corner before the finish line.

“I was thinking in my head how to do it, and I was in the last few kilometres. I was just thinking about this corner, and I was thinking to take the first position, but then he understood my plan, and he made the acceleration just before.”

But Evenepoel took a wide line through the final corner, leaving the inside open for Ciccone, who immediately accelerated and briefly opened up a few metres.

“Then my plan was just go full after the corner. In one moment I was really believing it. But then, yeah, this is the race, and it's like this.”

It was the ninth podium finish this year.

“I think it's one of the hardest years of my career. I don't know how many times I've finished second or on the podium. Eight, nine, or I don't know how many times.”

“Today I think was really close, but then another time second. So now for the last two races, I just want to you know, race without pressure and let's see what just to enjoy the bike.”

Ciccone will line up at Il Lombardia, the fifth and final monument of the year next weekend.

items.title: ‘My Shape Is Really Bad’: Tadej Pogačar Sorry/Not Sorry to Miss Euro Champs
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Speculation growing about when and where Pogačar could return to racing in 2027. His team and others comment.
items.lbText:
Tadej Pogačar and his partner Urska Žigart attend the elite men's European road race championships as spectators (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski/Getty Images) (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski)

There was much chatter recently that Tadej Pogačar might defy team orders and ride the European championships , both to defend his title and also because it was held in his home country of Slovenia.

His team denied it and said his recovery was too important, and so it proved: the 28 year old was at the race, but only as a guest.

Winning a major title on home soil is likely a once in a lifetime possibility for a Slovenian but, in this case at least, it’s one ambition he may have to let go of.

Ditto for his partner Urška Žigart, who is also sidelined after a jawbone fracture reoccurred again.

“For sure even yesterday when we were watching the women’s race, Urška was like, ‘damn, I should be there,” Pogačar told Eurosport after the finish of Sunday’s race.

“Especially she has been feeling super good so it is tough. When you have good shape it is tough to look at the race and know you could be part of it.”

Pogačar has been in dominant form this year, winning a record-equaling fifth Tour de France plus multiple other races. He looked to be en route for victory at the Vuelta a España but crashed heavily on stage 8 and withdrew.

He was diagnosed with a fractured vertebra and collarbone, as well as concussion. And while he’s recovered rapidly from that fall, he’s also realistic about how he would have got on had he defied his team and ridden on Sunday.

“Today I am riding my bike for one week now outside. I know my shape is really bad,” he said. “I don’t wish to be riding out today. But one week ago or two weeks ago, I would be really eager to be on the start today.”

The question of when Pogačar will be on a startline again still remains to be seen.

El Pais recently suggested he would contradict UAE Team Emirates-XRG advice and line out in the European championships, something the team denied.

And while he ultimately didn’t take part in the race, the Spanish publication stated that competing in the Santos Tour Down Under would be the team’s preferred first race back.

That’s something we at Velo previously argued , noting that both the rider himself and Pogačar’s own agent Alex Carera had said earlier this season that the Slovenian was planning to ride—and win—the race at some point in the coming years.

He has made winning every WorldTour stage race a big career goal and the early finish to his racing in 2026 seems to tee things up perfectly for an early season start.

Such a buildup could also put him in prime form for Paris-Roubaix, a race he has been trying to win.

Velo reached out in recent weeks to the race organisers, to Carera and to UAE Team Emirates-XRG.

His agent didn’t reply as yet, but Santos Tour Down Under organisers were non-committal about the prospect of him competing there.

“Our only thought right now, like every cycling fan in the world, is for Tadej and Urska in their recovery from their injuries,” a spokesperson told Velo in late August. “We hope to see them back on their bike soon and wish them all the best, but anything beyond that is secondary to their health and wellbeing.”

A spokesperson in recent days said it was far too early to get confirmation of his plans, noting that the first indications of his schedule would be given out at the team’s December camp.

He may well decide to head to Australia, a race he previously rode in 2019. But it seems confirmation of that is still a couple of months away.

For now, watching races and rebuilding his fitness will be as close as he will get to pinning on a number.

items.title: New WRC champion Evans relieved after “surreal” Sardinia title showdown
‘I know my shape is kind of really bad’- Tadej Pogačar comes to terms with missing European Championships in Slovenia
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
But, of course, Pogačar still returned home to soak up the cheers. Riding in the race director’s car, he waved to fans lining the road on the Možjanca climb and gathered at the finish in Šenčur.

The UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider said he had no regrets about sitting out the race, but admitted he felt differently two weeks earlier, just weeks after crashing out of the Vuelta a España.

“I'm here riding my bike for one week now outside [since the crash], and I know my shape is kind of really bad, and I don't wish to be riding out today,” he told with a chuckle.

“A week or two ago, though, I was really eager to be on the start today.”

But it was a tougher call for his fiancée, Urška Žigart, who refractured her jaw in a crash at Faun Tour Femmes in September. The AG Insurance-Soudal rider was also forced to miss Saturday’s women’s race on home soil.

“Even yesterday, when we were watching a women's race, Urška was like, ‘ah, damn, I should be there’, and she's been feeling super good,” Pogačar said. “When you have good shape. It's tough to look at the race and know that you could be part of it.”

“Luka has been a big part of my career,” said Pogačar who was present at Mezgec biggest win of his career, when he was around 15 years old at the 2014 Giro d’Italia in Trieste.

“Since then, he was kind of my idol and mentor in the national team, and I learned a lot from him. And he had a really amazing career. I think a lot of young kids, young cyclists, should aim more to have a career like him as a lead-out man and a helper and a road captain in the team," he added. "So to be here today with him is really nice and I'm honoured to be sitting next to him.”

Mezgec went out in style, going into the early break and then high-fiving the crowd once he was caught before calling it a day.

items.title: Was it 'unfair' not to penalise stricken F1 cars in Malaysia?
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Fernando Alonso believes it was unfair that the stricken cars were allowed to start Formula 1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, as "they never stopped a race" for an Aston Martin grinding to a halt this year.

There was chaos at the attempted start of F1's first race in Malaysia in nine years as several cars encountered issues, crawling or coming to a halt, for what's now been diagnosed as a "software bug" with the 2026 power units.

But it did not affect Alonso's Aston Martin Honda. He'd overtaken the ailing Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton and would have taken the restart 11th, on the fringes of the points. 

But with that start abandoned, the order was reset to that of the starting grid for the next (successful) attempt to start the race - a decision Alonso still wasn't pleased with after the race, despite finishing eighth.  

He said: "I think I had 50% DNF this year. They never stopped the race for us." 

Asked by The Race if it was unfair, Alonso said: "100%. I mean, this is motor racing…if it's a safety concern, I get it. If there are five cars in the middle of the road or whatever, we have to stop the race and we need to see what's going on. 

"But I think they were out of the race. They were out, even on the [start/finish pit]wall. They had to push it two metres, the marshals, and retire the car - like we do in 50% of the races. 

"It's the first time I see it, but right now I don't have all the info, so maybe there is a clear explanation and it's OK. I'm not too concerned."

What was going through his mind when he saw other cars stranded?

Alonso said: "The same thing that goes through their mind when they see the Aston Martin stop, I guess. Sad on one side because they have a problem, good because you have one car less in the race."

Alonso was speaking before the FIA publicly explained that there was a software bug. It sent a software update for all teams to download before the actual race start, so it's possible he'll revise his opinion in the days to come now he knows the cause of the problem.

The key difference to Alonso's DNFs - he's retired from 37.5% of grands prix this year - is that they have all been down to Aston Martin Honda's own reliability issues. The software glitch issue that struck the likes of Hamilton was an issue with an FIA-supplied software, outside of the team or drivers' control.

There are specific regulations over starting procedures being suspended, as was the case after the formation lap chaos. 

Article B5.14.1 of the FIA's sporting regulations says: "If at any time after the formation laps behind the safety car have commenced, track conditions are considered unsuitable to start the [session], the message "STARTING PROCEDURE SUSPENDED" will be sent to all competitors.

"Red flags will be shown at all marshal posts and at the control line, and the orange lights on the start gantry will be illuminated. 

"All F1 cars must enter the pitlane behind the safety car. 

"The first F1 car to arrive in the pitlane should proceed directly to the pitlane exit…All the other F1 cars should form up in a line behind the first F1 car in the order they entered the pitlane behind the safety car when the starting procedure was suspended."  

But that order is subject to change by the time the race is properly restarted, which is what allowed Hamilton to reclaim his second place.

There are rules around "Any driver who caused an aborted start and is then subsequently able to start must start from the end of the pitlane", but this didn't apply to Hamilton because the start was aborted for multiple drivers' issues, outside of their or their cars' control. 

So it could have been a different story had Hamilton spun off by himself and caused the suspended start. Instead a common-sense decsion was taken to reset things.

Aston Martin's chief trackside officer Mike Krack called it "a difficult subject" when The Race put Alonso's comments to him.

"I think it was really the only thing the FIA could have done at that point. The race had not started, so this was the formation lap. The race had not started, and they aborted.

"Obviously, we need to review the whole thing. It was a bit chaotic. I think for everyone, nobody really knew what was going on.

"But, at the end of the day, if you zoom out, I think it was the right thing to do." 

Mercedes would have also benefited as Hamilton's demise would have been a place gained for both Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, but deputy team boss Bradley Lord felt the right decision was made. 

"I think it was a slightly unprecedented situation," Lord said. 

"Likewise, formally speaking, the starting procedure hadn't happened, we were in the middle of formation laps before a call had been made, and so it felt like the, in the moment maybe if you felt advantaged or disadvantaged, it felt right or wrong, but overall it was the common sense thing to do.

"If you think of the millions of people watching around the world, they tune in for the start and suddenly the cars are all in a jumbled-up order because of something that happened 40 minutes earlier and was behind the safety car on a formation lap.

"I think that would have been a much harder thing to explain than resetting and then going from where we did, and it was pretty exciting when that happened."

items.title: Solberg has no regrets after WRC title near-miss: “It hurts a lot”
Charm City Cross Day 1: Manon Bakker and Tofik Beshir take solo victories in C1 races
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Manon Bakker and Tofik Beshir (CXD Trek Bikes) soloed to win the C1 races of Charm City Cross in Baltimore, Maryland, on day 1 of the third round of the 2026 US Cyclocross Series (USCX). Each rider took their fourth victory in five races in the series on Saturday.

In the women’s race, Bakker leaned into the same strategy that has served her well throughout the series, leading from the first lap. Bakker was coming off her first loss of the season on Day 2 at GO Cross.

“Today, I had a lot better focus and made no mistakes in the race,” Bakker said.

Lauren Zoerner led the front group going up the decisive Mansion Hill and across the long off-camber section on lap one. Going into the downhill, Bakker saw an opportunity to create some space ahead of her USCX rival, Sidney McGill.

From that point on, Bakker was untouchable. Behind her, McGill, Zoerner, Mia Aseltine (Competitive Edge Racing), Nico Knoll (PRO.FWD) and Kaya Musgrave (Competitive Edge Racing) formed the early chase, but the demanding course quickly turned the race into a war of attrition. Just past the halfway point of the six-lap race, McGill and Aseltine had emerged together in the battle for the remaining podium spots.

With two laps to go, McGill gapped Aseltine on the climb and rode on to secure second place, crossing the line 34 seconds behind the winner. Aseltine was third, a further 14 seconds down.

“I overtook Lauren right before the corner, going back down, and I knew that, normally, she couldn't hold my wheel,” Bakker added. “Probably Sydney is the only one who can. So, I wanted to have somebody in between me and Sydney to make it a little bit harder for her.”

The elite men’s race marked a homecoming for 19-year-old Beshir, who first lined up at Charm City six years ago during his inaugural cyclo-cross season. Baltimore is also the hometown of Marc Frazer, who mentored Beshir early in his career as team director at Kelly Benefits Strategies Cycling.

“To win in his hometown—that’s special,” Beshir says. “He’s the one that got me into the sport and it really means a lot to me.”

Struggling to return to form since an injury earlier in the year, Pan-American champion Andrew Strohmeyer (Competitive Edge Racing) put in a massive acceleration from the start, building a gap of 15 seconds to his closest pursuers by the third lap.

Beshir, who had been forced to fight his way through traffic after crashing on a corner earlier in the race, chased solo before finally catching Strohmeyer and settling onto his wheel. But a tiring Strohmeyer soon dropped back to the chase group, where he joined teammates Ryan Drummond and Dylan Zakrajsek, along with Tyler Clark (Caledon Hills Cycling Armada) and Miles Mattern (CXD Trek Bikes). Beshir continued alone with three laps to go.

One lap later, Clark attacked the group and crossed the line 18 seconds behind the winner for second place. The battle for third place heated up the final time up Mansion Hill, where Zakrajsek was able to pull away and hold on for third place.

“I knew Strohmeyer wasn’t going to slow down because he’s legit,” Beshir said. “I knew I needed to pull him back slowly. I didn’t want to burn myself out.”

“I wanted to follow him [Strohmeyer] because he is incredible,” he added. “I know he's not having a great season, but, just following him, you can tell he has a lot of experience and I've always admired him. I was definitely excited to follow his lines and learn new things from him.”

The UCI C2 race on day two at Charm will create some different dynamics, as parts of the course will be reversed and overnight rain could create slick conditions. Series champions will be officially crowned, as Sunday’s race will be the finale of the three-event series.

items.title: Tour de Vendée: Alexis Renard sprints to first professional victory of his career
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Alexis Renard sprinted to victory in the Tour de Vendée, doubling up on wins this week for Cofidis this weekend after his teammate Jenthe Biermans won Cholet Agglo Tour on Saturday. It was the first professional victory for the 27-year-old Frenchman who typically is a lead-out man for Bryan Coquard.

After the final breakaway was caught inside of seven kilometres to go, teams jostled for position on two laps of the 3km finishing circuit featuring three main corners, and peppered with road furniture in between, with Cofidis making a big push to come together as a team before the final decisive corner.

Xabier Berasategi (Euskatel-Euskadi) took second and Giovanni Lonardi (Polti VisitMalta) was third in Saint-Gilles-Croix-de-Vie.

“I was leading Bryan out again today, but I came past him a bit too quickly in the finale; when I launched, or rather, when I intended to launch him, I saw the 200m sign and thought, ‘Right, this should work’,” Renard said.

“I was strong yesterday, too. I broke my derailleur but managed to get back to the peloton from a long way back. So, we had high ambitions this weekend for the team and Bryan, and that I’m the one who won today is just incredible. It’s my first professional victory, something I’m really going to savour.”

 Renard and his teammate Paul Ourselin has made their way into an early 18-rider breakaway that escaped after some 50 kilometres of racing.

 “Honestly, I thought it [the break] was going to go to the end, but TotalEnergies wasn't rolling so it's a bit disorganised. In the end, we tried to re-mobilise with Jenthe and Bryan to try to lead him out. Finally I managed to get the victory, so it stays in the team and that’s always good.”

Clément Venturini (Unibet Rose Rockets) secured the FDJ United Series title for the second consecutive year, finishing 15th in the 13th and final races of the season. The series was formerly known as the Coupe de France.

Starting in Saint-Jean-d’Hermine, the 198.2km course passed through several villages before reaching a landmark of Vendée cycling: Chantonnay and its famous "Côte du Gîte" climb, which has played a pivotal role in several French National Championships. The peloton then headed west to the seaside resort of Saint-Gilles-Croix-de-Vie, a first-time coastal finish for the Tour de Vendée. The finale was contested over two large 10km laps, followed by three shorter 3km laps.

A number of large groups tried to get away in the early kilometres, but a split in the bunch finally allowed a huge break to form, with 18 riders, including Renard, quickly building a lead of more than a minute, with 50km ridden.

The gap hovered around the one-minute mark for the large group before they were reeled in after spending 87 kilometres off the front. Two riders, Léandre Huck (Van Rysel Roubaix) and Enzo Paleni (Groupama-FDJ United), countered and pulled away only to be reeled in after the first small lap.

The two French WorldTour teams, Decathlon CMA CGM and Groupama-FDJ United, put riders at the front, but it was hard to control the pace in the criterium-style finale.

items.title: 'Finished the season on a high' – Riley Pickrell and Modern Adventure reap the rewards of a season of building the lead out at Le Tour de Langkawi
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
It may not have been another stage victory on Sunday's final day of racing at Le Tour de Langkawi for Riley Pickrell (Modern Adventure) but, once again, it wasn't that far off in a tour where the consistency of the Canadian's presence in the top two spots has delivered a clear reminder of just how far the squad has come in the space of 12 months.

Pickrell has undoubtedly been impressive in his turn of speed, though he is far from taking sole credit for the three second places and one win he gathered from the four sprint contests that unfolded at the Malaysian ProTour race this week. And there was also a fifth place when he sprinted from the group after the break had already soaked up the top four spots.

"If I have consistency, it means my teammates are always dropping me off in a good position where I can sprint to a top three," Pickrell told s after the race finale in Putrajaya. "So this week I can really only say thanks to my team because they're the reason why it's so consistent."

That hasn't always been the case, as given Modern Adventure ProTeam is only in its first season it meant that they were starting fresh, and had to find their feet both together as a team and also within the peloton and it's a process that clearly continued through the eight-day tour.

"We didn't have this kind of consistency at the beginning of this year because we had never worked with each other before," explained Pickrell. "We didn't have the processes. We have spent so many hours post-race being pretty critical on where we've made mistakes in these lead outs and how to read the read the race better.

"So now when we're exposed to those situations again and again, we know what the other rider wants out of it and how to adjust accordingly. And that's why the consistency is really coming out. I'm super excited for next year. Most of us here are going into offseason now but we definitely finished the season on a high and I think all the guys are really eager to already get started for next season."

There was more to being satisfied with the outcome than the consistent top placings, there was a first win of the season for Pickrell and sixth for the squad. It also went beyond the improvements within the team lead-out, as this race perhaps felt a little more like a coming of age.

As sports director Alex Howes put it just before the squad pulled off the win on stage 6, "We're figuring stuff out as a team so honestly, we're just happy to be in a position where we get to have this conversation about beating a team like Astana. They're a good team and we have got a lot of respect for them, but I think we can get around them."

Then when they did, XDS Astana clearly didn't consider it a fluke, as they were determined to put the responsibility for the chase of the break on the new squad's shoulders after they had won a stage

"We kind of went into this season kind of being like 'we're just gonna be like the little shit team that nobody respects and it's gonna be really hard to do anything' whereas I really feel like by the end of this season we have a lot of respect," Pickrell said, adding that if the team wasn't respected XDS-Astana would never have tried to hand over the responsibility for chasing down the break to the squad.

"I think that says a lot for what we've accomplished this year and the trajectory we are on is really impressive."

*Cyclingnews attended Le Tour de Langkawi on an invitation/media package from the race that included travel and accommodation. items.title: Remco Evenepoel to skip the European Championships time trial to concentrate on next Sunday's Il Lombardia
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Recently crowned time trial World Champion Remco Evenepoel is to skip the defence of his European title to concentrate on winning Il Lombardia, he revealed on Sunday.

"Wednesday? No, no, I'm going to focus on Lombardia now," he responded when the interviewer said he’d see the Belgian star on Wednesday for the TT.

Evenepoel is without doubt the best time trialist of the current era, not only does he have four rainbow jerseys to his name, but he’s won the European title twice, including last year in France. He’s also a multiple Belgian champion and, of course, the current Olympic champion after taking gold in Paris, just days before doing the same in the road race.

This week’s Slovenian course would certainly have suited the 26-year-old, covering as it does the same 22km lap on which he won Sunday’s road race, but he clearly has other priorities.

Though he has two Monument victories to his name, winning Liège-Bastogne-Liège in both 2022 and 2023, he has never won Il Lombardia, instead finishing the last two editions behind Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), with three other participations dating back to 2020.

However, with Pogačar still recovering from the injuries he sustained in a crash on stage 8 of the Vuelta a España, Evenepoel has the perfect opportunity to add the Italian Classic to his palmarès.

There had been rumours Pogačar was to start the European Championships road race in Slovenia on Sunday, but he was unable to take the start despite it being in his home country. He was, however, at the race to see Evenepoel win, waving to crowds from one of the race direction cars. Evenepoel will certainly be hoping he doesn’t change his mind.

Evenepoel's ride to win the European road race was an excellent one. His Belgian team did much of the riding and covered any threatening move all day long. He then managed to catch Giulio Ciccone after crashing, then did most of the work to take the pair to the line.

Before his appointment in Il Lombardia, Evenepoel has something else on his mind, "I’m gonna celebrate tonight because it's a special one. Like I said, it's now I won all the championships in pro cycling, so I think this one we can celebrate it big time."
