items.title: Hamilton & Verstappen bemused after glitch turns F1 into 'Lego race'
items.content: <article>Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton liken the effects of a software bug that affected multiple cars before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to a "Lego race".</article>
items.lbText:
Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton likened the effects of a software bug that affected multiple cars before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to a "Lego race".

The problem led to several cars, including those of the two multiple world champions who were sharing the front row of the grid, not working in the wet conditions that preceded the race.

A tropical downpour delayed attempts to get the grand prix under way for the best part of an hour. And when the cars set off on formation laps behind a safety car to test the conditions, audiences were treated to the bizarre sight of many of them struggling to move.

A bug in the software that mandates how the engines' electrical power can be used in wet conditions had been triggered by a combination of low engine speeds, low grip and specific aspects of the circuit layout.

Verstappen, who went on to take a dominant win that was his first victory of the year, said: "These engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented.

"I triggered [the problem] first and then I looked in my mirror, I was like, 'Wait, are they waiting for me or what's going [on]...?' It was like the Lego race."

Verstappen was referring to a show run in battery-powered Lego F1 cars that was held before the British Grand Prix in July.

Hamilton, sitting beside Verstappen in the post-race news conference after finishing third, interjected to say: "Yeah, we had the same speed. I had to stop on track and stop the car and engine and restart it. I've never done that before."

Verstappen added: "It was insane. Like, it's the Lego power. At some point we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on.

"Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still, and I saw you (Hamilton) by yourself crawling. That's not what you want, right, for the sport."

Mercedes driver George Russell, who retired from the race with an engine failure, said: "It didn't feel very F1."

Nikolas Tombazis, the single-seater director for governing body the FIA said there would be a full investigation.

The issue arose, he added, because, while the software had been tested, it had not been tested in these specific conditions. Largely because there has been so little running in the wet this year.

"Cars are complicated," Tombazis said. "We would all like it to be simpler, but when you have electrical energy and combustion energy all working together, and obviously when you want to ensure that there's sporting fairness between the teams, that is complicated.

"We haven't done a full debrief of the situation and see how we can avoid such an issue. Every race, we have a long debrief afterwards, where we identify criticalities.

"Obviously, that was a major criticality, and we need to make sure we avoid it. Can I guarantee it will never happen again? This specific problem, yes. A problem, no, but we will do our best to avoid it, of course."

This is far from the first issue created by the huge complexity of the latest hybrid engines introduced this year, with their near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power.

Because the engines are fundamentally energy starved, and so cannot deploy their full combined power output at all times, a series of complexities were added into the management of the engines to try to sticking-plaster solutions.

Many of these led to the counter-intuitive driving about which many of the sport's stars have been complaining all season - and more changes have been added since.

Off-track conversation has been dominated by this all year, and rules are changing for next year to alter the energy split to try to ameliorate the issue.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "What happened at the start obviously is not ideal in terms of presentation of the sport.

"But at the same time it is the first year of new regulations, quite complex from a regulatory point of view, and it was also the first time we started in such conditions.

"So we have to concede that F1 has done an excellent job in making some new regulations that came with some question marks from a power-unit behaviour point of view when it came to racing for instance.

"We have to acknowledge there has been really good work to make the show and racing work, and if there are some glitches occasionally, we have to accept they are glitches for everyone, be supportive and make sure it doesn't happen again."

The problem had a secondary consequence - the field order was jumbled up, and one reading of the rules could have meant the grid order should change for any restart.

But while the FIA's software engineers were rewriting the code as fast as possible, it was determined that, as this situation had never occurred before, and as the problem was out of any competitor's control, the most appropriate order was to revert to the original grid.

Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "If you think of the millions of people watching around the world, they tune in for the start and suddenly the cars are all in a jumbled up order because of something that happened 40 minutes earlier and it was behind a safety car on a formation lap. That would have been a much harder thing to explain than resetting and then going from where we did."

"Amazing" was the word Verstappen chose to describe his and Red Bull's first win of the 2026 season at a chaotic, bizarre and, in some ways, unprecedented race.

It would be wrong to say the victory was a complete surprise, as it came after three consecutive podium finishes in which the four-time champion appeared to be edging closer and closer to such an achievement.

But it certainly adds a fresh twist to a season of fluctuating fortunes at the front, in which the only real constant has been Kimi Antonelli, as the championship heads into its final stretch.

It was Verstappen's 72nd victory and it came in a manner entirely familiar to those who have followed his career - but entirely unfamiliar to this season.…

items.title: Evenepoel Pips Ciccone in Desperate Sprint to Become European Champion
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Remco Evenepoel, crashes, recovers, attacks, does all the work and finally pips Ciccone in photo finish.
items.lbText:
Remco Evenepoel beats Giulio Ciccone to become European road race champion in Sencur, Slovenia. (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski/Getty Images) (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski)

Remco Evenepoel found redemption after a disappointing road race at the world championships, becoming European road race champ for the first time in his pro career after a dramatic finale.

The Belgian outsprinted Giulio Ciccone (Italy) at the line but had to wait for the result of a photo finish to confirm the win. Ciccone got a better line through the last corner and opened a lead of several bike lengths, but lost out by a tiny margin.

Evenepoel was fueled by pride and stubbornness, being determined to show well after his worlds disappointment and going into hulk mode after he went clear with Ciccone on the penultimate lap but crashed.

He took an uphill bend too fast and lost his front wheel, with his Belgian team keeping him within range and enabling him to jump up to Ciccone once again.

The Italian declined to work on the final lap, taking only one brief turn near the finish, and took the final corner better.

This gave him an important gap over Evenepoel but the Belgian wouldn’t be denied, chasing furiously all the way to the line and then lunging past. His throw to the line was better than that of Ciccone and this was just enough to give him the victory.

Christian Scaroni raced in 59 seconds back to make it an Italian silver and bronze, while Toms Skujiņš (Lavia) leap clear of a chase group to nab fourth, 1:13 back and three seconds ahead of Iván Romeo (Spain) and others.

Evenepoel was lucky not to be too affected by his fall. “It was a bit of a tricky situation the second last time on the climb. I put a nice attack but I went a bit too fast in the corner and I just slipped away,” he said.

“I think there I could have gone, but in the end we stayed calm and we came back to the plan. Then I put in an attack just before the descent and then I was with Cicco in the front.

“We worked together pretty well. The sprint was looking a bit…I thought I was not going to get it anymore, but then I saw him slowing down quite a lot with 100 meters to go and I just came just over him on the finish line.”

Evenepoel won the junior European road race championships in 2018 but this was his first time to take the distinctive blue and white jersey as a pro.

He took the time trial twice, in 2019 and 2025.

The elite men’s road race was 197km in distance and, like the women’s race, featured a mostly flat opening section of 85km prior to the start of the finishing circuit. The men would complete five laps compared to the women’s two, with the climb of Možjanca the main obstacle.

Six riders went clear very early on and had over a minute the first time over the finish line, but they were all caught with 82km remaining. The climb saw a large number of riders dropped from the peloton, including Juan Ayuso (Spain), and the contenders continued to dwindle with each passing lap.

Roglič’s Slovenia team took control of the pace the penultimate time up the climb but rather than the multiple Vuelta winner attacking, it was instead Giulio Ciccone (Italy) who leaped clear on with 36.3km remaining.

Evenepoel joined him almost immediately and then went past, launching a very aggressive surge, but went too fast into a right hand curve and lost the front wheel, crashing.

Ciccone went over the summit alone, chased by Roglič, while behind Evenepoel’s Belgium team were chasing hard and kept the Italian leader within range. He subsequently jumped clear and got up to Ciccone, with the two of them 12 seconds ahead of a group of chasers with 25km left.

Those behind trying to get across included Roglič, Toms Skujiņš (Latvia), Emil Herzog (Germany), Iván Romeo (Spain), Evenpoel’s teammates Ramses Debruyne and Maxim Van Gils, French trio Léo Bisiaux, Manhys Rondel and Clément Braz Afonso plus Christian Scaroni (Italy).

Roglič was under pressure as the home rider and did a lot of the chasing, but these were 26 seconds behind starting the final lap.

Rondel and Scaroni leaped clear in pursuit but with Evenepoel setting the pace out front the whole way up the climb, those two chasers were almost a minute back.

Scaroni attacked Rondel close to the summit in an attempt to bridge. Evenepoel was on a mission, though, and he had no chance of bridging. However there was still an advantage as once this information was passed on from a race moto, Ciccone made clear to Evenepoel that he couldn’t contribute. The Belgian wasn’t happy but continued driving onwards, hoping to win the sprint.

Ciccone finally started to ride inside the final 3km, making the decision after his team car drew alongside. However his contribution was minimal, with the Italian clearly trying to stay as fresh as possible.

Evenepoel led into the final corner but Ciccone got a better line and came past him. He launched early, opened several lengths, but Evenepoel chased hard all the way to the line and took the photo finish.

items.title: How to follow the Singapore Grand Prix on the BBC
items.content: <article>All the key BBC coverage details for the Singapore Grand Prix, the sixth and final sprint event of the season, which takes place from 9-11 October.</article>
items.lbText:
Round 17 of the 2026 Formula 1 season heads to the Marina Bay Street Circuit for the Singapore Grand Prix, from 9-11 October.

The weekend is also the sixth and final sprint event of the campaign.

At the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Max Verstappen took his first victory of the year, with title leader Kimi Antonelli second and Lewis Hamilton third.

Italian Antonelli leads Mercedes team-mate George Russell by 84 points in the drivers' championship after the Briton retired from race with an engine issue.

Sunday's 62-lap grand prix, that takes place at night in Singapore, starts at 13:00 BST.

Verstappen wins Bahrain GP in Malaysia after long delays

Andrew Benson Q&A: Send us your questions

Commentary of the race will be available across 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

You can also ask your smart speaker to "play 5 Sports Extra".

Make sure to listen to every episode of the Chequered Flag podcast. For the first time this year, the post-race show for every grand prix is available to watch on BBC iPlayer and YouTube. , external

First practice: 09:30-10:30 - 5 Sports Extra

Sprint qualifying: 13:30-14:14 - 5 Sports Extra

Sprint race: 10:00-11:00 - 5 Sports Extra

Qualifying: 14:00-15:00 - 5 Sports Extra

Race: 13:00 with build-up from 12:45 - 5 Sports Extra

The early forecast predicts some rain could fall in Singapore for the final race of this triple-header.

Thundery showers and light winds are predicted across all three days of track action, but conditions should clear by the time the later racing takes place.

Temperatures across the weekend will remain high at about 33C.

Marina Bay is hosting a sprint weekend for the very first time this year.

Sprint qualifying has three sessions, where the six slowest cars are knocked out from the first two - like normal qualifying.

These sessions, known as SQ1, SQ2 and SQ3, and last 12, 10 and eight minutes respectively.

This will make up the grid for the sprint race.

Only the top eight finishers score points, with eight points awarded for first place down to one point for eighth, which will get added to the overall drivers' championship standings.

items.title: Winners and losers from F1's 2026 Bahrain GP in Malaysia
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
A very strange start was followed by a race full of curveballs in Formula 1's 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix, held in Malaysia.

Here's our pick of the stars and flops.

Winner: Max Verstappen & Red Bull (1st)

A first pole and win of the season for Red Bull, its engine division and the absolute star of today's show, Max Verstappen.

He was almighty at every turn today. He completed a lovely, intricate move at Turns 1-3 around the outside of Kimi Antonelli early on, was absolutely rapid as the track dried, and - after a briefly alarming moment when he stopped late on and lost the lead before the Mercedes followed suit a lap later - held off Antonelli for the win.

While you wouldn't expect to see Isack Hadjar on par with Verstappen, the gap between the two Red Bulls today shows the level at which Verstappen is operating in these scenarios. The car helped, but the driver made the ultimate difference.

And a word for Red Bull Powertrains. Both Audi and Honda (for Aston Martin) have had engine struggles this year. RBPT has produced what is F1's best internal combustion engine at its very first attempt, so that's a big positive for future years as it improves its battery and deployment abilities.

Loser: Isack Hadjar (5th)

The obvious loss for Hadjar here is being mugged by both Ferraris on the four-lap shootout after the safety car at the end.

However, look earlier and the problems were already there. He was jumped by Liam Lawson at the start, and after he got that place back he rarely matched team-mate Verstappen's pace. He was as much as three seconds per lap slower at times even when he had a certain amount of clean air.

We're not expecting Verstappen-level performances from Hadjar less than two years into his F1 career, but he looked like he was driving a different brand of car today.

Remember two safety cars reset the field. He was almost 10 seconds behind Verstappen at the lap nine safety car, and 28s behind before the one on lap 42.

Loser: George Russell (classified 20th)

Such a deeply nasty ending to what was already a disappointing-but-manageable weekend.

Even before the 'grand finale' of losing third in the final laps due to a power unit issue, George Russell had suffered a couple of ignominies at Sepang - one was the qualifying defeat to Mercedes team-mate Antonelli (who was limited to one Q3 run), the other was being reeled in and overtaken by Antonelli with what looked like unbefitting ease.

If anything, the late-race issue can almost soothes a little what had come before - because there's nothing you can do. Just wasn't his weekend. Just isn't his year.

Winner: Lewis Hamilton (3rd)

Merely changing Lewis Hamilton's tyres to inters at the start may have made him a victory contender, but watching the laptimes during the race I don't think Hamilton had an answer for Verstappen or Antonelli, especially with Hamilton's ill-chosen stint on the poorer mediums, so really I believe this was the best result possible even if Hamilton reckons second was doable.

I think it would be fair to criticise another Ferrari mismanagement of a race though, because the inters were the right choice. It was only a Hamilton masterclass and a bit of luck elsewhere away from barely breaching the points.

Hamilton carved through from 16th to fifth in the second stint after a great call to stay out on his original softs and not switch to new ones under the first safety car.

Then he reduced an 11 second gap to Hadjar down to 3.5s before stopping, struggled on the mediums then nailed a pass on the faster Red Bull shortly after the final safety car when back on his favoured softs. Unbelievable performance.

Team-mate Charles Leclerc had to overcome an extra stop, for the inters early on, but when things were level he took much longer to fight through the pack than Hamilton did. He was about 15s behind before the final safety car, but getting to fourth was still a very nice recovery. One you might celebrate if Hamilton hadn't done what he did.

Loser: Williams (17th & DNF)

In a race where it ran sixth and seventh early on with the correct choice of inters at the start, everything pretty much fell apart for Williams under the first safety car caused by Valtteri Bottas's spin on lap nine.

In the double-stack pitstop which followed for Williams, Alex Albon was the second car and had to wait for his stop, costing him three positions.

Carlos Sainz, in the leading car, was tagged by Gabriel Bortoleto on the restart. A hilarious radio sequence followed where Bortoleto said Sainz left him no room and Sainz said he left all the room in the world. The 10-second penalty for Bortoleto showed the stewards' opinion on it.

That left Sainz struggling to recover from the back, and Albon was well out of reach of the points in 19th when his gearbox later broke.

Winner: Fernando Alonso (8th)

It felt like there was never any doubt, once the restart order had taken shape during the final safety car, that Fernando Alonso would score 'something' for Aston Martin. 

He is still the go-to man on the grid when it comes to a situation like that - and the only question was whether he would be able to fend off the McLaren of Lando Norris, which, of course, he was.

It's a big result for Aston Martin (not just because Alonso was over a minute off five laps in due to the starting tyre call), and a big example of the value its star driver brings when you need to simply keep the programme afloat.

Clearly, the AMR26 has improved - but things would sure have looked a lot bleaker in the results table without Alonso's endless opportunism.

Loser: Alpine (13th and 16th) 

No intra-team collision this time for Alpine but a “very painful” couple of wrong tyre calls across both cars, which left Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly well outside the top 10. 

Gasly explained: “We thought the track could dry a lot quicker. The team was willing to take the gamble, I supported it because, to me, it sort of made sense, and our worst-case scenario was still a lot better than, unfortunately, what the reality was. 

“When we went out there, we're losing a huge amount of laptime, and then it's a choice of coming back on your decision or trying to stay out there and make it work. But we tried that and unfortunately it cost us a lot of laptime. 

“Then after the virtual safety car, we had the safety car, and everything went the other way; nothing really came our way. We never could capitalise on anything, and it was just very painful.” 

Painful because Racing Bulls scooped seven points and extended its advantage over Alpine in their battle for fifth in the championship to 22 points.

Winner: Racing Bulls (7th and 10th)

OK, so things didn’t end as well as they started for Racing Bulls, considering Liam Lawson was duelling with Verstappen for the final place on the podium on the opening lap, but Lawson still walked away with the top midfield honours. 

That’s despite some frightful formation laps where Lawson didn’t have team radio.

“I knew I had no radio before I even pulled away for the formation lap, so I was very stressed because there's a lot of procedures, especially in this year's car, that you have to do, and I literally was like, no idea what's going on, no idea what mode I was meant to be in,” Lawson explained.

“I had to look at my pit board on the way by to read a certain switch change I had to do, and then it brought the radio back. So, yeah, very stressful. 

“That was probably the most alone I've ever felt, and obviously very confusing when all the cars were slowing down, but again, I couldn't talk to the team. I didn't know if I was allowed to overtake or what. Just a lot of confusion.”

Lawson bounced back from that strongly to drive to seventh place with strong pace that made him regret not defending against Oscar Piastri’s McLaren harder. 

Team-mate Arvid Lindblad picked up the final point late on by passing Nico Hulkenberg’s Audi.

Loser: Audi (11th and 18th) 

The upgraded Audi performed much better at Sepang than it did in Baku, with Bortoleto making it into Q3, but that progress didn’t translate into any points.

Bortoleto misjudged how wet Turn 2 was and went steaming into Sainz’s Williams, picking up damage on his car as well as a 10-second time penalty that ruined any chance of points.

Audi made the wrong call fitting Hulkenberg with slicks at the start, something he admitted was “too ambitious”, but that was quickly rectified with a move back to the intermediates.

It then got the timing right to go back to slicks, but the safety car coming out right after that nullified its advantage from doing so.

“I was eating my steering wheel at that,” was how Hulkenberg described his feelings. “That sucked because I was feeling brave and like a hero in that moment.

“I think we could have undercut a few people, but unfortunately, the safety car had other plans.”

Hulkenberg ultimately ended up finishing 11th - the ninth time an Audi has finished there this season.

Winner: Kimi Antonelli (2nd)

A couple of high-profile errors at Turn 15 made Verstappen's job easier today, but Antonelli's Mercedes wasn't as fast as the Red Bull and the outcome was successfully being best of the rest and extending his points lead.

That's up to 84 now, and while the race was a bit scruffy, it didn't affect the outcome. Team-mate Russell's retirement only adds to the impending feeling that Antonelli is within reach of a first title.

Even if Russell hadn't retired, Antonelli had caught and passed Russell to show he was the quicker and better driver on the day, and even if Russell hadn't retired, it wouldn't change the expectation of where the title's going, he still would have extended his lead.

Loser: Esteban Ocon (15th)

Esteban Ocon has been in strong form lately and he made the most of starting on the correct intermediate tyre for the start to jump well into the top 10 from 17th - all after he'd pulled over to the side on the original formation lap which could have ruined his race.

He made quick work of the two Williams as well, overtaking them on merit in the early running to go as high as sixth in a "mega" stint.

But that was as good as it got as the track dried and the relative pace of the Haas showed. Spirited battles, but faster cars came through and he returned back down to 15th and behind his Haas team-mate Ollie Bearman again.

Loser: McLaren (6th and 9th) 

Like Ferrari, McLaren got the tyre call wrong at the start of the race, though it at least partly rectified that on Piastri’s side by bringing him into the pits at the end of formation laps to ditch the slick tyres.

But unlike Ferrari, the McLarens didn’t have the raw pace to make the progress it would have liked, looking fourth best and vulnerable to the midfield.

Norris was caught out by the cars ahead of him braking behind Russell’s stricken Mercedes under safety car, but it looked like an avoidable error. 

It was an error that ensured he finished behind Lawson’s Racing Bulls and even Alonso’s Aston Martin Honda. 

And the meagre points tally of 10 means Red Bull is now just 18 points adrift of it in the constructors’ championship, and Verstappen now ties Norris in the drivers' points.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I think he has endless upside’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Paying homage to my biggest brain fart…

Would you believe the Knicks play basketball tomorrow!?

Here’s the latest from around Tarrytown and those places.

On Mohamed Diawara’s increased comfort and development entering Year 2:

“Last year, you could see he was a little jittery when he was out there, because he didn’t quite know what to do, and he knew when he did it, he just had to go hard. So a lot of times, he would just play at one speed. There’s a comfort level now, so his cadence is better, especially offensively. His ability to communicate on the floor is at a little bit of a higher level, because he has a better feel not just offensively, but defensively — not just what he should do, but what he should be telling his teammates to do, especially if he’s on the backside or bottom side of the defense, because he sees everything in front of him. He’s one of those players that needs to take a step forward.”

On his plans for the preseason opener:

“(Starters will play,) but not much. We’ll try to ease them in. The last game is always a dress rehearsal, but we’ll try to build them up leading to that game.”

On accepting preseason mistakes and emphasizing next-play speed:

“Any time you have new guys, because we have new guys on this team that we’re trying to mix in with guys that have been here, you’re gonna make some mistakes. I’m 100 percent OK with that. Once somebody makes a mistake, I’m looking for how quickly do they try to make up for the same mistake? I’m huge on the next-play speed.

“So there’s gonna be a a lot of mistakes, but are guys gonna drop their head a little or hesitate? It happened anyway. Move on, try to correct it. and then address it during the day also.”

On what he’ll prioritize seeing in preseason:

“Overall effort, the little things like boxing out every single time, competing, offensively, to offensive rebound, and then sprinting corner-to-corner in transition.”

On ending practices with a must-make free throw:

“It puts pressure on guys, you know, and then everybody’s standing there watching. So if you miss it, everybody’s got to run. I got it from Pop. It also, at the end of the day, brings the group together.”

On Tony Bradley making the final free throw on Saturday:

“You see everybody came and gave him love. So you feel good when you do it.”

On being followed home by a family of Knicks fans after the championship:

“I stopped at the red light. The first vehicle was kind of honking at me and I could see the kids waving out. So I go through and they turn into a driveway three or four houses past the red light and the father and kids jump out of the car and start waving and they had their Knicks gear on and I gave them a wave.

“But I had my helmet and my sunglasses, so I didn’t think anybody noticed me. So I ride home and I’ve got my country music blasting, and I pull into my driveway in my garage, and the next thing you know, that car was pulling into my driveway. They followed me home.

“I don’t know how they got back in their car that quickly and followed me home. But they followed me home. And the guy owns a company and he had some food products, so he brings out a box of cereal and all that. And he’s got his three kids and they just start telling me what the championship meant . . .

“This is like August, two months after the championship, but you could still feel that passion. So was it scary? Yes. It was scary. Any time you get followed home, it is very, very scary, but just to see the joy and excitement, especially on kids’ faces.

“The dad was more excited than the kids, by the way, but to see that, you realize this is not just a championship. This is special.”

On falling out of the Knicks’ rotation during his rookie season:

“Honestly, It didn’t really need explanation. I think I was a rookie. That was my first year. So you just got to be ready, whatever the team wants you to do. We have a great team with big players, so if I was in the rotation and I’m not in the rotation anymore, I think it’s just part of the game for the whole team. I wasn’t really thinking about that, I was just ready to take any opportunity. I wasn’t thinking about not playing and stuff.”

On better understanding how to prepare his body for the NBA:

“Now that I know a little bit more the physicality that I need in the league, how I need to prepare my body. … I think now that I have a year in the league, it’s a little bit easier to see how I can prepare for the new season.”

On the Knicks’ championship parade and his offseason:

“I always knew Knicks fans were another kind of fans…I was prepared for it to be a big thing. But I was surprised, it was great to see.

“Best summer of my life… went back to Paris, it was nice. Everybody was happy about it.”

On Mohamed Diawara’s potential:

“I think he has endless upside. He’s very talented, can do a lot: shoot, defend, pass. He can do everything; a really versatile player. I’m excited to see him grow. I think he’s going to keep getting better and better, so I’m really excited for him.”

On receiving the key to his hometown of Jefferson City:

“Yeah, they just told me they were going to do it. I grew up in Jeff City, went to high school out there, have lifelong friends, and I just — I grew up there.

“So Jeff City, Missouri is special to me. So it’s an honor.”

On believing more recognition will come after the Knicks’ championship run:

“Throughout the season, that’s where more recognition will come. This next season, I think I put it on display every night, the versatility, being able to guard anyone and affect the game offensively and defensively. I’m a two-way player, that’s what I take pride in, helping the team win games. I think I’ve always done it.

“Maybe there’s more of an eye on it right now because we just won the championship. That’s what I pride myself in.”

On Mike Brown’s coaching chops:

“He deserves all the praise… he’s always been a great coach. When you win, you get more recognition. Everything is coming together for him.”

On his work with Pacome Dadiet and Mo:

“I encourage them when they’re doing well… be there for them any way I can.”

“It was fun, we were there for Jalen. Was really cool that he got to host it. We were there for the intro. It was cool to see him do that, some funny skits. It was a good time.”

On not falling for his flowers:

“I really do appreciate it and I respect the hell out of them. It’s honestly really cool and it’s a sign of respect. To hear that from those guys, I really do appreciate it.

“It’s just like a lot of things. When you hear praise, when you hear negativity, it has to go through one ear and out the other. You got to continue to be the best version of yourself or people are going to pass you. I really do appreciate it. It shows where I’ve grown, but still got a lot of work to do.”

items.title: How FIA software bug caused chaos in Bahrain GP in Malaysia – and the emergency fix that saved the race
Dominant Verstappen & superb Hamilton recovery - driver ratings
items.content: <article>BBC Radio 5 Live F1 commentator Harry Benjamin rates how the drivers performed during the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. </article>
items.lbText:
Max Verstappen secured his first win of the 2026 season with victory at a chaotic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton had an eventful race and finished third, while Kimi Antonelli extended his championship lead to 84 points over Mercedes team-mate George Russell with his second place at Sepang.

Russell retired from the grand prix while in third place with a power unit failure.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Malaysia...

Verstappen wins Bahrain GP in Malaysia after long delays

Hard to find much wrong this weekend. Dominant through every part of qualifying for his first pole of the season. A poor start but then recovered after losing out to both Mercedes drivers to control a hugely difficult race.

Proving Baku was just a blip for the championship leader. Produced an excellent start to take the lead and ultimately brought home second on a weekend where Mercedes never looked entirely comfortable.

A superb recovery after Ferrari's decision to start on slick tyres sent him tumbling from the front row to 18th. Hamilton fought all the way back to the podium and passed Isack Hadjar after the final safety car to complete one of his best drives of the season.

Close to team-mate Hamilton in qualifying before suffering the same early tyre nightmare in the race. Recovered impressively through the field to fourth and ensured Ferrari salvaged a huge result from a strategy that initially looked disastrous.

Third fastest in qualifying was an excellent performance before his engine penalty dropped him to eighth on the grid. A great battle with Hamilton even if he did lose out with Leclerc denying him fourth at the end too.

Never quite had McLaren at the sharp end but made the right early call to abandon the slicks and start from the pit lane on intermediate tyres. Recovered to sixth and comfortably beat Norris on a day when simply keeping everything clean counted for plenty.

One of his strongest races of the year. Just missed Q3 and then made a sensational start in the wet conditions, gaining seven positions and briefly running fourth before eventually bringing his Racing Bulls home in seventh.

Aston Martin finally showed some signs of life and Alonso made sure to capitalise. Reached Q2 on merit and converted 12th on the grid into an excellent eighth-place finish. Comfortably the team's best result for some time.

A frustrating weekend that ended with an avoidable mistake. Qualified ahead of Piastri and was right behind his team-mate before the final restart, only to lose control behind the safety car and ran through the gravel, dropping him to ninth.

A really impressive recovery considering he started at the very back because of his power unit penalty. Helped Lawson with a tow on Saturday and then charged through to score the final point on Sunday.

Andrew Benson Q&A: Send us your questions

Missing Q2 was disappointing but he responded with a strong recovery on Sunday. Climbed from 15th on the grid to finish just outside the points and comfortably ahead of Audi team-mate Bortoleto after the Brazilian's penalty.

A much more competitive weekend for Aston Martin generally. Stroll joined Alonso in Q2 and kept himself out of trouble through a chaotic race to finish 12th, even if his team-mate ultimately extracted more from the opportunity.

Started 21st due to grid penalties, so 13th represented a very respectable recovery. Kept things clean after his costly mistake last time out and made up plenty of ground in difficult conditions.

Another fairly anonymous weekend for Haas. Knocked out in Q1 and although he gained a couple of places during the race, 14th was about all there was to show for it.

Frustrated with Haas' qualifying run plan after going out in Q1 and never really recovered from there. Great start and was fighting well inside the top 10. Ultimately finished behind Bearman and was unable to make the changing conditions work sufficiently to threaten the points.

Qualifying ninth was an excellent start but Sunday unravelled almost immediately. Nearly lost the car on slicks during the formation procedure and ultimately fell all the way to 16th as Alpine's gamble failed to pay off.

Williams struggled for pace throughout the weekend but 13th represented a good qualifying. His race was then further compromised by contact with Bortoleto, for which the Audi driver was penalised, so 17th doesn't tell the whole story.

There was plenty to like about reaching Q3 in the Audi, but the race undid that good work. Contact with Sainz earned him a penalty and left him 18th after starting inside the top 10.

Qualified last and never looked likely to make meaningful progress even amid all the chaos. Reaching the chequered flag was at least something for Cadillac, but 19th completed another difficult weekend.

A far better race than his eighth place in qualifying suggested. Made an excellent start, ran inside the top three for virtually the entire afternoon and, even if he couldn't match Mercedes team-mate Antonelli, was heading for another podium before a power-unit failure stopped him with five laps remaining.

Williams lacked pace from the outset and qualifying 20th left him with an enormous amount of work to do. His eventual retirement was caused by a gearbox problem rather than a driving error, but there had been little sign of any kind of meaningful challenge before then.

A weekend to forget. Qualified ahead of Cadillac team-mate Perez but admitted his decision to run slicks was a risk before spinning into the gravel on lap nine and triggering the first safety car.

items.content: <article>Max Verstappen takes his and Red Bull's first win of the year with a dominant drive in a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that started amid chaotic and unprecedented scenes.</article>
items.lbText:
Max Verstappen took his and Red Bull's first win of the year with a dominant drive in a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that started amid chaotic and unprecedented scenes.

Verstappen led home the Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli, who took a giant leap towards his first world title when team-mate George Russell retired from third place with a power unit failure with five laps to go.

Antonelli now leads Russell by 84 points with either six or seven races remaining.

Lewis Hamilton drove an extraordinary race after dropping towards the back with an incorrect tyre choice for a wet start to fight back to pass Red Bull's Isack Hadjar for third place with three laps to go.

All that came after a delay of an hour and a half caused initially by heavy rain and then by a series of bizarre technical problems that left several cars crawling as they completed formation laps on the wet track behind the safety car.

After that problem, it took some time for governing body the FIA to decide the order in which the cars should take the start.

The key stories of a madcap afternoon were:

Verstappen's dominant win in a revived Red Bull

The effective death knell for Russell's already faint title hopes

A series of questions over race organisation, particularly over the start

Once the race got under way, with the cars in their original order, Verstappen and Hamilton on the front row immediately lost ground and the Mercedes of Antonelli and Russell swept past them into first and second places.

Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers took the start on intermediate tyres on the still-wet track after a torrential tropical downpour had delayed the start.

Hamilton chose soft-compound slicks and immediately regretted the decision as it became apparent that the track was still far too wet for that option. He and others who chose slicks immediately dropped to the back of the field, and lost nearly a minute to the leaders in the early laps.

Meanwhile, Verstappen repassed Russell for second place on lap six, and was on Antonelli's tail when a safety car was deployed to allow marshals to recover the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas, who had spun off at Turn 13 on lap nine.

The leaders took the opportunity of the safety car to pit for slick tyres, and when the race resumed four laps later, Verstappen immediately passed Antonelli at Turn Four, the Italian also losing out to Russell on the exit of the corner.

From that moment on, Verstappen was total in control and he edged away into a race of his own.

Behind him, Antonelli had pace on Russell and passed him on lap 21 at Turn Four, the move seemingly settling the top three positions.

A late safety car caused by Alex Albon's stricken Williams led to everyone switching to fresh tyres for a four-lap dash to the flag, but again Verstappen was supreme and remained unchallenged.

Even then, there was drama, as Russell pulled off just before Turn One with five laps to go before the safety car had even ended.

In the immediate aftermath, Lando Norris was apparently distracted by Russell's car and had to take to the gravel at Turn One to avoid running into the back of team-mate Oscar Piastri, dropping from eighth to 11th.

He recovered to ninth by the end, immediately behind Fernando Alonso, who scored points for Aston Martin for only the third time this year after their strongest performance of the year.

Hamilton and the others who chose to use dry tyres at the start immediately lived to regret their decision, as they were passed by all the cars on intermediates.

Within a few laps, Hamilton was nearly a minute behind the leaders and down in 17th place, his race apparently over.

But he stayed out during the safety car, sticking with the soft tyres he had chosen for the start, and when the race restarted he began to pick off the cars in front of him, driving an excellent race to get back into contention for serious points.

Hamilton passed car after car until by lap 24 he was on the tail of Isack Hadjar's fourth-placed Red Bull.

They pitted together on lap 31, Hadjar sticking to soft tyres, and Hamilton having no choice but to move to mediums.

Hamilton trailed the Frenchman for lap after lap, right on his tail, but was never quite able to get close enough to pass, despite a number of attempts, before the late safety car.

That gave Hamilton the chance to switch to the preferred soft tyres, and a lap after the restart he passed Hadjar into Turn One to take the final podium position.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc also passed Hadjar in the closing laps, with Oscar Piastri taking sixth after a dispiriting weekend for McLaren, ahead of Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Alonso.

Norris and the second Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.

After the tropical downpour, the race was initially started with formation laps behind the safety car. But immediately the problems started.

Verstappen and Hamilton were the first of a number of cars that were afflicted by a software issue that left them unable to do more than crawl along.

Governing body the FIA said this was caused by a combination of the weather, low speed, the mandated wet-weather energy management settings and the circuit layout.

A software update removing the constraint on energy limits was issued by governing body the FIA during the subsequeby start delay to enable teams to resolve the issue.

Most teams who were afflicted managed eventually to get their cars going, but the field order was jumbled, and that led to a debate as to the positions in which the cars should take the restart.

The rules did not cover the situation, which was unprecedented. And although they outline positional penalties for any driver who is not able to regain his position by a certain place on the track having lost it on a formation lap, this was ignored in restarting the race in its original order.
